I am advertising [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], and the main benefit or offer is [YOUR BENEFIT OR OFFER]. Generate several distinct ad creative concepts, each with a different angle such as the problem it solves, the desired outcome, social proof, curiosity, or a bold claim. For each concept, describe the visual idea, the headline or hook, and why that angle would work for my audience. Give me a range to test rather than one idea. Mark the two or three most promising concepts. Give me the ad creative concepts.
description: Generate a range of distinct ad creative concepts with different angles to test.
useCase: Use this when planning ads and needing strong creative directions. A range of concepts with different angles gives you options to test, which is essential since ad performance is hard to predict and testing several angles finds the winner far faster than betting everything on one idea you assume will work.

title: Generate Ad Hooks
promptText: Generate scroll stopping hooks for my ad. I am advertising [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], and the key message is [YOUR MESSAGE]. Give me 12 hook options, meaning the opening line or headline that stops the scroll and pulls people in. Vary them: some that call out the audience, some that name the pain, some that promise the outcome, some that spark curiosity, and some that challenge an assumption. Keep them short and punchy for an ad. Mark the strongest few. The hook determines whether the ad gets seen at all. Give me the ad hooks.
description: Generate scroll stopping ad hooks across multiple proven angles to test.
useCase: Use this because the hook decides whether an ad gets seen. Scroll stopping opening lines earn the attention everything else depends on, and testing varied hooks finds what grabs your audience, since even a great offer and visual fail if the hook does not stop people from scrolling past.

title: Write an Image Prompt for an Ad
promptText: Help me write an image generation prompt for an ad visual. The ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE], the concept is [YOUR AD CONCEPT OR ANGLE], the mood is [MOOD], and my brand colors are [YOUR COLORS OR WRITE NONE]. Write a clear image prompt describing a scroll stopping ad visual, its style, mood, composition, and colors, leaving space for headline text if I will add it. Specify the aspect ratio for [PLATFORM]. Give me the main prompt plus a couple of variations. Remind me the visual needs to stop the scroll and support the ad message, and to verify it is suitable and accurate for advertising.
description: Write an image prompt for a scroll stopping ad visual with room for text.
useCase: Use this to generate an attention grabbing ad visual. A clear prompt specifying the concept, mood, and aspect ratio, with space for text, produces a scroll stopping image that supports the message, giving your ads custom visuals that perform better than generic stock, which audiences increasingly recognize and scroll past.

title: Explore Different Ad Angles
promptText: Help me explore different angles to advertise my [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE]. The same product can be sold many ways, so help me brainstorm distinct advertising angles: leading with the problem, the outcome or dream result, fear of missing out, social proof, a surprising insight, a specific use case, price or value, or an us versus the old way angle. For each, explain how the ad would frame the product and which audience mindset it targets. Then recommend which angles are most worth testing for my offer. Give me the ad angles and a recommendation.
description: Explore distinct advertising angles for the same product and pick which to test.
useCase: Use this to find the angle that sells your product best. The same offer can be advertised many ways, and exploring distinct angles like problem, outcome, or social proof reveals which resonates, since often the difference between an ad that flops and one that converts is not the product or visual but the angle it leads with.

title: Write Ad Copy
promptText: Write ad copy for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am advertising [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM]. The main benefit is [KEY BENEFIT], the offer is [YOUR OFFER OR WRITE NONE], and the action I want is [DESIRED ACTION]. Write ad copy that hooks with a strong opening, speaks to what my audience wants or struggles with, conveys the benefit clearly, and drives the action with a clear call to action. Match the length and style to [PLATFORM]. Give me two or three versions with different tones or angles to test. Keep it compelling, not generic. Give me the ad copy.
description: Write compelling ad copy that hooks, conveys the benefit, and drives action.
useCase: Use this to write ad copy that converts. Copy that hooks fast, speaks to the audience's wants, and drives a clear action turns attention into clicks, and having a few versions to test finds the strongest, since ad copy is a major lever on performance and small wording changes can meaningfully shift results.

title: Plan a Video Ad Concept
promptText: Help me plan a short video ad for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], and the key message is [YOUR MESSAGE]. Help me plan the video concept: a hook in the first few seconds that stops the scroll, how the ad unfolds to hold attention and convey the value, the key beats or scenes, and a clear call to action at the end. Note that the first seconds are critical since most viewers drop off fast. Keep it achievable to produce simply. Give me the video ad concept and a rough shot or beat outline.
description: Plan a short video ad concept with a strong hook and clear beats.
useCase: Use this to plan a video ad that holds attention. A concept with a strong opening hook and clear beats keeps viewers watching, which matters because most drop off in the first seconds, and a video ad that fails to hook immediately wastes its budget no matter how good the rest of it is.

title: Design a Scroll Stopping Ad Visual
promptText: Help me design an ad visual that stops the scroll for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM]. Help me plan a visual built to grab attention in a busy feed: what makes people stop scrolling, how to use contrast, movement, faces, or pattern interrupts, how to make it stand out from typical polished ads without looking like spam, and how to support the message. Note the balance between attention grabbing and on brand. Give me the scroll stopping visual concept and what makes it stop the scroll.
description: Design an ad visual engineered to stop the scroll in a busy feed.
useCase: Use this to design an ad visual that earns attention in a crowded feed. Understanding what actually stops the scroll, like contrast, faces, or pattern interrupts, makes your ad get noticed, since the visual's only job in the first instant is to halt the scroll, and one that blends in never gets the chance to sell anything.

title: Plan a User Generated Style Ad
promptText: Help me plan a user generated content style ad for my [BUSINESS TYPE], the authentic looking kind that does not feel like a polished ad. I am promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM]. Help me plan a natural, authentic feeling ad concept: how to make it feel like a genuine recommendation or real person sharing rather than a corporate ad, what to show and say, and the casual style that builds trust. This style often outperforms polished ads because it feels real. Note how to keep it honest. Give me the UGC style ad concept and script or talking points.
description: Plan an authentic user generated style ad that does not feel like an ad.
useCase: Use this to create ads that feel authentic rather than corporate. A user generated style ad that feels like a real recommendation builds trust and often outperforms polished production, since audiences increasingly tune out obvious ads but engage with content that feels genuine and human, making this style highly effective when done honestly.

title: Generate an Ad Visual with Gemini
promptText: Help me write a prompt to generate an ad visual. The ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE], the concept is [YOUR CONCEPT], the mood is [MOOD], and my brand colors are [YOUR COLORS OR WRITE NONE]. Write a clear detailed image prompt describing an eye catching ad visual, its style, composition, mood, and colors, with space for headline text if needed. Specify the aspect ratio for [PLATFORM]. Give me the main prompt and a couple of variations to test different looks. Remind me to check the generated image is attention grabbing, on brand, accurate, and suitable for a paid ad.
description: Write a detailed prompt to generate an eye catching ad visual to test.
useCase: Use this to generate ad visuals to test. A detailed prompt describing the concept, mood, and aspect ratio produces attention grabbing imagery, and generating variations lets you test different looks cheaply, which suits advertising where testing multiple visuals is how you find the creative that actually performs rather than guessing.

title: Write and Optimize Ad Calls to Action
promptText: Help me write strong calls to action for my ad promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM]. The action I want is [DESIRED ACTION, E.G. SHOP, LEARN MORE, SIGN UP, BOOK]. Give me several call to action options that clearly tell people what to do next and motivate the click, varying the urgency, framing, and wording. Note which suit a cold audience seeing me for the first time versus a warmer one. The CTA converts attention into action, so it needs to be clear and compelling. Give me the ad CTA options and when to use each.
description: Write clear, compelling ad calls to action matched to audience temperature.
useCase: Use this to convert ad attention into clicks. A clear compelling call to action tells people exactly what to do and motivates them, and matching it to a cold versus warm audience improves results, since a vague or weak CTA loses the action even after your hook and visual successfully earned the viewer's attention.
variables: DESIRED ACTION, E.G. SHOP, LEARN MORE, SIGN UP, BOOK

title: Create Ad Variations to Test
promptText: Help me create variations of my ad to test what works best. My base ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], with this hook and message: [YOUR CURRENT AD]. Create variations that each change one element so I can learn what drives performance: one with a different hook, one with a different angle, one with a different visual concept, and one with a different call to action. For each, note what it is testing and what a win would tell me. Testing one variable at a time reveals what actually moves results. Give me the ad variations to test.
description: Create controlled ad variations that isolate one variable to test performance.
useCase: Use this to improve ads through testing rather than guessing. Variations that each change one element reveal what actually drives performance, which is how profitable ad accounts are built, since systematic testing beats intuition and isolating variables tells you exactly what to keep and what to change in the next round.

title: Diagnose an Underperforming Ad
promptText: Help me diagnose why my ad is not performing. The ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], here is the ad: [DESCRIBE YOUR AD, HOOK, VISUAL, AND COPY], and the problem is [WHAT IS UNDERPERFORMING, E.G. LOW CLICKS, LOW ATTENTION, CLICKS BUT NO SALES]. Help me pinpoint the likely issue: whether the hook fails to stop the scroll, the visual is weak, the angle does not resonate, the copy is unclear, the CTA is weak, or there is a mismatch with the landing page. For the likely cause, suggest what to change. Give me a diagnosis and specific fixes.
description: Diagnose why an ad is underperforming and what specifically to fix.
useCase: Use this when an ad is spending but not delivering. Pinpointing whether the problem is the hook, visual, angle, copy, or CTA tells you what to fix rather than scrapping the whole ad, which saves budget and time, since ads usually fail at one specific point and fixing that is faster than starting over blindly.
variables: DESCRIBE YOUR AD, HOOK, VISUAL, AND COPY
WHAT IS UNDERPERFORMING, E.G. LOW CLICKS, LOW ATTENTION, CLICKS BUT NO SALES

title: Write a Problem Agitate Solve Ad
promptText: Help me write an ad using the problem agitate solve structure for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My audience [TARGET AUDIENCE] struggles with [THE PROBLEM], and my [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] solves it by [HOW IT SOLVES IT]. Write an ad that names the problem so they feel understood, agitates it briefly by touching on the frustration or cost of it, then presents my solution as the relief, ending with a clear call to action. Keep the agitation honest and empathetic, not manipulative. This structure works because it meets people in their pain. Give me the problem agitate solve ad.
description: Write a problem agitate solve ad that meets the audience in their pain.
useCase: Use this to write an ad using a proven persuasive structure. Naming the problem, briefly agitating it, then presenting your solution meets people in their pain and makes your offer feel like relief, which converts well when done empathetically, since prospects who feel understood are far more receptive to the solution that follows.

title: Plan a Carousel Ad
promptText: Help me plan a carousel ad for [PLATFORM] promoting my [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE]. My key selling points are [YOUR SELLING POINTS OR OFFER DETAILS]. Help me plan the carousel cards: a first card that hooks and earns the swipe, cards that each build the case with a benefit, feature, or proof point, a logical flow that leads toward the sale, and a final card with a strong call to action. Note what visual and text goes on each card. A carousel ad lets me tell a fuller story than a single image. Give me the carousel ad plan card by card.
description: Plan a carousel ad card by card that builds a case toward the sale.
useCase: Use this to plan a carousel ad, which tells a fuller story than a single image. Cards that hook then build the case with benefits and proof let you make a complete argument, useful for products that need more explanation, since the swipeable format holds attention while walking prospects from interest to the call to action.
variables: YOUR SELLING POINTS OR OFFER DETAILS

title: Plan a Retargeting Ad
promptText: Help me plan a retargeting ad for people who already engaged with my [BUSINESS TYPE] but did not buy. They previously [WHAT THEY DID, E.G. VISITED THE SITE, VIEWED THE PRODUCT, ABANDONED CART], and my offer is [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING]. Help me plan an ad tailored to a warm audience that already knows me: how to acknowledge they were interested, address the likely reason they did not act, add reassurance or an incentive, and bring them back to complete the action. Retargeting audiences convert well with the right nudge. Give me the retargeting ad concept and message.
description: Plan a retargeting ad that brings warm prospects back to complete the action.
useCase: Use this to convert warm prospects who engaged but did not buy. A retargeting ad tailored to people who already showed interest, addressing why they hesitated and adding a nudge, converts well, since these warm audiences are far closer to buying than cold ones and often just need a reminder or reassurance to complete what they started.
variables: WHAT THEY DID, E.G. VISITED THE SITE, VIEWED THE PRODUCT, ABANDONED CART

title: Plan an Ad Built on Social Proof
promptText: Help me plan an ad built around social proof for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My proof is [YOUR PROOF, E.G. TESTIMONIALS, RESULTS, NUMBER OF CUSTOMERS, REVIEWS], and I am promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE]. Help me plan an ad that puts the proof front and center: how to feature a testimonial or result as the hook, how to make the proof credible and relatable, and how to connect it to the action I want. Social proof reduces the skepticism that stops people buying from someone new. Keep it genuine. Give me the social proof ad concept and how to present the proof.
description: Plan an ad that leads with social proof to overcome buyer skepticism.
useCase: Use this to build an ad around proof, which overcomes the skepticism prospects feel toward an unfamiliar business. Leading with a genuine testimonial or result makes the ad credible and relatable, since people trust the experiences of others far more than a business's own claims, making social proof one of the most persuasive ad angles.
variables: YOUR PROOF, E.G. TESTIMONIALS, RESULTS, NUMBER OF CUSTOMERS, REVIEWS

title: Match Your Ad to Your Audience
promptText: Help me make sure my ad actually resonates with the specific audience I am targeting. My ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING], here is the ad concept: [DESCRIBE YOUR AD], and my target audience is [TARGET AUDIENCE AND WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT THEM]. Help me assess: whether the hook, angle, visual, and language actually fit how this audience thinks and what they care about, where it might miss or feel generic, and how to sharpen it to speak directly to them. An ad that feels made for the viewer outperforms a generic one. Give me the audience match check and how to tailor the ad more tightly.
description: Check whether your ad truly resonates with your specific target audience.
useCase: Use this to ensure an ad speaks directly to its audience rather than generically. Checking whether the hook, angle, and language fit how your audience thinks, and tightening it to them, lifts performance, since an ad that feels made specifically for the viewer resonates far more than a generic one trying to appeal to everyone.
variables: TARGET AUDIENCE AND WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT THEM

title: Balance Visual and Text in an Ad
promptText: Help me get the balance of visual and text right in my ad creative. My ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] on [PLATFORM], and my concept is [YOUR CONCEPT]. Help me decide: how much text should be on the visual itself versus in the caption or copy, what the essential words on the image should be, how to keep the visual clean and attention grabbing rather than cluttered with text, and how the on image text and the caption should work together. Too much text on an ad image hurts both attention and reach. Give me guidance on the visual and text balance for my ad.
description: Balance on image text and caption so your ad stays clean and attention grabbing.
useCase: Use this to get the text balance right on an ad. Deciding what belongs on the image versus in the caption keeps the visual clean and attention grabbing, which matters because too much text on an ad image hurts both attention and reach on many platforms, while the right minimal on image text lands the message fast.

title: Get a Quick Ad Concept Fast
promptText: I need a quick ad concept. My [BUSINESS TYPE] is promoting [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], and the key benefit is [KEY BENEFIT]. Give me a fast, clear ad concept: the hook, the visual idea, and the call to action, ready to create or test. Keep it simple and actionable, no long explanation. Just give me a solid ad concept I can use right now.
description: Get a fast, complete ad concept with hook, visual, and CTA ready to test.
useCase: Use this when you need an ad concept quickly. A fast complete concept with hook, visual, and CTA lets you launch or test without a long process, useful for capitalizing on a timely moment or getting a test running, since a solid concept acted on quickly often beats a perfect one that takes too long to develop.

title: Frame Your Offer in an Ad
promptText: Help me frame my offer compellingly in an ad. My offer is [YOUR OFFER AND ITS DETAILS], for [TARGET AUDIENCE], and the real value is [THE VALUE OR OUTCOME]. Help me frame it in the ad for maximum appeal: how to present the offer so the value feels obvious, whether to lead with the price, the saving, the outcome, or the transformation, how to add urgency or reason to act now if genuine, and how to make it feel like a clear yes. The same offer can be framed weakly or powerfully. Give me the strongest way to frame my offer in the ad and the wording.
description: Frame your offer in an ad so its value feels obvious and compelling.
useCase: Use this to present an offer so it feels like an obvious yes. Framing it around the right element, whether outcome, saving, or transformation, and adding genuine urgency makes the value clear, since the same offer can be framed weakly or powerfully, and how you present it in the ad heavily influences whether people act.

title: Storyboard a Video Ad
promptText: Help me storyboard my video ad so I know exactly what to film or create. My video ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE] on [PLATFORM], and the concept is [YOUR CONCEPT]. Help me break it into a shot by shot storyboard: the opening hook shot, each following scene or shot with what it shows and any text or voiceover, the pacing, and the closing call to action shot. Keep it simple enough to produce with basic tools or a phone. A storyboard makes filming efficient and the ad coherent. Give me the shot by shot storyboard for my video ad.
description: Storyboard a video ad shot by shot so it is efficient to film and coherent.
useCase: Use this to plan a video ad before filming. A shot by shot storyboard covering the hook, scenes, and CTA makes production efficient and the ad coherent, saving time and frustration, since filming without a plan leads to wasted effort and a disjointed result, while a clear storyboard means you know exactly what to capture.

title: Check an Ad for Policy and Claim Issues
promptText: Help me check my ad for issues that could get it rejected or cause problems. My ad promotes [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] on [PLATFORM], and here is the ad: [DESCRIBE YOUR AD AND COPY]. Help me spot potential issues: claims that are too strong or unsubstantiated, anything that could violate common ad platform policies, misleading framing, or wording that promises results I cannot guarantee. Suggest how to keep the ad compelling while making the claims honest and defensible. Note this is general guidance, not legal or platform specific advice. Give me the check and any wording to fix.
description: Check an ad for overreaching claims and policy issues before running it.
useCase: Use this before running an ad to catch claim and policy problems. Spotting overreaching claims or misleading framing helps you avoid rejections and the trust damage of overpromising, keeping the ad both compelling and defensible, since exaggerated claims risk platform rejection and the disappointed customers and complaints that follow when reality falls short.

title: Turn a Winning Post into an Ad
promptText: Help me turn a post that performed well organically into a paid ad for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The post was about [POST TOPIC] and did well because [WHY YOU THINK IT WORKED, OR WRITE NOT SURE]. Here is the post: [DESCRIBE OR PASTE THE POST]. I want to promote [WHAT YOU ARE PROMOTING] to [TARGET AUDIENCE]. Help me adapt it into an ad: what made it resonate that I should keep, how to add a clear offer and call to action without killing what worked, and how to frame it for a paid audience that does not already follow me. Proven organic content often makes the best ads. Give me the ad adaptation.
description: Adapt a well performing organic post into a paid ad that keeps what worked.
useCase: Use this to turn proven organic content into ads. A post that already resonated is validated creative, and adapting it into an ad while keeping what worked and adding an offer often outperforms concepts built from scratch, since real audience response is the best signal of what will convert when you put budget behind it.
variables: WHY YOU THINK IT WORKED, OR WRITE NOT SURE

title: Write a Professional Invoice
promptText: Help me write a clear professional invoice for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the work or products are [WHAT YOU DELIVERED], the amount is [AMOUNT], and my payment terms are [PAYMENT TERMS, E.G. DUE IN 14 DAYS]. Help me lay out an invoice that includes everything it needs: a clear description of what they are paying for, the amount and any breakdown, the due date, how to pay, my details, and an invoice number. Keep it professional and easy to understand so there is no confusion or reason to delay payment. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the invoice content and layout.
description: Write a clear, professional invoice that leaves no confusion about what is owed.
useCase: Use this to send invoices that get paid without back and forth. A clear professional invoice with an obvious amount, due date, and payment method removes the confusion and friction that delay payment, which matters for a solo operator whose cash flow depends on getting paid promptly and looking organized to clients.
variables: PAYMENT TERMS, E.G. DUE IN 14 DAYS

title: Write an Invoice Email
promptText: Write a friendly professional email to send with an invoice to my client. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the invoice is for [WHAT IT IS FOR], the amount is [AMOUNT], and it is due [DUE DATE]. Write an email that thanks them, clearly notes the invoice is attached with the amount and due date, states how to pay, and keeps a warm professional tone that makes paying feel easy and expected. Keep it brief. The email should reduce any friction to prompt payment while maintaining the relationship. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the subject line and the email.
description: Write a warm invoice email that makes prompt payment feel easy and expected.
useCase: Use this when sending an invoice, since the email framing affects how fast you get paid. A warm professional note that clearly states the amount, due date, and how to pay reduces friction and sets the expectation of prompt payment, while keeping the client relationship positive rather than transactional.

title: Write a Gentle Payment Reminder
promptText: Write a gentle payment reminder for an invoice that is due soon or just past due. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the invoice is for [WHAT IT IS FOR], the amount is [AMOUNT], and it was due [DUE DATE OR HOW OVERDUE]. Write a friendly, low pressure reminder that assumes good faith, such as it simply slipping their mind, restates the invoice details and how to pay, and makes it easy to resolve without any awkwardness. Keep it warm and professional so it protects the relationship. This is an early reminder, not a demand. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the subject line and the reminder.
description: Write a friendly, good faith payment reminder for a recently due invoice.
useCase: Use this for a first reminder on a due or slightly late invoice. A gentle good faith nudge that assumes the client simply forgot gets most invoices paid without damaging the relationship, since many late payments are honest oversights and a warm reminder resolves them while keeping the client comfortable.

title: Write a Firm Payment Reminder
promptText: Write a firm but still professional payment reminder for an invoice that is now clearly overdue after earlier gentle reminders. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the invoice is for [WHAT IT IS FOR], the amount is [AMOUNT], and it is now [HOW OVERDUE]. Write a reminder that is more direct and firm than a gentle nudge, clearly states the invoice is overdue and needs to be paid, notes any late terms or next steps if relevant, and requests prompt payment, while remaining professional rather than hostile. Firmness is warranted now, but keep the door open. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the subject line and the reminder.
description: Write a firm but professional reminder for a clearly overdue invoice.
useCase: Use this when gentle reminders have not worked and an invoice is meaningfully overdue. A firm professional message that clearly states the invoice must be paid signals you are serious without burning the relationship, which is often what finally prompts payment from a client who has been letting it slide.

title: Build a Payment Reminder Sequence
promptText: Help me build a sequence of payment reminders that escalates appropriately for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My payment terms are [YOUR TERMS], and I want a repeatable set of reminders to send at the right intervals. Build the sequence: a friendly reminder just before or at the due date, a gentle nudge shortly after, a firmer reminder further out, and a final notice, each with suggested timing and the tone shift. Give me the messages I can reuse for any client by filling in the details. A consistent reminder system means I get paid without agonizing over each message. Give me the full reminder sequence with timing.
description: Build a reusable, escalating payment reminder sequence with the right timing.
useCase: Use this once to systematize chasing payment so you never dread it. A ready sequence that escalates from friendly to firm at set intervals means you follow up consistently on every late invoice without writing each message from scratch, which is how a solo operator keeps cash flowing without letting invoices slip.

title: Write a Final Payment Notice
promptText: Write a final payment notice for a seriously overdue invoice where earlier reminders have failed. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the invoice is for [WHAT IT IS FOR], the amount is [AMOUNT], and it is now [HOW OVERDUE]. Write a serious, professional final notice that clearly states this is a final request before I take further steps such as [YOUR NEXT STEP, E.G. PAUSING WORK, LATE FEES, OR OTHER ACTION], gives a clear deadline, and remains firm and factual rather than emotional or threatening. This is a last attempt to resolve it directly. Note this is general guidance, not legal advice. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the subject line and the final notice.
description: Write a serious, professional final notice for a seriously overdue invoice.
useCase: Use this as a last direct attempt before escalating a badly overdue invoice. A firm factual final notice with a clear deadline and stated next step often prompts payment when softer reminders failed, and keeping it professional rather than emotional protects you while making clear you will not simply absorb the loss.
variables: YOUR NEXT STEP, E.G. PAUSING WORK, LATE FEES, OR OTHER ACTION

title: Set Clear Payment Terms
promptText: Help me set clear payment terms for my [BUSINESS TYPE] serving [TARGET AUDIENCE]. My work is [WHAT YOU DO], and my current terms are [YOUR TERMS OR WRITE NONE]. Help me define terms that protect my cash flow and reduce late payments: when payment is due, whether to require deposits or upfront payment, whether to charge late fees, accepted payment methods, and how to communicate the terms upfront so they are agreed before work starts. Explain how each choice affects getting paid on time. Note this is general guidance, not legal or accounting advice. Give me recommended payment terms and how to state them.
description: Set clear payment terms that protect cash flow and reduce late payments.
useCase: Use this to establish terms that get you paid reliably. Clear terms agreed upfront, covering due dates, deposits, and late fees, prevent the payment problems that come from vague arrangements, since most late payment issues trace back to terms that were never clearly set or communicated before the work began.

title: Request a Deposit or Upfront Payment
promptText: Write a message requesting a deposit or upfront payment before I begin work for a client. The client is [CLIENT NAME], the project is [THE PROJECT], the total is [TOTAL AMOUNT], and the deposit I want is [DEPOSIT AMOUNT OR PERCENTAGE]. Write a message that requests the deposit confidently and professionally, frames it as standard practice that protects both sides, explains what happens once it is paid, and makes it easy to pay. Requesting a deposit should feel normal, not awkward. Keep it warm but clear. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the deposit request message.
description: Confidently request a deposit or upfront payment as standard practice.
useCase: Use this to request deposits without awkwardness. Framing a deposit as standard practice that protects both sides makes it feel normal and secures payment before you invest work, which protects your cash flow and filters out clients who were never serious, a key safeguard for a solo operator.

title: Write a Late Fee Policy
promptText: Help me write a clear late fee policy for my [BUSINESS TYPE] to encourage on time payment. My payment terms are [YOUR TERMS], and the late fee I am considering is [YOUR LATE FEE OR WRITE NOT SURE]. Help me write a policy that states when a payment is considered late, what the late fee is and how it applies, and how it is communicated to clients upfront so it is fair and expected. Explain how to enforce it without damaging good client relationships, and when to waive it. Note this is general guidance, not legal advice, and late fee rules can vary by location. Give me the late fee policy and how to communicate it.
description: Write a fair late fee policy that encourages on time payment.
useCase: Use this to add a late fee that motivates prompt payment. A clear policy communicated upfront gives clients a real incentive to pay on time and compensates you when they do not, and knowing when to enforce versus waive it lets you protect cash flow without souring relationships with otherwise good clients.
variables: YOUR LATE FEE OR WRITE NOT SURE

title: Build a Reusable Invoice Template
promptText: Help me build a reusable invoice template for my [BUSINESS TYPE] so I can invoice quickly and consistently. My work is [WHAT YOU INVOICE FOR], and my payment terms are [YOUR TERMS]. Create a clean invoice template with all the standard fields I need and fill in the blank spots for what changes each time, such as the client, description, amount, and dates. Include everything a proper invoice should have so I never leave out something important. The goal is a professional template I can fill in fast for any client. Give me the reusable invoice template.
description: Build a reusable invoice template you can fill in fast for any client.

useCase: Use this when an email needs to land a certain way. Tone is easy to misjudge in writing since there is no voice or expression to soften it, and catching that your draft reads as cold, passive aggressive, or overly apologetic before sending prevents a lot of unnecessary friction.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP
DESIRED TONE, E.G. WARMER, FIRMER, MORE FORMAL, MORE CASUAL

promptText: Help me cut this email down. Here is my draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]. Trim it to the essentials: cut the padding, throat clearing, unnecessary context, and over explanation, while keeping everything that actually matters and preserving the tone. Make the ask clearer and easier to spot. Long emails get skimmed, so a shorter one is usually more effective. Tell me what you cut and why. Give me the shortened email.
description: Cut a long email down to the essentials without losing what matters.
useCase: Use this when your email has grown too long. Cutting the padding and over explanation while keeping the substance makes it more likely to be read and acted on, since a long email invites skimming and the request buried in paragraph four often gets missed entirely.

title: Write a Cold Email That Gets a Reply
promptText: Help me write a cold email to someone who does not know me, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The recipient is [WHO THEY ARE AND WHY YOU ARE REACHING OUT], what I want is [YOUR ASK], and what I know about them is [ANY RELEVANT CONTEXT, OR WRITE NOT MUCH]. Write a short email that opens with something specific to them rather than a generic pitch, explains quickly why I am reaching out, makes a small easy ask rather than a big one, and respects their time. Keep it short, since long cold emails get deleted. Be genuine rather than salesy. Give me a subject line and the cold email.
description: Write a short, specific cold email that respects their time and gets a reply.
useCase: Use this when reaching out to someone who does not know you. A short email that opens with something specific to them and makes a small easy ask gets replies, unlike the generic pitch that gets deleted, since the bar for a stranger's attention is high and brevity plus relevance is what clears it.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND WHY YOU ARE REACHING OUT
ANY RELEVANT CONTEXT, OR WRITE NOT MUCH

title: Make Your Ask Clear in an Email
promptText: Help me make my ask clear in an email, because I tend to bury it or be vague. Here is my draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT], and what I actually want is [WHAT YOU REALLY WANT THEM TO DO]. Help me: state the ask explicitly rather than hinting at it, put it somewhere they will actually see it, make it specific and easy to say yes to, and remove the hedging that makes it sound optional. Being direct about what I want is not rude, it is helpful. Give me the revised email with a clear ask.
description: Make your ask explicit and easy to act on instead of buried or hedged.
useCase: Use this when you hint at what you want rather than asking. A buried or hedged ask often gets no response simply because the recipient did not register that anything was needed, and being direct about what you want is helpful rather than rude, since it lets them act.
variables: WHAT YOU REALLY WANT THEM TO DO

title: Draft a Reply to an Email
promptText: Help me reply to an email. Here is the email I received: [PASTE THEIR EMAIL], my relationship with them is [YOUR RELATIONSHIP], and what I want to convey is [YOUR RESPONSE OR POSITION]. Draft a reply that addresses what they actually said rather than talking past it, answers any questions they asked, conveys my position clearly, and moves things forward. Note anything in their email I should address that I might overlook. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the reply.
description: Draft a reply that addresses what they actually said and moves things forward.
useCase: Use this when a reply needs care. Addressing what they actually said, answering their questions, and catching the point you might have overlooked prevents the frustrating exchange where two people talk past each other across three rounds of email.

title: Soften an Email That Reads Too Harsh
promptText: Help me soften an email that might read harsher than I intend. Here is my draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT], the recipient is [WHO THEY ARE], and the situation is [ANY CONTEXT, E.G. YOU ARE FRUSTRATED, IT IS BAD NEWS, YOU ARE PUSHING BACK]. Soften it so it stays clear and firm on the substance but does not read as cold, blunt, or annoyed. Keep the message intact rather than watering it down into vagueness. Point out the specific phrases that were landing badly. Softening tone is not the same as backing down. Give me the softened email.
description: Soften a harsh sounding email without watering down the message.
useCase: Use this when frustration or bluntness has crept into a draft. Softening how it reads while keeping the substance firm prevents an email that damages a relationship over tone, and knowing which phrases were landing badly helps you catch it yourself next time.
variables: ANY CONTEXT, E.G. YOU ARE FRUSTRATED, IT IS BAD NEWS, YOU ARE PUSHING BACK

title: Make an Email Firmer Without Being Rude
promptText: Help me make an email firmer, because my draft is too soft and apologetic. Here it is: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT], and what I need is [WHAT YOU NEED TO HOLD FIRM ON]. Rewrite it to be clear and confident: cut the excessive apologizing, hedging, and qualifiers that undermine my position, state what I need directly, and sound professional and assured rather than tentative. Remaining polite while being firm is entirely possible. Point out the phrases that were weakening me. Give me the firmer email.
description: Make a soft, apologetic email firm and confident while staying polite.
useCase: Use this when your draft undermines you with hedging and apology. Cutting the qualifiers that weaken your position and stating what you need directly reads as confident rather than rude, and it matters because a tentative email invites the other side to push back on things that were not negotiable.
variables: WHAT YOU NEED TO HOLD FIRM ON

title: Check an Email for Clarity Before Sending
promptText: Help me check this email before I send it. Here is my draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT], and the recipient is [WHO THEY ARE]. Check it for: anything unclear or open to misreading, whether my point and ask are obvious, whether the tone matches my intent, anything that could be taken the wrong way, and anything missing they would need to respond. Read it as the recipient would rather than as I meant it. Flag what to fix. Give me the feedback and a tightened version.
description: Check an email for clarity and misreading risk before you send it.
useCase: Use this before sending an email that matters. Reading it as the recipient would rather than as you meant it catches the ambiguity and unintended tone that cause misunderstandings, which is the main gap in email since you cannot clarify in the moment the way you can in conversation.

title: Write an Introduction Email
promptText: Help me write an email introducing myself for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The recipient is [WHO THEY ARE], the context is [WHY YOU ARE INTRODUCING YOURSELF, E.G. NEW CLIENT, REFERRAL, NETWORKING], and what I want from the introduction is [YOUR GOAL]. Write an email that introduces me clearly without a life story, explains why I am reaching out and any connection between us, conveys what I do briefly and relevantly, and suggests a clear next step. Keep it warm and short. Give me a subject line and the introduction email.
description: Write a warm, short introduction email that leads to a clear next step.
useCase: Use this when introducing yourself to someone new. An introduction that stays brief, names any connection, and suggests a next step lands far better than a long self description, since the recipient's question is simply why this matters to them and how much of their time it will take.
variables: WHY YOU ARE REACHING OUT, E.G. NEW CLIENT, REFERRAL, NETWORKING

title: Write an Email Using a Referral
promptText: Help me write an email to someone I was referred to, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The referrer is [WHO REFERRED YOU AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP TO THEM], the recipient is [WHO THEY ARE], and what I want is [YOUR ASK]. Write an email that leads with the referral since that is my strongest credential here, mentions the referrer naturally rather than name dropping, explains why I am reaching out, and makes a clear reasonable ask. A referral opens doors, so use it well without overplaying it. Give me a subject line and the email.
description: Write a referral email that uses the connection well without overplaying it.
useCase: Use this when someone referred you to a contact. Leading with the referral gets the email read since it is your strongest credential with a stranger, and mentioning the referrer naturally rather than name dropping keeps it from feeling like you are trading on someone else's relationship.
variables: WHO REFERRED YOU AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP TO THEM

title: Write a Thank You Email
promptText: Help me write a thank you email for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am thanking [WHO] for [WHAT THEY DID], and my relationship with them is [YOUR RELATIONSHIP]. Write a genuine thank you that is specific about what I am grateful for rather than generic, feels sincere rather than formulaic, and where natural keeps the relationship warm for the future. Keep it short, since a brief genuine thank you beats a long performative one. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the thank you email.
description: Write a specific, genuine thank you email that does not feel formulaic.
useCase: Use this to thank someone properly. Being specific about what you are grateful for makes a thank you feel genuine rather than obligatory, and these small notes quietly build the goodwill that leads to referrals and repeat work, which most people skip sending entirely.

title: Write an Apology Email
promptText: Help me write an apology email for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What happened is [WHAT WENT WRONG], who it affected is [WHO], and what I am doing about it is [YOUR FIX OR RESPONSE]. Write an apology that takes clear responsibility without excessive self flagellation or defensive explaining, acknowledges the actual impact on them, states what I am doing to fix it and prevent it recurring, and moves forward constructively. Avoid the non apology of sorry you feel that way. Own it and move on. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the apology email.
description: Write an apology that owns the mistake without excessive grovelling or excuses.
useCase: Use this when you need to apologize professionally. Taking clear responsibility and focusing on the fix, rather than defensive explaining or excessive grovelling, is what actually repairs trust, and handling a mistake well often leaves a client with more confidence in you than if it had never happened.

title: Write an Email Delivering Bad News
promptText: Help me write an email delivering bad news for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The bad news is [WHAT YOU NEED TO TELL THEM, E.G. A DELAY, A PROBLEM, A PRICE INCREASE, DECLINING SOMETHING], the recipient is [WHO THEY ARE], and any context or solution is [WHAT YOU CAN OFFER, OR WRITE NOTHING]. Write an email that delivers the news clearly and early rather than burying it, explains briefly without over justifying, offers a solution or path forward where possible, and respects them enough to be direct. Do not bury bad news at the bottom of a cheerful email. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the email.
description: Deliver bad news clearly and early rather than burying it in padding.
useCase: Use this when you must tell someone something they will not like. Delivering it clearly and early respects them and preserves trust, since burying bad news under cheerful padding is transparent and makes the recipient trust you less, while directness paired with a path forward usually lands better than expected.
variables: WHAT YOU NEED TO TELL THEM, E.G. A DELAY, A PROBLEM, A PRICE INCREASE, DECLINING SOMETHING
WHAT YOU CAN OFFER, OR WRITE NOTHING

title: Write an Email Saying No
promptText: Help me write an email declining something for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. description: Write a clear, warm no that does not leave false hope or invite negotiation.
useCase: Use this when you need to decline something. A clear warm no is kinder than a vague maybe that leaves someone waiting, and over explaining tends to invite negotiation, so a brief reason and a firm answer serves both sides better than a softened response that is not actually a yes.

title: Write an Email Sharing Good News
promptText: Help me write an email sharing good news for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The news is [THE GOOD NEWS], the recipient is [WHO THEY ARE], and what I want from it is [YOUR GOAL, E.G. JUST SHARING, BUILDING MOMENTUM, PROMPTING NEXT STEPS]. Write an email that leads with the good news, conveys genuine energy without overhyping, notes anything they need to know or do next, and where natural strengthens the relationship. description: Write an email sharing good news with genuine energy and a clear next step.

title: Build a Library of Email Templates

INQUIRIES, QUOTES, ONBOARDING, FOLLOW UPS, INVOICES]. For each, draft a template with clear fill in the blank spots for what changes each time, written in my voice and covering what that email needs to accomplish. Note where personalization matters so they do not feel canned. The goal is to stop rewriting the same emails from scratch. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the template library.
description: Build reusable templates for the emails you write over and over.
useCase: Use this once to stop rewriting the same emails. Templates for your recurring messages save real time and ensure your best wording gets used every time rather than whatever you improvise when tired, while noting where personalization matters keeps them from feeling canned.
variables: YOUR REPEATED EMAILS, E.G. INQUIRIES, QUOTES, ONBOARDING, FOLLOW UPS, INVOICES

title: Respond to an Inquiry
promptText: Help me respond to an inquiry from a potential customer in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is their inquiry: [PASTE THEIR MESSAGE], and my service is [WHAT YOU OFFER]. Write a response that answers what they actually asked, conveys competence and warmth, gives them what they need to move forward, asks any question I need answered, and proposes a clear next step. Respond promptly and helpfully, since the first reply shapes whether they choose me. Do not dump my entire pitch on them. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the response.
description: Respond to a customer inquiry helpfully with a clear next step.
useCase: Use this when a potential customer reaches out. The first reply shapes whether they choose you, so answering what they actually asked and proposing a clear next step converts better than a generic pitch dump, which reads as though you did not read their message.

title: Define Your Email Voice
promptText: Help me define a consistent voice for my emails in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My audience is [WHO YOU EMAIL], how I want to come across is [YOUR DESIRED IMPRESSION, E.G. WARM AND PROFESSIONAL, DIRECT AND EFFICIENT, FRIENDLY AND CASUAL], and here are examples of emails I have written: [PASTE A FEW OF YOUR EMAILS, OR WRITE NONE]. Help me define my email voice: the tone, level of formality, typical greetings and sign offs, sentence style, and what to avoid. Give me a short voice guide I can apply consistently so my emails sound like me rather than varying with my mood. Give me the email voice guide.
description: Define a consistent email voice so your messages sound like you every time.
useCase: Use this to make your emails consistently sound like you. A defined voice covering tone, formality, and sign offs keeps your emails coherent rather than swinging between stiff and casual depending on your mood, which is what makes a small business feel professional and recognizable.

title: Draft an Email You Are Dreading

Help me draft it: what to actually say, how to be honest without being harsh, how to handle my own discomfort without letting it make the email worse, and how to keep it professional. Being direct is usually less painful than the avoidance. Note anything I should not say. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the email.
description: Draft the difficult email you have been avoiding, honestly and professionally.
useCase: Use this for the email you keep putting off. Getting it drafted honestly and professionally breaks the avoidance, and being direct is almost always less painful than the delay, since the situation rarely improves while you postpone and the discomfort compounds.

title: Get a Quick Email Draft Fast
promptText: I need a quick email. It is to [WHO], about [WHAT IT IS ABOUT], and I want them to [DESIRED ACTION]. Give me a short clear professional email with a subject line, ready to send with minor edits. Keep it concise, no padding. Just give me a solid email I can send right now.
description: Get a fast, concise, ready to send email draft.
useCase: Use this when you just need an email written and sent. A quick clear draft gets it off your list without deliberation, which matters on a busy day when the alternative is the email sitting unwritten for hours while you avoid the small friction of starting it.

title: Proofread an Email Before Sending
promptText: Proofread this email before I send it: [PASTE YOUR EMAIL]. Check for typos, grammar errors, awkward phrasing, wrong names or details, and anything that would look careless or unprofessional. Fix what needs fixing while keeping my voice and tone intact rather than rewriting it into something generic. Flag anything that reads oddly. Give me the corrected email and note what you changed.
description: Proofread an email for errors while keeping your voice intact.
useCase: Use this before sending an email where a typo would look bad. Catching errors and awkward phrasing while preserving your voice protects your professionalism, since a misspelled name or sloppy sentence in a client email quietly undermines the impression you are working to build.

title: Write a Meeting Request Email
promptText: Help me write an email requesting a meeting for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The person is [WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP], the purpose is [WHY YOU WANT TO MEET], and what I want out of it is [YOUR GOAL]. Write a short email that states clearly why I want to meet and what is in it for them, proposes a specific length so they know the commitment, offers concrete times or an easy way to book, and makes saying yes simple. Keep it brief, since a long meeting request signals a long meeting. My tone is [TONE]. Give me a subject line and the email.
description: Write a short meeting request that makes the purpose and commitment clear.
useCase: Use this when asking someone for a meeting. Stating the purpose, the length, and what is in it for them makes yes easy, since vague open ended requests get ignored, and naming a specific short duration reassures a busy person that this will not eat their afternoon.

title: Clarify Why the Meeting Should Happen
promptText: Help me clarify the purpose of a meeting I want to request in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I want to meet [WHO] because [YOUR ROUGH REASON], and what I hope comes out of it is [YOUR HOPED OUTCOME]. Help me sharpen this: what the meeting is genuinely for, what specific outcome would make it worthwhile, whether the purpose is clear enough to state in one sentence, and how to frame it so it sounds worth their time rather than vague. A meeting request without a clear purpose usually gets declined or wasted. Give me a clear one sentence purpose and how to frame it.
description: Sharpen a vague meeting purpose into one clear sentence worth someone's time.
useCase: Use this before requesting a meeting you have not fully thought through. Sharpening the purpose into one clear sentence is what gets it accepted and makes it productive, since a request that cannot state its own purpose gets declined, and a meeting without one wastes everyone's time even when accepted.

title: Check Whether a Meeting Is Needed at All
promptText: Help me decide whether I actually need a meeting or whether this could be handled another way in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I need is [WHAT YOU NEED TO ACCOMPLISH OR DECIDE], the people involved are [WHO], and the context is [ANY CONTEXT]. Help me assess honestly: whether a live conversation genuinely adds something here, or whether an email, a message, a shared document, or a short recorded update would do it faster for everyone. If a meeting is warranted, say what makes it so. If not, suggest the better alternative. Do not default to yes. Give me an honest recommendation.
description: Honestly check whether a meeting is needed or could be handled async.
useCase: Use this before putting a meeting on anyone's calendar. Honestly checking whether a live conversation adds anything, or whether an email or shared doc would be faster, protects your time and theirs, since much of what becomes a meeting could have been resolved in writing in a fraction of the time.
variables: WHAT YOU NEED TO ACCOMPLISH OR DECIDE

title: Propose an Alternative to a Meeting
promptText: Help me propose handling something without a meeting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Someone wants to meet about [WHAT THEY WANT TO MEET ABOUT], and I think it could be handled by [YOUR PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE, E.G. EMAIL, A DOC, A QUICK MESSAGE]. Write a message that suggests the alternative without seeming dismissive or unwilling to engage, frames it as saving them time rather than avoiding them, offers to meet if the alternative does not resolve it, and keeps the relationship warm. Declining a meeting gracefully is a skill. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the message.

useCase: Use this when someone requests a meeting that does not need to be one. Suggesting an alternative framed as saving their time, while offering to meet if it does not resolve, protects your calendar without damaging the relationship, which is what makes declining a meeting gracefully a genuinely useful skill.

YOUR PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE, E.G. EMAIL, A DOC, A QUICK MESSAGE

title: Propose Meeting Times Without the Back and Forth

My availability is [YOUR AVAILABILITY], the meeting length is [HOW LONG], and the person is [WHO THEY ARE AND WHERE, IF TIMEZONES MATTER]. Write wording that offers a few specific concrete options rather than asking when works for you, handles timezones clearly if relevant, gives an easy fallback if none work, and makes it a one reply decision. Vague availability questions cause the endless email tennis. Give me the scheduling wording.
description: Propose specific times so scheduling takes one reply instead of five emails.
useCase: Use this to end scheduling ping pong. Offering a few concrete options rather than asking when works for you turns scheduling into a one reply decision, since open ended availability questions force the other person to do the work and generate the email tennis everyone hates.

title: Frame a Meeting as Worth Their Time
promptText: Help me frame a meeting request so it sounds worth the other person's time in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I want to meet [WHO THEY ARE], the meeting is about [THE TOPIC], and honestly what is in it for them is [THE BENEFIT TO THEM, OR WRITE HELP ME FIND IT]. Help me frame it around their interest rather than mine: what they would gain, why it is relevant to them, and how to convey that briefly and honestly without overselling. If the meeting mainly benefits me, help me be upfront about that rather than dressing it up. Give me the framing and wording.
description: Frame a meeting request around their benefit rather than yours.
useCase: Use this when requesting time from someone busy or senior. Framing the meeting around what they gain, rather than what you want, is what earns a yes, and being upfront when the meeting mainly benefits you reads as more honest than a thin pretext they will see through anyway.
variables: THE BENEFIT TO THEM, OR WRITE HELP ME FIND IT

title: Request a Meeting with a Stranger

The person is [WHO THEY ARE AND WHY YOU WANT TO MEET THEM], what I know about them is [ANY CONTEXT], and my ask is [WHAT YOU WANT]. Write a short request that opens with something specific to them rather than a generic pitch, explains briefly why I am reaching out to them specifically, asks for a small amount of time rather than an hour, and makes it easy to say yes or no. Keep it short and respectful of the fact they owe me nothing. Give me a subject line and the request.

useCase: Use this to ask a stranger for time. Opening with something specific to them and asking for a small amount of time rather than an hour respects that they owe you nothing, which is exactly why short specific requests get accepted while generic pitches for an hour get deleted.

title: Follow Up on an Ignored Meeting Request
promptText: Help me follow up on a meeting request that got no reply in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I asked [WHO] about [WHAT YOU ASKED FOR] on [WHEN YOU ASKED], and I have heard nothing. Write a brief follow up that assumes good faith rather than sounding annoyed, adds something useful rather than just bumping the thread, makes it even easier to respond, and gives them an easy out if they are not interested. Keep it light and short. Note how many follow ups is reasonable before letting it go. Give me the follow up message.
description: Follow up on an unanswered meeting request without sounding annoyed.
useCase: Use this when a meeting request gets no reply. A light follow up that assumes good faith and offers an easy out often gets a response, since most silence is a busy inbox rather than rejection, though knowing when to stop matters as much as sending the first nudge.

title: Decline a Meeting Request Gracefully

Write a message that declines clearly without leaving false hope, stays warm and respectful, gives a brief reason without over explaining, and where appropriate offers an alternative such as a shorter call, an async option, or another time. description: Decline a meeting clearly and warmly without leaving false hope.
useCase: Use this to say no to a meeting. A clear warm decline is kinder than an indefinite maybe that leaves someone chasing you, and offering a smaller alternative where appropriate lets you protect your time without shutting the relationship down entirely.

title: Reschedule a Meeting Gracefully

title: Cancel a Meeting Professionally
promptText: Help me cancel a meeting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Write a message that cancels clearly and promptly, apologizes proportionately to the disruption caused, explains briefly, and either proposes a new time or closes it out cleanly so they are not left wondering. Cancelling late deserves a real apology, cancelling early just needs clarity. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the message.
description: Cancel a meeting clearly with an apology proportionate to the disruption.
useCase: Use this when cancelling a meeting. Cancelling promptly and clearly, with an apology sized to the actual disruption, handles it well, and either proposing a new time or closing it out cleanly prevents the limbo where the other person does not know whether to expect you to follow up.

title: Confirm a Meeting Before It Happens
promptText: Help me write a meeting confirmation message for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The meeting is [WHAT, WHEN, AND HOW LONG], with [WHO], and it is happening [WHERE OR ON WHAT PLATFORM]. Write a brief confirmation that restates the time clearly including timezone if relevant, confirms the location or link, notes what we will cover so they arrive prepared, and mentions anything they should bring or think about. Keep it short. A confirmation reduces no shows and makes the meeting more productive. Give me the confirmation message.
description: Confirm a meeting with the time, link, and what will be covered.
useCase: Use this after a meeting is booked. A brief confirmation restating the time, link, and agenda reduces no shows and means people arrive prepared rather than asking what this is about in the first five minutes, which is where a lot of meeting time quietly disappears.

title: Send a Meeting Reminder
promptText: Help me write a short reminder for an upcoming meeting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The meeting is [WHAT AND WHEN], with [WHO], and it is [WHERE OR THE LINK]. Write a brief friendly reminder that restates the time and link, keeps it light rather than nagging, and includes anything they need to have ready. Keep it very short. A quick reminder the day before meaningfully cuts no shows. Give me the reminder message.
description: Send a short, friendly meeting reminder that cuts no shows.
useCase: Use this the day before a meeting. A brief reminder with the time and link meaningfully reduces no shows, which protects the slot you reserved, and keeping it light rather than nagging means it reads as helpful rather than as chasing someone who already committed.

Write a message that assumes good faith rather than sounding annoyed, checks whether everything is okay, offers to reschedule if I still want to, and keeps the door open or closes it gracefully. Note when a no show is worth another attempt versus a signal to move on. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the message.
description: Follow up after a no show without sounding annoyed, and know when to move on.
useCase: Use this when someone misses a meeting. Assuming good faith rather than firing off an annoyed note is usually right since things genuinely come up, though recognizing when a no show is a signal to stop investing matters too, especially with a prospect who was never that interested.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP

title: Ask for a Shorter Meeting
promptText: Help me ask to shorten a meeting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The meeting is [WHAT AND HOW LONG IT IS SCHEDULED FOR], with [WHO], and I think it needs [HOW LONG YOU THINK IT NEEDS]. Write a message that proposes the shorter length without seeming dismissive of them or the topic, frames it as keeping things focused rather than as me being too busy for them, and suggests how to make the shorter time work such as a tight agenda. Most meetings expand to fill the time booked. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the message.
description: Ask to shorten a meeting without seeming dismissive of the person or topic.
useCase: Use this when a meeting is booked for longer than it needs. Proposing a shorter slot framed as keeping things focused protects your time without insulting anyone, and it works because meetings genuinely expand to fill whatever was booked regardless of what the topic actually requires.
variables: WHAT AND HOW LONG IT IS SCHEDULED FOR
HOW LONG YOU THINK IT NEEDS

title: Request a Discovery Call with a Prospect
promptText: Help me request a discovery call with a potential client for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The prospect is [WHO THEY ARE AND HOW THEY CAME TO YOU], my service is [WHAT YOU OFFER], and what I want from the call is [YOUR GOAL]. Write a message that proposes a short call framed around understanding their situation rather than pitching at them, sets a clear expectation of what the call is and how long, makes booking easy, and removes any sense of a hard sell. People avoid calls they think are pitches. My tone is [TONE]. Give me a subject line and the message.
description: Request a discovery call framed around them, not as a disguised pitch.
useCase: Use this to get a prospect on a call. Framing it around understanding their situation rather than pitching, with a clear short duration, removes the resistance people have to sales calls, since the fear of being pitched at for an hour is exactly what makes prospects avoid booking.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND HOW THEY CAME TO YOU

title: Include an Agenda in a Meeting Request
promptText: Help me include a brief agenda in my meeting request for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The meeting is about [THE TOPIC], with [WHO], for [HOW LONG], and what needs to be covered is [WHAT TO COVER]. Write a short agenda to include in the request that shows the meeting has a plan and will not ramble, sets the expectation of what we will and will not cover, and helps them prepare. Keep it to a few lines rather than a formal document. An agenda in the request itself makes acceptance more likely. Give me the request wording with the agenda.
description: Include a brief agenda in a meeting request to show it has a plan.
useCase: Use this to make a meeting request more likely to be accepted. A few lines of agenda signal that the meeting has a plan and will not ramble, which reassures a busy person, and it also means both sides arrive knowing what will and will not be covered.

title: Request a Meeting with Someone Senior
promptText: Help me request a meeting with someone significantly more senior or busy than me, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The person is [WHO THEY ARE], my connection to them is [YOUR CONNECTION, OR WRITE NONE], and what I want is [YOUR ASK]. Write a request that is respectful of their time without being obsequious, gets to the point in the first line, asks for a small specific amount of time, makes clear why them specifically, and gives an easy no. Confidence without arrogance is the balance. Do not apologize for existing. Give me a subject line and the request.
description: Request time from someone senior with confidence rather than obsequiousness.
useCase: Use this when asking someone senior or very busy for time. Getting to the point immediately and asking for something small reads as confident and respectful, while excessive apologizing for taking their time actually makes the ask harder to say yes to by signalling you do not think it is worth it.

title: Propose a Recurring Meeting
promptText: Help me propose a recurring meeting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The meeting would be [WHAT IT IS FOR], with [WHO], at a cadence of [HOW OFTEN], lasting [HOW LONG]. Write a proposal that explains why a regular rhythm helps rather than ad hoc meetings, proposes the cadence and length, notes what each session would cover, and builds in a check to review whether it is still worth it later. Recurring meetings tend to outlive their usefulness, so proposing a review point upfront is smart. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the proposal message.
description: Propose a recurring meeting with a built in point to review whether it still earns its place.
useCase: Use this when proposing a standing meeting. Explaining why a rhythm helps and building in a review point upfront is smart, since recurring meetings reliably outlive their usefulness and become far harder to cancel once they are simply part of everyone's week.

title: Fix the Tone of a Meeting Request
promptText: Help me fix the tone of my meeting request in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT], and the person is [WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP]. Check whether it reads as I intend: whether it sounds desperate, presumptuous, apologetic, or demanding, whether the ask is proportionate to the relationship, and whether it makes yes easy. Point out the specific phrases that land badly and why. Meeting requests fail on tone more often than on substance. Give me the feedback and a fixed version.
description: Fix a meeting request that reads as desperate, presumptuous, or apologetic.
useCase: Use this before sending a meeting request that matters. Meeting requests fail on tone more often than substance, and catching that your draft reads as desperate or presumptuous, and which specific phrases cause it, is what turns an ignored request into an accepted one.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP

title: Share a Booking Link Without Seeming Cold
promptText: Help me share my booking link in a way that does not feel cold or presumptuous in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The person is [WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP], and the meeting is [WHAT IT IS FOR]. Write wording that offers the booking link as a convenience for them rather than as me being too important to check my calendar, keeps the human warmth around it, and offers to just pick a time manually if they prefer. Note when a booking link is appropriate versus when it reads as dismissive, such as with someone senior. Give me the wording.
description: Share a booking link warmly rather than in a way that reads as dismissive.
useCase: Use this when sending someone a booking link. Framing it as a convenience for them, with an offer to just pick a time manually, keeps the warmth, and knowing when a link reads as dismissive matters, since sending one to a senior contact can land as though their time matters less than yours.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP

title: Get a Quick Meeting Request Fast
promptText: I need a quick meeting request. It is to [WHO], about [THE PURPOSE], and I want [HOW LONG] of their time. Give me a short clear message with a subject line that states the purpose, proposes a specific length, and offers a couple of times. Keep it brief and ready to send. Just give me a solid meeting request I can send right now.
description: Get a fast, ready to send meeting request with a clear purpose and times.
useCase: Use this when you just need a meeting request written and sent. A quick message stating the purpose, length, and a couple of times covers everything a good request needs without deliberation, which is all most meeting requests actually require.

title: Decide When to Ask for the Meeting
promptText: Help me decide when and how to time a meeting request in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The person is [WHO THEY ARE], the context is [WHAT IS GOING ON, E.G. YOU JUST MET THEM, THEY JUST BOUGHT, YOU HAVE BEEN TALKING A WHILE], and my ask is [WHAT YOU WANT]. Help me think about timing: whether now is the right moment or too early, what would make them more receptive, whether to build more rapport first, and how the timing changes the framing. Asking too early can burn a contact who would have said yes later. Give me a recommendation on timing and framing.
description: Decide whether now is the right moment to ask for a meeting.
useCase: Use this before asking someone for time, especially a new contact. Timing matters because asking too early can burn a relationship that would have produced a yes later, and thinking about what would make them receptive is often worth more than perfecting the wording of a premature ask.
variables: WHAT IS GOING ON, E.G. YOU JUST MET THEM, THEY JUST BOUGHT, YOU HAVE BEEN TALKING A WHILE

title: Write a Follow Up Email
promptText: Help me write a follow up email for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I originally contacted [WHO THEY ARE] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT] on [WHEN], and I have heard nothing back. Write a short follow up that assumes good faith rather than sounding impatient, adds something useful rather than just saying bumping this, restates the ask clearly and simply, and makes it easy to reply even with a no. Keep it brief, since a long follow up on an ignored email rarely lands better. My tone is [TONE]. Give me a subject line and the follow up.
description: Write a brief follow up that assumes good faith and makes replying easy.
useCase: Use this when someone has not replied. A short follow up that adds something useful rather than just bumping the thread gets responses, since most silence is a busy inbox rather than rejection, and making it easy to reply with a no often produces the clarity you actually needed.

title: Decide When to Follow Up
promptText: Help me decide when to follow up in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I contacted [WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT] on [WHEN], and the urgency is [HOW TIME SENSITIVE IT IS]. Help me judge: whether enough time has passed to follow up without seeming impatient, how the right timing changes based on who they are and what I asked for, whether the urgency justifies moving sooner, and what a sensible gap looks like here. Following up too fast reads as pushy, too slow and the thread goes cold. Give me a recommendation on timing and why.
description: Judge the right moment to follow up without seeming pushy or letting it go cold.
useCase: Use this when unsure whether it is too soon to chase. Timing depends on who they are and what you asked, and getting it right matters because following up too fast reads as pushy while waiting too long lets the thread go cold and the context fade from their memory.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP

title: Add Value to a Follow Up Instead of Just Bumping
promptText: Help me make my follow up worth opening rather than just a bump in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am following up with [WHO THEY ARE] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT], and what I could offer or share is [ANYTHING USEFUL YOU COULD ADD, OR WRITE HELP ME FIND SOMETHING]. Help me find a genuine reason to reappear in their inbox: a useful resource, a relevant update, a new angle, an answer to a likely objection, or something that makes the follow up feel helpful rather than needy. If I have nothing to add, tell me and suggest how to follow up honestly anyway. Give me the value adding follow up.
description: Find a genuine reason to follow up rather than sending an empty bump.
useCase: Use this when your follow up would otherwise just say checking in. Adding something genuinely useful makes reappearing in someone's inbox feel helpful rather than needy, and being told honestly when you have nothing to add is more useful than manufacturing a thin pretext they will see through.
variables: ANYTHING USEFUL YOU COULD ADD, OR WRITE HELP ME FIND SOMETHING

title: Replace Just Checking In with Something Better
promptText: Help me write a follow up without falling back on just checking in, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I am following up with [WHO THEY ARE] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT], and the situation is [WHERE THINGS STAND]. Explain briefly why just checking in and similar phrases are weak, since they put the work on the recipient and give them nothing to respond to, then write a follow up that has an actual purpose, a specific question they can answer easily, or a concrete next step. Give them something to react to rather than a vague nudge. Give me the improved follow up.
description: Write a follow up with an actual purpose instead of a vague checking in nudge.
useCase: Use this to stop sending follow ups that give the recipient nothing to work with. Just checking in puts the effort on them and invites no response, whereas a specific question or concrete next step is easy to answer, which is why purposeful follow ups reliably outperform vague nudges.

title: Plan a Follow Up Sequence
promptText: Help me plan a follow up sequence for my [BUSINESS TYPE] so I stop following up randomly or forgetting entirely. The situation is [WHAT YOU FOLLOW UP ON, E.G. PROPOSALS, INQUIRIES, QUOTES], and my typical contact is [WHO THEY ARE]. Plan a sequence: how many follow ups is reasonable, the gap between each, how the message and tone should shift across them, what each one should add, and a clear final one that closes the loop. Give me the messages I can reuse. A planned sequence means I follow up consistently without agonizing each time. Give me the sequence with timing.
description: Plan a reusable follow up sequence with timing so you never chase randomly.
useCase: Use this once to systematize following up. A planned sequence with set gaps and reusable messages means you follow up consistently without deciding from scratch each time, which is how a solo operator stops losing deals to the simple failure of never sending the second email.
variables: WHAT YOU FOLLOW UP ON, E.G. PROPOSALS, INQUIRIES, QUOTES

title: Write a Final Follow Up That Closes the Loop
promptText: Help me write a final follow up to close out a thread in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I have followed up with [WHO THEY ARE] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT] [HOW MANY TIMES] with no reply. Write a final message that closes the loop gracefully: notes I will stop following up, keeps the door genuinely open for them to come back, avoids guilt tripping or passive aggression, and leaves a good impression. Note that a clean closing message often gets a reply when nothing else did, since it releases the pressure. My tone is [TONE]. Give me the final follow up.
description: Write a graceful final follow up that closes the loop without guilt tripping.
useCase: Use this to end a thread you have chased enough. A clean closing message that releases the pressure often gets a reply when nothing else did, and even when it does not, it leaves a good impression rather than the resentment a passive aggressive last word would create.

title: Decide When to Stop Following Up
promptText: Help me decide whether to keep following up or let it go in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I have contacted [WHO THEY ARE] about [WHAT IT WAS ABOUT] [HOW MANY TIMES] over [HOW LONG], and the signals so far are [ANY RESPONSE OR SILENCE]. Help me assess honestly: whether the silence means no, whether more follow up would help or just annoy them, whether this is worth more of my energy, and when persistence turns into pestering. Be honest rather than encouraging me to keep chasing something dead. Note that my energy may be better spent elsewhere. Give me an honest read on whether to continue.
description: Honestly assess whether to keep following up or let a dead thread go.
useCase: Use this when you are not sure whether to keep chasing.
