Flag anything I kept that they probably will not understand. Note that jargon feels professional to write and reads as evasive, and that the terms my peers use are often invisible to my customers. Give me the plain version.
description: Replace industry jargon with the words your audience actually uses.
useCase: Use this when your page reads like an industry brochure. Jargon feels professional to write and reads as evasive to a visitor, and the vocabulary that impresses your peers is frequently invisible to the customers you are trying to reach.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND HOW MUCH THEY KNOW

title: Match the Page to Where They Came From
promptText: Help me check whether my landing page matches what brought people there, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What they clicked was [THE AD, SEARCH RESULT, OR LINK THEY CAME FROM], and my page says [PASTE YOUR OPENING COPY]. Check the match: whether the page delivers what the click promised, whether the language carries over, and whether someone would feel they landed in the right place. Note that a mismatch between the promise and the page is one of the fastest ways to lose a visitor, since they bounce before reading anything. Give me the gaps and how to close them.
description: Check that your page delivers what the click that brought them promised.
useCase: Use this when traffic arrives and bounces instantly. A mismatch between what the ad or search result promised and what the page says loses people before they read a word, since the first job of a landing page is confirming they landed in the right place.
variables: THE AD, SEARCH RESULT, OR LINK THEY CAME FROM

title: Adapt Copy to How Warm the Visitor Is
promptText: Help me adapt my landing page copy to how warm my visitors are, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My traffic comes from [WHERE, E.G. COLD ADS, SEARCH, YOUR EMAIL LIST, A REFERRAL], my offer is [WHAT YOU OFFER], and my current copy is [PASTE IT]. Help me adjust: how much explaining a cold visitor needs versus how much a warm one finds patronizing, where to start the argument, and what to assume. Note that copy written for a cold stranger bores someone who already trusts me, and copy written for a warm lead baffles someone who just arrived. Give me the adapted version.
description: Adapt copy to whether visitors arrive cold or already trusting you.
useCase: Use this when one page serves different traffic sources. Copy written for a cold stranger bores someone who already trusts you, and copy for a warm lead baffles someone who just arrived, so knowing which you are writing for changes where the argument starts.
variables: WHERE, E.G. COLD ADS, SEARCH, YOUR EMAIL LIST, A REFERRAL

title: Say Who the Page Is For
promptText: Help me make clear who my landing page is for in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My offer is [WHAT YOU OFFER], my ideal customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and who it is not for is [WHO SHOULD NOT BUY, OR WRITE HELP ME WORK THIS OUT]. Write copy that names the right person so they recognize themselves immediately, and where useful says plainly who this is not for. Note that naming who it is not for makes the right person trust it more, and that a page trying to appeal to everyone speaks to nobody in particular. Give me the copy.
description: Name who the page is for so the right person recognizes themselves.
useCase: Use this when your page tries to appeal to everyone. Naming the right person makes them recognize themselves immediately, and saying plainly who it is not for makes the right person trust it more rather than fewer people buying.
variables: WHO SHOULD NOT BUY, OR WRITE HELP ME WORK THIS OUT

title: Write the Copy Around a Form
promptText: Help me write the copy around a form on my [BUSINESS TYPE] landing page. The form asks for [WHAT FIELDS YOU REQUEST], what they get is [WHAT THEY RECEIVE], and what happens after is [WHAT FOLLOWS]. Write the copy: the line above explaining what they get, the field labels, the button, and the reassurance underneath about what I will and will not do with their details. Also tell me honestly which fields I could drop. Note that every field costs completions, and asking for a phone number when I only need an email quietly halves the response. Give me the form copy.
description: Write form copy that explains the trade and cuts fields you do not need.
useCase: Use this on any form. Every field costs completions, and asking for a phone number when you only need an email quietly halves your response, while the reassurance line underneath about what happens to their details is often what tips someone into filling it in.

title: Remove What Is Pulling People Away
promptText: Help me find what is pulling visitors away from the action on my [BUSINESS TYPE] landing page. My page has [DESCRIBE EVERYTHING ON IT, INCLUDING NAVIGATION, LINKS, SIDEBARS, AND FOOTERS], and my goal is [THE ONE ACTION]. Help me identify every exit route competing with my goal, which are genuinely necessary, and which exist only because they are on every other page of my site. Note that a landing page with full site navigation gives people fifteen ways to leave before deciding. Give me what to remove and what to keep.
description: Find the links and navigation quietly pulling visitors off your landing page.
useCase: Use this if your landing page carries your normal site navigation. Full navigation gives visitors fifteen ways to leave before they decide, and much of what sits on a landing page is there only because it is on every other page rather than because it earns its place.
variables: DESCRIBE EVERYTHING ON IT, INCLUDING NAVIGATION, LINKS, SIDEBARS, AND FOOTERS

title: Decide How Long the Page Should Be
promptText: Help me decide how long my landing page should be for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Help me judge: whether this needs a short page or a long one, what determines it, and what my page actually needs to include. Note that short versus long is the wrong question, since the real one is whether the page answers everything a person needs before deciding, and a high commitment offer to a cold visitor needs more than a free download does. Give me a recommendation.
description: Decide page length based on what the visitor needs before deciding.
useCase: Use this when unsure whether to write short or long. Short versus long is the wrong question, since what matters is whether the page answers everything someone needs before deciding, and a high commitment offer to a cold visitor needs far more than a free download.

title: Cut the Copy That Is Not Working
promptText: Help me cut the copy that is not earning its place on my [BUSINESS TYPE] landing page. Here is my copy: [PASTE IT], and my goal is [THE ACTION YOU WANT]. Cut hard: the throat clearing intro, the paragraphs that say nothing, the section about my company history nobody asked for, and anything that does not move someone toward the action. Tell me what you cut and why. Note that most landing pages are long because nobody edited them rather than because the length was needed. Give me the trimmed version.
description: Cut landing page copy that does not move anyone toward the action.
useCase: Use this on a page that grew without editing. Most landing pages are long because nobody cut anything rather than because the length was needed, and the company history section nobody asked for is usually sitting exactly where the argument should be building.

title: Match the Page to How You Actually Sound
promptText: Help me make my landing page sound like me rather than a template, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my copy: [PASTE IT], here is how I actually talk about my work: [PASTE AN EMAIL OR DESCRIBE HOW YOU EXPLAIN IT IN PERSON], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Rewrite the page in my actual voice while keeping it clear and persuasive. Note that most landing pages sound like every other landing page because people switch into marketing voice when they start writing, and the way I explain my work in an email is usually better than what I put on the page. Give me the rewrite.
description: Rewrite a page in your real voice instead of default marketing tone.
useCase: Use this when your page sounds like every other landing page. People switch into a borrowed marketing voice the moment they start writing copy, and the way you explain your work in a normal email is almost always clearer and more convincing than what ends up on the page.
variables: PASTE AN EMAIL OR DESCRIBE HOW YOU EXPLAIN IT IN PERSON

title: Work Out Why Nobody Is Converting
promptText: Help me work out why my landing page is not converting in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My page is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], my traffic is [HOW MUCH AND FROM WHERE], and my conversion rate is [WHAT IT IS, OR WRITE ALMOST NOTHING]. Help me diagnose honestly: whether the copy is the problem, whether the traffic is wrong for the offer, whether the offer itself is the issue, or whether I simply do not have enough traffic to tell yet. Be honest if the answer is that the offer is the problem and no copy will fix it. Give me the likely cause and what to check.
description: Diagnose whether the copy, the traffic, or the offer itself is the problem.
useCase: Use this when a page is not converting and you assume it is the copy. Often the traffic is wrong for the offer, or the offer itself is the problem and no rewrite will fix it, and being told that honestly saves you three rounds of edits that were never going to work.

title: Balance Landing Page Copy Against SEO
promptText: Help me balance writing for conversion against writing for search on my [BUSINESS TYPE] landing page. My target keyword is [YOUR KEYWORD], my page is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], and my main traffic source is [WHERE PEOPLE ACTUALLY COME FROM]. Help me judge: whether this page needs to rank at all or just convert the traffic I send it, where the two goals genuinely conflict, and which should win. Note that a page stuffed with keywords converts worse, and a page nobody can find converts nothing, so the answer depends on where the traffic comes from. Give me a recommendation.
description: Judge whether a landing page needs to rank or just convert the traffic you send.
useCase: Use this when torn between keywords and conversion. A page stuffed with keywords converts worse while a page nobody finds converts nothing, so the honest answer depends entirely on whether your traffic comes from search or from ads and links you control.

title: Get Quick Landing Page Copy
promptText: I need quick landing page copy. My offer is [WHAT YOU OFFER], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the action I want is [WHAT THEY SHOULD DO]. Give me a headline, a subheadline, three benefit points, and a call to action. Keep it clear and specific, no marketing filler. Just give me copy I can put up right now.
description: Get a fast, complete set of landing page copy ready to use.
useCase: Use this when you need a page up rather than perfect. A headline, subheadline, three benefits, and a call to action covers the structure most simple pages need, and a live page you improve later beats a perfect one still sitting in a draft.

title: Find Internal Linking Opportunities
promptText: Help me find internal linking opportunities across my [BUSINESS TYPE] site. My pages and what each covers are [LIST YOUR PAGES AND THEIR TOPICS]. Note that internal links are for guiding readers first and search engines second, so a link that helps nobody read further is not worth adding. Give me the linking opportunities as pairs with a reason for each.
description: Find internal linking opportunities across your pages based on how topics relate.
useCase: Use this when your pages sit disconnected from each other. Finding where a link would genuinely help a reader continue matters more than link count, since internal links serve readers first and search engines second, and a link that helps nobody read further earns its place nowhere.

promptText: Help me write anchor text for internal links on my [BUSINESS TYPE] site. Write anchor text that describes where the link goes so a reader knows what they will get, reads naturally in the sentence, and avoids both click here and awkwardly stuffed keywords. Note that anchor text is a promise about the destination, so click here breaks that promise and keyword stuffing reads as spam. Give me a few options.
description: Write anchor text that tells the reader where the link goes and reads naturally.
useCase: Use this whenever you add a link. Anchor text is a promise about the destination, so click here tells the reader nothing while a keyword jammed in awkwardly reads as spam, and describing where the link actually goes serves both the reader and search engines at once.

Tell me which to keep, move, or cut. Note that a page cluttered with links nobody wants trains readers to ignore all of them, including the ones that matter. Give me the verdict on each.
description: Check whether each internal link helps the reader or just exists for SEO.
useCase: Use this on a page stuffed with links. A page cluttered with links nobody wants trains readers to ignore all of them, including the useful ones, so being honest about which serve the reader and which exist only for search engines is what keeps the important links visible.

Note that a well linked cluster signals depth on a topic and helps a reader move through it, while scattered unlinked pages on the same subject waste that depth. Give me the linking structure.
description: Link a group of related pages into a connected cluster with clear structure.
useCase: Use this when you have several pages on one topic sitting unconnected. Linking them into a cluster with a central page and supporting siblings signals depth on the subject and helps readers move through it, whereas the same pages scattered and unlinked waste the depth you built.

Help me design a hub: what the hub page itself should say, how it should organize and link to the pieces, what order or grouping helps a reader, and whether I have gaps a hub would expose. Note that a hub page gives readers one place to find everything on a topic and gives search engines a clear map of how my content fits together. Give me the hub structure and what it should link to.
description: Plan a hub page that organizes and links all your content on a topic.
useCase: Use this to give readers one entry point to everything on a topic. A hub page organizes scattered content into a clear map that helps readers find what they need and shows search engines how your pages fit together, and planning it often exposes the gaps in your coverage.

title: Bring Buried Pages Closer to the Surface
promptText: Help me bring buried pages closer to the surface on my [BUSINESS TYPE] site. My site structure is [DESCRIBE HOW PAGES NEST, E.G. Help me work out: which important pages sit too many clicks from the homepage, why that weakens them, and how to link them closer to the surface. Note that a valuable page five clicks deep is both hard for readers to find and treated as less important by search engines. Give me which pages to surface and how.
description: Bring important pages that sit too deep closer to the homepage.
useCase: Use this when valuable pages are buried deep in your structure. A page five clicks from the homepage is hard for readers to reach and treated as less important by search engines, so surfacing your money pages with closer links is a quiet but real improvement.

Pointing internal links at your service or product pages from relevant content tells search engines those pages matter, provided the links fit the context, since a forced link jammed in where it does not belong helps neither the reader nor the ranking.

title: Link Blog Posts to Your Service Pages
promptText: Help me link my blog posts to my service or product pages on my [BUSINESS TYPE] site. My blog post is about [THE POST TOPIC], and my relevant service or product page is [WHAT IT OFFERS]. Help me find the natural bridge: where in the post a reader would genuinely be ready to learn about my offer, how to link there without it feeling like a jarring sales insert, and the anchor text that fits. Note that a reader learning about a problem is a reader who might want it solved, but a sales link dropped mid explanation breaks trust. Give me where and how to link.

A reader learning about a problem is a reader who might want it solved, so linking from the post to your relevant service at the right moment converts interest, while a sales link dropped mid explanation breaks the trust the post was building.

title: Place Links Where They Fit the Content
promptText: Help me place internal links naturally within a piece of content on my [BUSINESS TYPE] site. Help me find the spots where each link genuinely fits the flow of what I am saying, rather than bolting a links section onto the end. Tell me if a page does not fit anywhere naturally. Note that a link woven into the point being made gets clicked, while a related links list at the bottom mostly gets ignored. Give me where each link belongs.
description: Weave links into the content where they fit rather than listing them at the end.
useCase: Use this instead of dumping a related links list at the bottom. A link woven into the point being made gets clicked while a list at the end mostly gets ignored, and being told a page fits nowhere naturally saves you forcing a link that would only clutter the piece.

title: Fix a Page with Too Many Links

Help me cut it back: which links are essential, which are redundant because several point to the same place, which distract from the main path, and which just clutter. Note that when every other word is a link, readers stop trusting any of them and the important links lose their weight among the noise. Give me which links to keep and which to cut.
description: Cut a page with too many links back to the ones that matter.
useCase: Use this on a page where every other word is a link. When links are everywhere readers stop trusting any of them and the important ones lose their weight in the noise, so cutting back to the essential links is what makes the ones that remain actually get clicked.

promptText: Help me integrate a new page into my [BUSINESS TYPE] site with internal links. Help me plan: which existing pages should link to the new one so it does not launch as an orphan, which pages the new one should link out to, and the anchor text for each. title: Plan Navigation and Menu Links

title: Decide What Belongs in the Footer
promptText: Help me decide what internal links belong in my [BUSINESS TYPE] site footer. My pages are [LIST YOUR PAGES], and what is in my footer now is [WHAT IS THERE, OR WRITE NOTHING YET]. title: Find Broken Things on Your Site
promptText: Help me find broken things on my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND YOUR PLATFORM], and what has changed recently is [ANY RECENT CHANGES, OR WRITE NOTHING SPECIFIC]. Give me a checklist to find what is broken: dead links, buttons that do nothing, forms that fail, images that do not load, pages that error, and anything that stopped working after a change. Tell me how to check each without technical tools. Note that things break silently and I am usually the last to know, since visitors just leave rather than telling me a link is dead. Give me the checklist.
description: Find dead links, broken forms, and other silent failures on your site.
useCase: Use this to catch what breaks silently. Visitors rarely tell you a link is dead or a form failed, they just leave, so you are usually the last to know, which makes a deliberate check for broken things the only way to find what is quietly turning people away.
variables: ANY RECENT CHANGES, OR WRITE NOTHING SPECIFIC

title: Audit Your Forms and Contact Methods
promptText: Help me audit the forms and contact methods on my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My forms and contact options are [LIST THEM, E.G. CONTACT FORM, BOOKING FORM, EMAIL LINK], and my platform is [YOUR PLATFORM]. Give me a checklist: actually submitting each form myself to confirm it works, checking the submission actually reaches me, confirming the confirmation message and any auto reply fire, and making sure my contact details are correct everywhere. Note that a broken contact form loses leads invisibly and I might not notice for months, so testing them myself is the only way to be sure. Give me the checklist and how to test each.
description: Audit forms by actually submitting them and confirming they reach you.
useCase: Use this because a broken form loses leads invisibly. You might not notice for months that submissions stopped reaching you, so actually submitting each form and confirming it arrives is the only reliable check, and it is the single audit item most worth doing.
variables: LIST THEM, E.G. CONTACT FORM, BOOKING FORM, EMAIL LINK

title: Audit Your Content for What Is Stale
promptText: Help me audit my [BUSINESS TYPE] website content for what has gone stale. My pages are [LIST OR DESCRIBE THEM], and what has changed in my business is [WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW, E.G. SERVICES, PRICING, TEAM, POSITIONING]. Give me a checklist to find outdated content: old dates and years, services I no longer offer, prices that changed, mentions of people who left, dead references, and anything that no longer reflects reality. Note that content ages silently and a visitor finding outdated information wonders what else is wrong, so stale content quietly damages trust. Give me the checklist and where stale content usually hides.
description: Audit content for outdated dates, services, prices, and dead references.
useCase: Use this because content ages silently. A visitor who finds outdated information wonders what else on the site is wrong, so stale prices, dropped services, and old years quietly damage trust, and they hide in exactly the pages you stopped looking at long ago.
variables: WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW, E.G. SERVICES, PRICING, TEAM, POSITIONING

title: Audit Your SEO Basics
promptText: Help me audit the SEO basics across my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND YOUR PLATFORM], and my SEO knowledge is [HOW MUCH YOU KNOW]. Give me a plain checklist covering the fundamentals: whether pages have titles and descriptions, whether headings are used properly, whether images have alt text, whether the site is indexed by search engines at all, and whether anything is accidentally blocking search engines. Flag the one or two things that would be genuinely serious if wrong. Note that most small sites have a couple of basic SEO problems rather than needing a deep technical audit. Give me the checklist.
description: Audit SEO fundamentals with a plain checklist, flagging the serious ones.
useCase: Use this to cover SEO fundamentals without a deep technical audit. Most small sites have a couple of basic problems rather than complex ones, and flagging the genuinely serious issues like accidentally blocking search engines tells you where an easy oversight could be quietly hiding your whole site.

title: Check Whether Search Engines Can Find You
promptText: Help me check whether search engines can actually find and index my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND YOUR PLATFORM], and my situation is [E.G. NEW SITE, NOT SHOWING UP, RECENTLY REBUILT, OR JUST CHECKING]. Help me check the things that could make my site invisible to search: whether it is being indexed at all, whether a setting is accidentally blocking search engines, whether a leftover setting from building the site is still live, and how to confirm. Note that a single wrong setting can hide an entire site from search, and this is the first thing to rule out when a site gets no search traffic. Give me what to check and how.
description: Check whether a wrong setting is hiding your whole site from search.
useCase: Use this first when a site gets no search traffic. A single leftover setting from when the site was built can hide it entirely from search engines, so ruling that out before anything else saves you optimizing content on a site search engines were never allowed to see.
variables: E.G. NEW SITE, NOT SHOWING UP, RECENTLY REBUILT, OR JUST CHECKING

title: Audit Whether Your Site Is Easy to Use
promptText: Help me audit whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] website is actually easy to use. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND ITS MAIN PAGES], and what I want a visitor to do is [THE MAIN GOAL]. Give me a checklist to assess usability as a first time visitor would: whether it is obvious what I do, whether navigation makes sense, whether the path to the main action is clear, whether anything confuses or frustrates, and where a visitor might get stuck. Note that I know my site too well to see its confusions, so I should test this by watching someone unfamiliar try to use it if I can. Give me the checklist and what to watch for.
description: Audit usability from a first time visitor's perspective, not your own.
useCase: Use this because you know your own site too well to see its confusions. A checklist assessing whether a stranger could tell what you do and find the main action surfaces the friction you are blind to, and watching an unfamiliar person try to use it reveals even more.
variables: DESCRIBE IT AND ITS MAIN PAGES

title: Audit the Path to Your Main Action
promptText: Help me audit the path a visitor takes to my main action on my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. The action I want is [WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO], and the steps to get there are [DESCRIBE THE PATH, FROM LANDING TO COMPLETING THE ACTION]. Walk through the path as a visitor: where the next step is unclear, where friction or doubt creeps in, how many clicks it takes, and where people likely drop off. Note that every extra step and unclear moment loses people, and the fix is often removing steps rather than adding persuasion, since a clear short path converts better than a clever long one. Give me the weak points and fixes.
description: Walk the path to your main action and find where visitors drop off.
useCase: Use this to find where your funnel leaks. Every extra step and unclear moment on the path to your main action loses people, and the fix is often removing steps rather than adding persuasion, since a short clear path converts better than a clever long one.
variables: WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO
DESCRIBE THE PATH, FROM LANDING TO COMPLETING THE ACTION

title: Audit Your Calls to Action
promptText: Help me audit the calls to action across my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My main pages and what I want visitors to do on each are [LIST PAGES AND THEIR INTENDED ACTION]. Give me a checklist: whether every important page has a clear next step, whether the calls to action are obvious rather than buried, whether pages have too many competing actions, and whether any important page leaves the visitor with nowhere to go. Note that a page with no clear next step is a dead end where the visitor leaves, and a page with five competing actions is one where they choose none. Give me what to check and fix.
description: Audit calls to action so every page has one clear next step.
useCase: Use this to find pages that dead end or overwhelm. A page with no clear next step is where a visitor leaves and a page with five competing actions is where they choose none, so checking that every important page offers one obvious next step is a quiet conversion win.
variables: LIST PAGES AND THEIR INTENDED ACTION

title: Audit Whether Your Message Is Clear
promptText: Help me audit whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] website makes clear what I do. Here is my homepage and key copy: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT]. Read it as a first time visitor who knows nothing about me: tell me whether it is instantly clear what I offer and who it is for, where jargon or vagueness lost you, and whether I lead with what I do or bury it under a clever tagline. Be blunt. Note that the most common website problem is that the visitor cannot tell what the business does within a few seconds, and no amount of design fixes a message that is not clear. Give me an honest read and what to fix.
description: Audit whether a first time visitor can tell what you do within seconds.
useCase: Use this on the most common website problem. Visitors who cannot tell what you do within a few seconds leave, and no amount of design fixes an unclear message, so a blunt read on whether your homepage leads with what you offer or buries it under a clever tagline is worth having.

title: Audit Your Images
promptText: Help me audit the images across my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My site uses [DESCRIBE YOUR IMAGES, E.G. STOCK PHOTOS, REAL PHOTOS, GRAPHICS], and my platform is [YOUR PLATFORM]. Give me a checklist: whether images are slowing the site with oversized files, whether they have alt text, whether generic stock photos are doing any work or just filling space, and whether the images actually help visitors understand or trust me. Note that huge image files are one of the most common self fixable speed problems, and a generic stock photo of a handshake adds nothing a visitor cares about. Give me the checklist and what to fix.
description: Audit images for oversized files, missing alt text, and useless stock photos.
useCase: Use this to catch a common speed and trust issue at once. Huge image files are one of the most self fixable speed problems, and a generic stock handshake photo adds nothing a visitor cares about, so an image audit often finds both easy speed wins and filler worth cutting.
variables: DESCRIBE YOUR IMAGES, E.G. STOCK PHOTOS, REAL PHOTOS, GRAPHICS

title: Audit Your Trust Signals
promptText: Help me audit the trust signals on my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My site currently has [WHAT YOU HAVE, E.G. TESTIMONIALS, CONTACT INFO, ABOUT PAGE, POLICIES], and my visitors are [WHO THEY ARE AND WHAT THEY WORRY ABOUT]. Give me a checklist: whether a stranger has reason to trust me, whether basic trust signals like real contact details and an about page are present, whether my proof is visible or hidden, and what a cautious visitor would look for and not find. Note that a visitor who cannot find a reason to trust me leaves, and missing basics like a real address or a way to reach a human quietly cost sales. Give me what to check and add.
description: Audit whether a cautious stranger has reason to trust your site.
useCase: Use this to see your site through a cautious visitor's eyes. Someone who cannot find a reason to trust you leaves, and missing basics like real contact details or an about page quietly cost sales, so checking what a careful visitor looks for and does not find is worth doing.
variables: WHAT YOU HAVE, E.G. TESTIMONIALS, CONTACT INFO, ABOUT PAGE, POLICIES
WHO THEY ARE AND WHAT THEY WORRY ABOUT

title: Check Your Legal and Policy Pages
promptText: Help me check whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] website has the legal and policy pages it should. My site does [WHAT IT DOES, E.G. COLLECTS EMAILS, SELLS PRODUCTS, RUNS ADS], my location is [WHERE YOU AND YOUR CUSTOMERS ARE], and what I have now is [WHAT POLICY PAGES EXIST, OR WRITE NONE]. Help me understand which basic pages a site like mine typically needs and why, such as a privacy policy or terms, and where they should be linked. Note that I am not a lawyer and neither are you, so this is a general checklist of what sites like mine usually have, not legal advice, and anything specific to my situation needs a professional. Give me the checklist with that caveat clear.
description: Check which basic legal and policy pages a site like yours usually has.
useCase: Use this to spot obviously missing policy pages. A general checklist of what sites like yours typically have catches gaps like a missing privacy policy, while being clear this is not legal advice, since anything specific to your jurisdiction and situation genuinely needs a professional rather than a checklist.
variables: WHAT IT DOES, E.G. COLLECTS EMAILS, SELLS PRODUCTS, RUNS ADS
WHERE YOU AND YOUR CUSTOMERS ARE
WHAT POLICY PAGES EXIST, OR WRITE NONE

title: Check Whether You Can Measure Anything
promptText: Help me check whether I can actually measure what happens on my [BUSINESS TYPE] website. My setup is [WHAT ANALYTICS OR TRACKING YOU HAVE, OR WRITE NONE OR NOT SURE], and what I want to know is [WHAT YOU WISH YOU KNEW, E.G. WHERE VISITORS COME FROM, WHAT THEY DO]. Help me check: whether tracking is installed and actually working, whether it is capturing the things that matter, whether my own visits are skewing the numbers, and what basic things I should be able to see but cannot. Note that flying blind means I cannot tell what is working, and that broken or missing tracking is common and easy to overlook. Give me what to check.
description: Check whether analytics are installed, working, and capturing what matters.
useCase: Use this before trusting or lamenting your numbers. Broken or missing tracking is common and easy to overlook, and flying blind means you cannot tell what works, so confirming analytics are installed, functioning, and not skewed by your own visits is worth doing early.
variables: WHAT ANALYTICS OR TRACKING YOU HAVE, OR WRITE NONE OR NOT SURE
WHAT YOU WISH YOU KNEW, E.G. WHERE VISITORS COME FROM, WHAT THEY DO

title: Audit Your Site Against Competitors
promptText: Help me audit my [BUSINESS TYPE] website against my competitors. My site is [DESCRIBE IT], my competitors are [WHO THEY ARE AND THEIR SITES], and what I want to learn is [YOUR GOAL]. Help me compare honestly: what their sites do that mine does not, where mine is actually better, what a customer comparing us would notice, and what is worth copying versus what is just different. Note that the goal is to learn from them rather than copy them, and that a competitor doing something does not make it right, since they may be making the same mistakes I am. Give me the comparison and what to act on.
description: Audit your site against competitors to learn rather than blindly copy.
useCase: Use this to learn from competitors without copying their mistakes. Comparing what a customer choosing between you would notice is useful, while remembering that a competitor doing something does not make it right keeps you from copying choices they may regret as much as you would.
variables: WHO THEY ARE AND THEIR SITES

title: Set Up a Recurring Audit Routine
promptText: Help me set up a simple recurring audit routine for my [BUSINESS TYPE] website so it does not rot. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND YOUR PLATFORM], and how often I realistically look at it is [BE HONEST]. Help me build a light routine: what to check weekly, monthly, and a few times a year, kept small enough that I actually do it. Note that a big audit once a year misses problems that appear and cost me for months, while a five minute monthly check catches most things early, and a routine only works if it is small enough not to get skipped. Give me a recurring check schedule.
description: Set up a light recurring audit routine small enough that you keep doing it.
useCase: Use this so your site does not quietly rot between big audits. A five minute monthly check catches most problems early, where a once a year audit misses issues that appear and cost you for months, and the routine only works if it stays small enough that you never skip it.

title: Get a Quick Audit Checklist
promptText: I need a quick website audit checklist. My site is [DESCRIBE IT AND YOUR PLATFORM], and my main concern is [WHAT WORRIES YOU, OR WRITE GENERAL CHECK]. Give me a short practical checklist of the most important things to check, the kind a non technical owner can actually work through, ordered by what matters most. No long explanation, just the checklist. Give me the list.
description: Get a short, practical audit checklist ordered by what matters most.
useCase: Use this when you just want a checklist to work through now. A short practical list ordered by importance covers what most small sites need, and actually running through the top items today beats planning a thorough audit you keep postponing.
variables: WHAT WORRIES YOU, OR WRITE GENERAL CHECK

title: Generate Hooks for a Post
promptText: Help me write opening hooks for a social media post in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My post is about [WHAT THE POST COVERS], my audience is [WHO THEY ARE], and the platform is [WHERE IT IS GOING]. Write several different hook options for the first line: some that open with a specific claim, some with a question, some with tension, some with a surprising fact. Make each one earn the next line rather than being clickbait that the post cannot deliver on. Note that the hook has one job, to stop the scroll and buy the second line, and a hook that overpromises loses the trust of anyone who keeps reading. Give me the options and mark the strongest.
description: Generate several distinct opening hook options that stop the scroll honestly.
useCase: Use this when you have a post but not an opening. The hook has one job, to stop the scroll and earn the second line, and generating several angles lets you pick one that fits rather than defaulting to whatever came first, which is rarely the strongest.

title: Fix a Weak First Line
promptText: Help me fix the weak first line of my social media post in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my current opening: [PASTE YOUR FIRST LINE OR TWO], and the post is about [THE TOPIC]. Tell me honestly why it is not working: whether it starts with throat clearing, buries the interesting part, states something obvious, or gives no reason to read on. Then rewrite it several ways. Note that most posts hide their best line in the third sentence, and the fix is often just moving what is already there to the front rather than inventing something new. Give me the diagnosis and rewrites.
description: Diagnose and rewrite a weak first line, often by surfacing what is buried.
useCase: Use this when a post is not landing and you suspect the opening. Most posts hide their best line in the third sentence, so the fix is often moving what is already there to the front rather than inventing something new, and a blunt diagnosis shows you which.
variables: PASTE YOUR FIRST LINE OR TWO

title: Find a Fresh Angle for a Tired Topic
promptText: Help me find a fresh hook angle for a topic everyone in my [BUSINESS TYPE] posts about. My topic is [THE TOPIC], the usual take is [WHAT EVERYONE SAYS], and my real view or experience is [WHAT YOU ACTUALLY THINK OR HAVE SEEN]. Help me find an angle that stops the scroll because it is not the expected one: the honest contrarian take, the thing nobody admits, the specific story, or the myth worth puncturing. Note that the tenth identical post on a topic gets scrolled past, while an unexpected angle on the same topic earns attention, and honesty is usually more interesting than the safe take. Give me angle options.
description: Find an unexpected hook angle on a topic everyone already posts about.
useCase: Use this when your topic is saturated. The tenth identical take gets scrolled past while an unexpected angle on the same subject earns attention, and honesty is usually more interesting than the safe version, so finding the angle that is genuinely yours is what makes a tired topic land.
variables: WHAT YOU ACTUALLY THINK OR HAVE SEEN

title: Write the First Three Seconds of a Video
promptText: Help me write the first three seconds of a short video in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My video is about [WHAT IT COVERS], my audience is [WHO THEY ARE], and the platform is [WHERE IT GOES]. Write opening line options for what I say and show in the first moments, since that is what decides whether anyone watches the rest. Cover both what I say and what should be on screen. Note that on video the first three seconds carry the whole thing, and a slow intro like hey guys welcome back is where most viewers swipe away before the content even starts. Give me the opening options.
description: Write the opening seconds of a video, covering both what you say and show.
useCase: Use this for short video. The first three seconds decide whether anyone watches the rest, and a slow intro like hey guys welcome back is where most viewers swipe away before the content starts, so opening on the actual hook rather than a greeting is what holds them.

title: Open a Curiosity Gap Honestly
promptText: Help me open a curiosity gap in my hook without it being cheap clickbait, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My post delivers [WHAT THE POST ACTUALLY GIVES THEM], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me write a hook that creates a genuine gap the reader wants closed, where the post actually closes it. Show me the difference between honest curiosity and the you will not believe what happened next bait that people have learned to ignore. Note that a curiosity gap the post genuinely pays off builds trust, while one that leads to a letdown trains people to never click me again. Give me hook options and why they are honest.
description: Open a genuine curiosity gap the post actually pays off, not cheap bait.
useCase: Use this to intrigue without the bait people learned to ignore. A curiosity gap the post genuinely closes builds trust while one leading to a letdown trains people never to click you again, so the honest version that pays off is the only kind worth using.
variables: WHAT THE POST ACTUALLY GIVES THEM

title: Build a Contrarian Hook You Can Defend
promptText: Help me write a contrarian hook I can actually stand behind, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The common belief I disagree with is [THE BELIEF], my actual position is [WHAT YOU THINK INSTEAD], and my reasoning is [WHY YOU THINK IT]. Write hook options that challenge the common view in a way I can defend in the post, not just for shock. Note that a contrarian take I cannot back up gets me attention and then destroys my credibility when I cannot support it, so the hook must be a real position rather than a hot take I do not mean. Give me hooks I can genuinely defend.
description: Build a contrarian hook that reflects a real position you can defend.
useCase: Use this when you genuinely disagree with a common belief. A contrarian take you cannot back up gets attention and then destroys your credibility when the post fails to support it, so the hook must reflect a real position rather than a hot take you do not actually mean.

title: Open with a Story
promptText: Help me open a post with a story hook in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The story is [WHAT HAPPENED], the point it leads to is [THE LESSON OR TAKEAWAY], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me write an opening line that drops the reader into the middle of the story rather than winding up to it, creating enough tension that they want to know what happened. Note that a story hook works when it starts at the tense moment, not with once upon a time context that nobody stays for, and the setup can come after the reader is already hooked. Give me story opening options.
description: Open with a story hook that drops into the tense moment, not the windup.
useCase: Use this when a real story illustrates your point. A story hook works when it starts at the tense moment rather than the setup nobody stays for, so dropping the reader into the middle and filling in context afterward is what holds them long enough to reach the lesson.

title: Find the Buried Lede in Your Draft
promptText: Help me find the buried lede in my social post draft, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my draft: [PASTE IT]. Read it and tell me: what the single most interesting or surprising line in it is, wherever it currently sits, and whether that should become the hook. Then show me how it reads with that line moved to the front. Note that writers often warm up for several sentences before saying the interesting thing, and the best hook is frequently already in the draft, just in the wrong place. Give me the buried lede and a reordered version.
description: Find the most interesting line already in your draft and move it to the front.
useCase: Use this on any finished draft. Writers warm up for several sentences before saying the interesting thing, so the best hook is frequently already written, just sitting in the wrong place, and finding it is faster than inventing a new opening from nothing.

title: Open on an Emotion Your Audience Feels
promptText: Help me write a hook that opens on a feeling my audience actually has, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My audience is [WHO THEY ARE], the feeling relevant to my post is [THE FRUSTRATION, WORRY, OR DESIRE THEY HAVE], and my post is about [THE TOPIC]. Write hooks that name that feeling so precisely the reader thinks that is exactly me. Note that a hook naming a feeling someone recognizes stops them cold, but only if it is specific and true, since a vague or manufactured emotion reads as manipulation and gets ignored. Give me hooks that name the real feeling.
description: Open on a specific real feeling your audience recognizes as their own.
useCase: Use this to make someone feel seen in the first line. A hook naming a feeling so precisely the reader thinks that is exactly me stops them cold, but only when it is specific and true, since a vague or manufactured emotion reads as manipulation and gets scrolled past.
variables: THE FRUSTRATION, WORRY, OR DESIRE THEY HAVE

title: Hook Using Your Audience's Own Words
promptText: Help me write a hook using the exact words my audience uses, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My audience is [WHO THEY ARE], how they actually describe the problem or topic is [THEIR WORDS, FROM COMMENTS, EMAILS, OR CONVERSATIONS], and my post is about [THE TOPIC]. Help me write a hook in their language rather than my professional framing. Note that a hook in my industry terms slides past, while one in the reader's own words feels like it was written for them specifically, and the phrases people use in comments and DMs are the best source of these. Give me hooks in their language.
description: Write a hook in your audience's exact words rather than industry framing.
useCase: Use this when your hooks sound like your industry rather than your audience. A hook in professional terms slides past while one in the reader's own words feels written for them, and the phrases people use in your comments and messages are the richest source of that language.
variables: THEIR WORDS, FROM COMMENTS, EMAILS, OR CONVERSATIONS

title: Write a Hook for a List Post
promptText: Help me write the hook for a list post in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My list is [WHAT THE LIST CONTAINS], the number of items is [HOW MANY], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Write opening line options that make the list feel worth reading: promising a specific payoff, hinting at the most surprising item, or framing why this list beats the generic version. Note that a list hook like five tips for X is generic and ignored, while one promising the specific valuable thing inside earns the read, and teasing the best item works better than just naming the topic. Give me hook options for the list.
description: Write a list post hook that promises the specific payoff, not just the topic.
useCase: Use this for list content. A generic list hook like five tips for X gets ignored while one promising the specific valuable thing inside earns the read, so teasing the best item or the payoff works far better than merely naming the topic and a number.

title: Make a Vague Hook Specific
promptText: Help me make my vague hook specific, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my hook: [PASTE IT], and the specifics behind it are [THE REAL NUMBERS, DETAILS, OR FACTS]. Rewrite it with the specificity added: replacing words like a lot or quickly or many with the actual figure, and swapping generic claims for concrete ones. Note that a specific hook is more believable and more arresting than a vague one, since I grew my list is forgettable while I added four hundred subscribers in nine days stops the scroll. Give me the specific version.
description: Replace vague words in a hook with concrete numbers and details.
useCase: Use this when a hook feels flat and generic. A specific hook is more believable and more arresting than a vague one, since I grew my list is forgettable while a concrete figure and timeframe stops the scroll, and the specifics are usually already sitting in your draft unused.
variables: THE REAL NUMBERS, DETAILS, OR FACTS

title: Adapt a Hook to Each Platform
promptText: Help me adapt my hook for different platforms in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My core hook or post is [PASTE IT], and the platforms are [WHERE YOU ARE POSTING, E.G. LINKEDIN, INSTAGRAM, X, TIKTOK]. Help me adjust the hook for each: how much context each platform's audience needs, how the tone shifts, how long the opening can be before it cuts off, and what works on one platform but flops on another. Note that the same hook rarely lands identically everywhere, since a LinkedIn audience and a TikTok audience want different openings, and pasting one hook across all platforms wastes the ones it does not fit. Give me a version per platform.
description: Adapt one hook to fit the different audiences and formats of each platform.
useCase: Use this when posting across platforms. The same hook rarely lands identically everywhere, since a LinkedIn audience and a TikTok audience want different openings, so adapting tone, length, and context per platform beats pasting one version everywhere and wondering why it only worked in one place.
variables: WHERE YOU ARE POSTING, E.G. LINKEDIN, INSTAGRAM, X, TIKTOK

title: Fit a Hook Before the Cutoff
promptText: Help me fit my hook into the space before the see more cutoff, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My hook is [PASTE IT], and the platform is [WHERE IT GOES, SO THE CUTOFF LENGTH IS KNOWN]. Trim it so the compelling part lands before the reader has to tap see more, since anything after the cutoff is invisible to someone deciding whether to expand. Keep what makes it work and cut what does not earn its place in that first visible window. Note that the hook only counts if it is visible before the fold, and a great line sitting just past the cutoff might as well not exist. Give me the trimmed hook.
description: Trim a hook so its compelling part lands before the see more cutoff.
useCase: Use this when your best line sits past the fold. The hook only counts if it is visible before the see more cutoff, since a great line just past it might as well not exist, so trimming to land the compelling part in the first visible window is what makes it work at all.
variables: WHERE IT GOES, SO THE CUTOFF LENGTH IS KNOWN

title: Check a Hook Against What You Deliver
promptText: Help me check whether my hook overpromises what my post delivers, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My hook is [PASTE IT], and what the post actually gives the reader is [WHAT IT DELIVERS]. Check honestly: whether the hook writes a cheque the post cannot cash, whether someone drawn in by the hook would feel let down, and whether it is exciting because it is true or because it is exaggerated. Then fix it if it overreaches. Note that a hook that overpromises might win one scroll stop and lose the follow, since people remember being baited and stop trusting my posts. Give me an honest read and a fix.
description: Check whether a hook promises more than the post actually delivers.
useCase: Use this before posting a hook that feels too good. A hook that overpromises might win one scroll stop and lose the follow, since people remember being baited and stop trusting your posts, so checking that the excitement comes from truth rather than exaggeration protects the relationship.

title: Open with a Question That Works
promptText: Help me write a question hook that actually works, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My topic is [THE TOPIC], my audience is [WHO THEY ARE], and what I want them to feel is [THE REACTION]. Write question hook options that make the reader answer in their head and want to know more, not the lazy kind. Note that a weak question hook like are you struggling with X gets ignored because everyone uses it and the answer is obvious, while a sharp specific question the reader has actually asked themselves stops them. Give me question hooks and flag any that are too generic to work.
description: Write a specific question hook the reader has actually asked themselves.
useCase: Use this when reaching for a question opener. The lazy kind like are you struggling with X gets ignored because everyone uses it and the answer is obvious, while a sharp question the reader has genuinely asked themselves stops them, so the specificity is what separates the two.

title: Cut the Cliches from Your Hooks
promptText: Help me cut the tired cliches from my hook, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my hook: [PASTE IT]. Flag the overused hook formulas people now scroll straight past, such as unpopular opinion, let that sink in, here is why, and the like, and rewrite the hook without them. Note that a formula that once worked stops working once everyone copies it, and openers that felt clever a year ago now signal generic content and get ignored. Tell me if my hook is fine as is rather than inventing a problem. Give me a cliche free version.
description: Cut worn out hook formulas your audience now scrolls straight past.
