description: Catch small formatting tells that make a business look like it does not know the platform.
useCase: Use this to find the formatting slips that quietly undercut you. Small tells like another app's watermark, a link in bio reference where there is no bio, or cropped text signal that someone does not know the platform, and fixing them costs almost nothing while noticeably raising how polished you look.

title: Format a Post for How Each Feed Sorts
promptText: Help me shape a post for how each platform decides what to show for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My post is about [WHAT THE POST IS], my platforms are [LIST YOUR PLATFORMS], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. For each platform tell me what the feed tends to reward, early engagement, watch time, saves, comments, or freshness, and how to shape the post to give that platform the signal it favors. Note that a chronological feed and a ranked feed reward completely different things, so the same post shaped the same way leans into one platform's strengths while working against another's, and knowing what each feed favors lets me shape for it. Give me the per platform shaping.
description: Shape a post around the signal each platform's feed actually rewards.
useCase: Use this when a post does well on one platform and vanishes on another. A chronological feed and a ranked feed reward different things, from watch time to saves to freshness, so shaping the post to give each feed the signal it favors matters as much as the content itself.

title: Build a Simple Formatting Cheat Sheet
promptText: Help me build a simple formatting cheat sheet for the platforms I use so I stop relearning each one every time for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My platforms are [LIST YOUR PLATFORMS], and the kind of content I usually post is [WHAT YOU POST]. Pull it into one short reference: per platform, the ideal length, hashtag norm, link handling, first line rule, and any format quirk to remember. Note that keeping the rules in my head means I re decide the same things every post and forget details on the platforms I use less, so a one page reference I can glance at makes formatting fast and consistent instead of a guess each time. Give me the cheat sheet.
description: Turn per platform formatting rules into one short reference you reuse.
useCase: Use this once so you stop relearning each platform every post. Keeping the rules in your head means re deciding the same things each time and forgetting details on platforms you use less, so a one page reference on length, tags, links, and quirks makes formatting fast and consistent.

title: Write Your Founder Origin Story
promptText: Help me write the origin story of my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Why I started it is [WHAT LED YOU TO IT], the moment or problem that pushed me to begin was [THE TURNING POINT], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Shape it into a short honest story that a customer would find believable and human, not a polished myth. Note that people connect with a real reason someone started, so the specific true details matter more than sounding impressive, and a story that quietly inflates the struggle to seem more heroic tends to ring false to the exact people I want to reach. Give me the origin story.
description: Turn why you started into a short, honest founder origin story.
useCase: Use this when you need the story behind why your business exists. People connect with a real reason someone started, so the specific true details land harder than a polished myth, and an honest origin gives customers a human reason to care that a list of services never will.

title: Define Why Your Business Exists
promptText: Help me put into words why my [BUSINESS TYPE] exists beyond making money. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], who it helps is [WHO THEY ARE], and the difference I want to make for them is [THE CHANGE YOU WANT TO CREATE]. Give me a clear why statement I could stand behind, plus a short explanation of it. Note that a why only helps if it is true and specific to me, since a generic mission about empowering everyone says nothing and customers see through it, so the useful version names a real belief I actually hold rather than borrowing one that sounds good. Give me the why statement.
description: Put into words the real reason your business exists beyond profit.
useCase: Use this when your business feels like a list of services with no center. A why only helps if it is true and specific to you, since a generic empower everyone mission says nothing, so naming a real belief you hold gives your brand a center customers can actually connect to.
variables: THE CHANGE YOU WANT TO CREATE

title: Write Your About Page Story
promptText: Help me write the story for my About page for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My background is [YOUR RELEVANT BACKGROUND], why I do this work is [YOUR REASON], and who I help is [WHO THEY ARE]. Write it so it is about the reader as much as me, connecting my story to why it matters for them, rather than a resume of everything I have ever done. Note that the About page is one of the most visited pages on a small site, and visitors read it to decide whether to trust me, so a story that quickly shows who I help and why beats a long timeline of my career that answers a question nobody asked. Give me the About page story.
description: Write an About page story that connects your background to the reader.
useCase: Use this when your About page reads like a resume. It is one of the most visited pages on a small site and people read it to decide whether to trust you, so a story that ties who you are to why it matters for them beats a career timeline that answers a question nobody asked.

title: Get a Quick Brand Story Draft
promptText: I need a quick brand story draft to work from. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], why I started is [SHORT REASON], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me a short honest paragraph telling my story that I can edit, no theory or long explanation, just the draft. Give me the paragraph.
description: Get a short editable brand story paragraph to start from.
useCase: Use this when a blank page is the problem. A short honest draft covering why you started and who you help gives you something concrete to react to and fix, and editing a rough paragraph is far faster than writing your story from nothing.

title: Make the Customer the Hero
promptText: Help me reframe my brand story so the customer is the hero and my [BUSINESS TYPE] is the guide, not the star. My current story is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the problem they face is [THEIR STRUGGLE]. Rewrite it so their journey and their win are at the center, with my business as the thing that helps them get there. Note that customers care about their own story far more than mine, so a brand story that makes them the hero and me the helpful guide connects better than one where I am the genius they should admire, and this shift usually makes the story more persuasive without making it less true. Give me the reframed story.
description: Reframe your story so the customer is the hero and you are the guide.
useCase: Use this when your story is all about you. Customers care about their own story far more than yours, so casting them as the hero and your business as the guide that helps them win connects better than positioning yourself as the genius, and the shift makes the story more persuasive while staying true.

title: Write a Short Elevator Version
promptText: Help me boil my brand story down to a few sentences I could say out loud for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The longer version is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE YOUR STORY], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me a short spoken version I could use when someone asks what I do, that captures the heart of the story without sounding rehearsed. Note that most of the time I will only get a sentence or two before someone decides if they are interested, so the short version is the one that actually gets used, and it should sound like something a real person would say rather than a memorized tagline. Give me the elevator version.
description: Boil your brand story down to a few natural spoken sentences.
useCase: Use this for when someone asks what you do. Most of the time you get only a sentence or two before someone decides if they are interested, so the short version is the one that gets used, and it should sound like a real person talking rather than a memorized pitch.

title: Write an Honest Mission Statement
promptText: Help me write a mission statement for my [BUSINESS TYPE] that does not sound like every other one. What I actually do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], who I do it for is [WHO THEY ARE], and what I genuinely care about in the work is [WHAT MATTERS TO YOU]. Give me a mission statement that is specific and true to my business, and steer me away from the empty buzzwords that make these all sound identical. Note that most mission statements are interchangeable because they reach for grand vague words, so the honest useful version says something specific enough that a competitor could not copy it word for word, and specific beats lofty here. Give me the mission statement.
description: Write a specific, honest mission statement free of interchangeable buzzwords.
useCase: Use this when you want a mission statement that means something. Most are interchangeable because they reach for grand vague words, so the useful version is specific enough that a competitor could not copy it, and specific and true beats lofty and empty every time.

title: Turn Your Values Into a Story
promptText: Help me show my business values through a story rather than just listing them for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The values I care about are [YOUR VALUES], and a real example of one of them in action was [A TIME YOU LIVED A VALUE]. Turn that into a short story that demonstrates the value instead of just claiming it. Note that anyone can list values like honesty and quality and they mean nothing on their own, while a specific story of a time I actually chose the harder honest option proves the value in a way a list never can, so showing beats telling here. Give me the story.
description: Demonstrate a value through a real story instead of listing it.
useCase: Use this when your values page is just words. Anyone can list honesty and quality and they mean nothing alone, while a specific story of a time you actually lived a value proves it in a way a list cannot, so showing beats telling when it comes to what you stand for.
variables: A TIME YOU LIVED A VALUE

title: Find the Emotional Core of Your Story
promptText: Help me find the emotional heart of my brand story for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My story so far is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Point me to the one feeling or truth at the center of it that people would actually connect with, and suggest how to bring that forward instead of burying it under facts. Note that a story full of dates and facts but no feeling does not stick, and often the most connecting part is the bit I am tempted to leave out because it feels too personal, so finding the real emotional core matters more than adding more detail. Give me the core and how to lead with it.
description: Find the one feeling at the center of your story and lead with it.
useCase: Use this when your story is accurate but flat. A story full of facts and no feeling does not stick, and often the most connecting part is the bit you want to leave out because it feels too personal, so finding the emotional core matters more than adding detail.

title: Tell the Story Behind Your Name
promptText: Help me tell the story behind my business name for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My name is [YOUR BUSINESS NAME], and where it came from is [THE REAL REASON OR ORIGIN]. Turn it into a short story I could share on my About page or in a post. If the real origin is not that interesting, tell me honestly and help me find a genuine angle rather than inventing a fake meaning. Note that a real story behind a name adds a little charm and memorability, but a made up profound meaning tends to feel forced, so an honest small origin beats a grand invented one, and if the name has no story it is fine to just say so. Give me the story or the honest verdict.
description: Turn the real origin of your business name into a short shareable story.
useCase: Use this when people ask about your name or you want a small story for your About page. A real origin adds charm and memorability, but an invented profound meaning feels forced, so an honest small story beats a grand fake one, and it is fine if the name simply has no story to tell.

title: Write a Vision of Where You Are Headed
promptText: Help me write a short vision of where my [BUSINESS TYPE] is headed that feels genuine rather than grandiose. What I want the business to become is [YOUR REAL AMBITION], who it will keep serving is [WHO THEY ARE], and what I do not want it to turn into is [WHAT TO AVOID]. Give me a vision statement grounded in what I actually want. Note that a vision of dominating the industry or changing the world rings hollow for most small businesses, while an honest picture of the kind of business I want to build and the difference it makes for a real group of people is both more believable and more useful to guide decisions. Give me the vision.
description: Write a grounded vision of where your business is headed, not a grandiose one.
useCase: Use this when you want a sense of direction without empty grandeur. A vision of dominating the industry rings hollow for a small business, while an honest picture of what you actually want to build and who it serves is more believable and more useful for guiding real decisions.

title: Decide How Much of Yourself to Share
promptText: Help me decide how personal to get in my brand story for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The personal part of my story is [WHAT YOU MIGHT SHARE], who my audience is [WHO THEY ARE], and how comfortable I am being open is [BE HONEST]. Help me find the line between a story that feels genuine and real versus oversharing something I will regret putting out publicly. Note that a bit of honest vulnerability makes a brand story connect, but there is a real limit, and something shared for connection can later feel exposing or attract the wrong attention, so the goal is the true detail that builds trust without handing over more of my private life than I actually want public. Give me where the line is for my situation.
description: Find the line between genuine vulnerability and oversharing in your story.
useCase: Use this when deciding how personal your brand story should get. A bit of honest vulnerability makes a story connect, but there is a real limit, and something shared for connection can later feel exposing, so this helps you find the true detail that builds trust without handing over more than you want public.

title: Stand Out Through Your Story
promptText: Help me use my story to stand apart from competitors who offer the same thing for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], my competitors are [WHO OR WHAT THEY ARE], and what is genuinely different about my path or approach is [WHAT SETS YOU APART]. Show me how to lead with the part of my story that competitors cannot copy, since they cannot have my exact history. Note that when the product is similar the story is often the real differentiator, because anyone can match a feature but no one else has my specific background and reasons, so leaning on what is true and unrepeatable about me is more durable than claiming to be better at the same things. Give me how to differentiate through story.
description: Use the unrepeatable parts of your story to stand apart from similar competitors.
useCase: Use this when competitors offer basically the same thing. When products are similar the story is often the real differentiator, because anyone can match a feature but no one has your exact history, so leaning on what is true and unrepeatable about you is more durable than claiming to be better at the same things.

title: Turn Your Story Into Ongoing Content
promptText: Help me break my brand story into smaller pieces I can share as content over time for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My full story is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], my platform is [WHERE YOU POST], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Pull out the moments, lessons, and turning points that could each become their own post, so my story becomes a well I draw from rather than a single About page nobody revisits. Note that a brand story tucked on an About page gets read once at most, while sharing pieces of it across my content is how people actually absorb who I am over time, so the story works hardest when it is spread out rather than filed away. Give me the content pieces.
description: Break your brand story into moments you can share as content over time.
useCase: Use this so your story does more than sit on an About page. A story filed away gets read once at most, while sharing its moments and turning points across your content is how people actually absorb who you are over time, turning one story into a well of posts.

title: Fix a Story That Feels Boring
promptText: Help me fix my brand story, which feels flat and forgettable, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my current story: [PASTE IT], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Tell me honestly why it is not landing, whether it is too generic, buries the interesting part, sounds like everyone else, or has no tension, then show me how to fix it. Note that most boring brand stories are not boring lives, they just lead with the dull parts and skip the real moment of doubt or change, so the fix is usually reordering and cutting rather than inventing drama, and I should not fabricate a struggle that did not happen. Give me the diagnosis and the fix.
description: Diagnose why a brand story falls flat and fix it without inventing drama.
useCase: Use this when your story is true but forgettable. Most boring brand stories are not boring lives, they just lead with the dull parts and skip the real moment of change, so the fix is usually reordering and cutting rather than adding fake drama you did not live.

title: Tell a Story Without a Dramatic Origin
promptText: Help me write a brand story when I do not have a dramatic origin for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The honest truth is [WHY YOU REALLY STARTED, EVEN IF ORDINARY], what I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me build a genuine story from ordinary beginnings rather than inventing a rags to riches tale. Note that plenty of good businesses started simply, because someone was good at something and decided to do it for themselves, and that plain truth told with a little care connects better than a fabricated dramatic backstory that I would then have to keep up, so honest and ordinary beats invented and grand. Give me the story.
description: Build a genuine brand story from ordinary beginnings, no drama required.
useCase: Use this when you feel your start was too plain for a story. Plenty of good businesses began simply, because someone was good at something and went out on their own, and that plain truth told with care connects better than a fabricated dramatic backstory you would have to keep up.
variables: WHY YOU REALLY STARTED, EVEN IF ORDINARY

title: Tell Your Story as a Solo or Small Team
promptText: Help me tell my brand story honestly about being a solo operator or small team for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The reality is [SOLO, OR HOW SMALL YOUR TEAM IS], what I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me frame my size as a genuine strength where it is one, without pretending to be a bigger company than I am. Note that many customers actively prefer working with the actual person or a small team and value the direct access and care, so being honest about my size and leaning into what that makes possible beats using we to imply a large company that a customer later feels misled by. Give me the story.
description: Frame being solo or a small team honestly, as a strength where it is one.
useCase: Use this when you feel pressure to seem bigger than you are. Many customers prefer working with the actual person and value the direct access, so being honest about your size and leaning into what it makes possible beats using we to imply a large company that a customer later feels misled by.
variables: SOLO, OR HOW SMALL YOUR TEAM IS

title: Check If Your Story Sounds True
promptText: Help me check whether my brand story sounds authentic or like marketing for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my story: [PASTE IT], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Point out any lines that sound like hollow marketing speak, exaggeration, or claims a skeptical reader would not believe, and suggest more honest wording. Note that people have a strong radar for brand stories that feel fake, and one inflated line can make them doubt the whole thing, so a story that stays believable throughout builds more trust than one with a few impressive but shaky claims, and cutting the parts that sound too good is usually the right move. Give me what to fix.
description: Check your story for lines that read as fake or exaggerated and fix them.
useCase: Use this before publishing your story. People have a strong radar for brand stories that feel fake, and one inflated line can make them doubt the whole thing, so catching the parts that sound too good and making them honest builds more trust than a few impressive but shaky claims.

title: Connect Your Story to What You Sell
promptText: Help me connect my brand story to what I actually sell for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My story is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], what I sell is [YOUR OFFER], and who buys it is [WHO THEY ARE]. Show me how to draw a clear line from my story to why my product exists and why I am the right person to provide it, so the story earns its place rather than being a nice tale that goes nowhere. Note that a brand story only pays off when it makes the offer make more sense, since a lovely story disconnected from what I sell is just entertainment, so the version that helps the business ties my why directly to why someone should buy from me. Give me the connection.
description: Draw a clear line from your story to why your offer exists and why you.
useCase: Use this when your story feels nice but disconnected from sales. A brand story only pays off when it makes the offer make more sense, since a lovely story that goes nowhere is just entertainment, so tying your why directly to why someone should buy from you is what makes the story work for the business.

title: Refresh a Story That No Longer Fits
promptText: Help me update a brand story that no longer matches where my [BUSINESS TYPE] is now. My old story was [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], what has changed since is [WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW], and who I serve today is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me refresh it so it reflects the business as it actually is, while keeping the true through line that has not changed. Note that businesses evolve and a story written at the start can quietly become inaccurate, which customers sense, but the fix is not throwing out the whole story, it is updating what changed while keeping the genuine core that still holds, so honesty about the evolution beats clinging to an outdated origin. Give me the refreshed story.
description: Update a brand story to match where the business is now, keeping the true core.
useCase: Use this when your story describes a business you no longer are. A story written at the start can quietly become inaccurate as you evolve, and customers sense it, but the fix is updating what changed while keeping the genuine core, not throwing out the whole thing.

title: Match Your Story to Your Brand Voice
promptText: Help me tell my brand story in a voice that matches the rest of my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My story is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], the tone I use elsewhere is [YOUR USUAL TONE, E.G. WARM, PLAYFUL, STRAIGHT TALKING], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Rewrite the story so it sounds like the same business a customer meets everywhere else, not a formal press release stapled onto a casual brand. Note that a story told in a stiff corporate voice on an otherwise warm and personal brand creates a jarring mismatch that makes the whole thing feel less genuine, so the story should sound like me, and matching the voice matters as much as the content of the story. Give me the story in my voice.
description: Rewrite your brand story so its voice matches the rest of your brand.
useCase: Use this when your story reads more formal than the rest of your brand. A stiff corporate voice on an otherwise warm personal brand creates a jarring mismatch that makes it feel less genuine, so the story should sound like the same business customers meet everywhere else.
variables: YOUR USUAL TONE, E.G. WARM, PLAYFUL, STRAIGHT TALKING

title: Build Your Core Value Proposition
promptText: Help me write the core value proposition for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], who it is for is [WHO THEY ARE], and the main result they get is [THE OUTCOME]. Give me a clear statement of what I offer, for whom, and why it is worth choosing, in plain language a customer would understand at a glance. Note that a value proposition is a promise about the result for the customer, not a description of my features, so the useful version leads with what they get rather than what I do, and it has to be specific enough to be believable rather than a vague claim to be the best. Give me the value proposition.
description: Write a clear core value proposition focused on the customer's result.
useCase: Use this when you cannot say in one line why someone should choose you. A value proposition is a promise about the customer's result, not a list of your features, so leading with what they get and staying specific enough to believe is what makes it land rather than a vague claim to be the best.

title: Turn Features Into Benefits
promptText: Help me turn the features of my [BUSINESS TYPE] into benefits customers actually care about. My features are [LIST WHAT YOU DO OR INCLUDE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. For each feature, tell me the real benefit behind it, the so what that matters to the customer, and flag any feature that has no meaningful benefit worth mentioning. Note that customers do not buy features, they buy what the feature does for them, so a list of specs leaves them to work out the value themselves while naming the benefit hands it to them, and a feature I cannot connect to a real benefit is probably not worth leading with. Give me the feature to benefit translation.
description: Translate your features into the benefits customers actually care about.
useCase: Use this when your marketing lists what you do but not why it matters. Customers do not buy features, they buy what the feature does for them, so naming the benefit behind each one hands them the value instead of leaving them to work it out, and a feature with no real benefit is not worth leading with.
variables: LIST WHAT YOU DO OR INCLUDE

title: Say What You Do in One Sentence
promptText: Help me say what my [BUSINESS TYPE] does in one clear sentence. What I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], who I help is [WHO THEY ARE], and the outcome is [THE RESULT]. Give me a few one sentence options that a stranger would immediately understand, without jargon or clever wordplay that hides the meaning. Note that if someone cannot tell what I do in one sentence they usually move on, so clarity beats cleverness here, and a plain sentence that lands beats a witty one that leaves people guessing what I actually sell. Give me the one sentence options.
description: Write a few plain one sentence explanations of what you do.
useCase: Use this when explaining your business takes a paragraph. If someone cannot tell what you do in one sentence they usually move on, so clarity beats cleverness, and a plain sentence that lands immediately beats a witty one that leaves people guessing what you actually sell.

title: Get a Quick Value Proposition Draft
promptText: I need a quick value proposition to work from. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the result they get is [THE OUTCOME]. Give me a short clear value proposition I can edit, plus one alternate version, no theory, just the drafts. Give me the two options.
description: Get two quick editable value proposition drafts to start from.
useCase: Use this when you just need something on the page to react to. Two short clear drafts covering what you do, for whom, and the result give you a concrete starting point, and sharpening a rough version is faster than writing your value proposition from scratch.

title: Get Specific About Who It Is For
promptText: Help me get specific about exactly who my [BUSINESS TYPE] is for in my value proposition. Right now I describe my customer as [YOUR CURRENT DESCRIPTION, MAYBE BROAD], what I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], and the people who most need it are [WHO GETS THE MOST VALUE]. Help me narrow the who so the value proposition speaks directly to the right person. Note that trying to appeal to everyone usually appeals to no one, because a message aimed at all small businesses feels generic to each, while naming a specific person makes that person feel it was written for them, so narrowing the who often makes the proposition stronger rather than smaller. Give me the sharper who and how it changes the proposition.
description: Narrow who your value proposition speaks to so it lands with the right person.
useCase: Use this when your value proposition tries to speak to everyone. A message aimed at all small businesses feels generic to each, while naming a specific person makes them feel it was written for them, so narrowing the who usually makes the proposition stronger rather than smaller.

title: Lead With the Outcome Customers Want
promptText: Help me rewrite my value proposition to lead with the outcome my customers actually want for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I do is [YOUR PROCESS OR SERVICE], and the deeper result the customer is really after is [WHAT THEY TRULY WANT]. Reframe the proposition around that end result rather than the process I use to deliver it. Note that customers care about the destination more than the vehicle, so leading with the outcome they want connects faster than explaining my method, though I still need to back the promise up, so the outcome should be one I can genuinely deliver rather than an inflated result. Give me the outcome led version.
description: Reframe your value proposition around the outcome, not your process.
useCase: Use this when your proposition explains your method instead of the result. Customers care about the destination more than the vehicle, so leading with the outcome they want connects faster than describing your process, as long as it is a result you can genuinely deliver.

title: Be Different, Not Just Better
promptText: Help me build a value proposition around being different rather than just claiming to be better for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], my competitors are [WHO OR WHAT THEY ARE], and what is genuinely different about my approach is [WHAT YOU DO DIFFERENTLY]. Help me lead with that real difference instead of a better or higher quality claim anyone could make. Note that everyone claims to be better and customers have learned to ignore it, while a specific difference gives them a concrete reason to choose me, so a true point of difference is more persuasive than a generic superiority claim, and if I cannot name a real difference that is worth knowing before writing the proposition. Give me the difference led proposition.
description: Build a value proposition on a real difference, not a better claim.
useCase: Use this when your proposition just says you are better. Everyone claims that and customers ignore it, while a specific difference gives a concrete reason to choose you, so leading with a true point of difference is more persuasive, and struggling to name one is worth knowing before you write.

title: Write a Value Proposition Headline
promptText: Help me write a headline for my homepage or landing page that carries my value proposition for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], who it is for is [WHO THEY ARE], and the main benefit is [THE BENEFIT]. Give me a few headline options that make the value clear in the few seconds a visitor spends before deciding to stay or leave, plus a supporting subhead for each. Note that the headline is often the only thing a visitor reads before deciding, so it has to communicate the value fast rather than be clever, and a clear headline with a specific benefit keeps people reading while a vague or cute one loses them. Give me the headline options.
description: Write homepage headline options that carry your value proposition fast.
useCase: Use this for the top of your homepage or landing page. The headline is often the only thing a visitor reads before deciding to stay, so it has to make the value clear fast, and a specific benefit keeps people reading while a vague or cute one loses them in seconds.

title: Cut the Jargon From Your Proposition
promptText: Help me cut the jargon and buzzwords from my value proposition for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is my current version: [PASTE IT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Point out the vague industry speak, the words that sound impressive but say nothing, and rewrite it in plain language a normal customer would use. Note that words like solutions, seamless, and cutting edge feel professional to write but wash over the reader without meaning, so plain concrete language communicates more than polished jargon, and if a phrase would sound odd said out loud to a customer it probably does not belong. Give me the plain language version.
description: Strip the buzzwords from your value proposition and make it plain.
useCase: Use this when your proposition sounds professional but says nothing. Words like solutions, seamless, and cutting edge feel impressive to write but wash over the reader, so plain concrete language communicates more, and a phrase that sounds odd said out loud to a customer probably does not belong.

title: Back Your Claim With Proof
promptText: Help me back up my value proposition with proof so it is believable for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My claim is [WHAT YOU PROMISE], and the evidence I actually have is [RESULTS, EXPERIENCE, GUARANTEES, TESTIMONIALS, OR HONESTLY LITTLE YET]. Show me how to support the promise with what I genuinely have, and if I am short on proof, how to make an honest claim I can back rather than one I cannot. Note that a bold promise with nothing behind it invites doubt, while a slightly smaller claim I can prove builds more trust, so matching the size of the claim to the proof I have is what keeps the proposition credible, and it is better to promise less and deliver than the reverse. Give me how to back the claim.
description: Support your value proposition with the proof you genuinely have.
useCase: Use this when your promise might sound too good to believe. A bold claim with nothing behind it invites doubt, while a slightly smaller one you can prove builds trust, so matching the size of the claim to your actual proof keeps the proposition credible, and promising less and delivering beats the reverse.
variables: RESULTS, EXPERIENCE, GUARANTEES, TESTIMONIALS, OR HONESTLY LITTLE YET

title: Match Your Proposition to a Real Pain Point
promptText: Help me anchor my value proposition to the real problem my customers have for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The problem they struggle with is [THEIR PAIN POINT], what I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], and how it helps is [HOW IT SOLVES THE PROBLEM]. Rewrite the proposition so it names the problem clearly and then presents my offer as the relief. Note that people feel their problem more sharply than they feel any solution, so leading with the pain they recognize pulls them in faster than opening with my offer, though I should name the problem honestly rather than exaggerating it into fear, since overstating the pain reads as manipulative. Give me the problem anchored proposition.
description: Anchor your value proposition to the real problem customers feel.
useCase: Use this when your proposition talks about your offer before the problem. People feel their problem more sharply than any solution, so naming the pain they recognize pulls them in faster than opening with what you sell, as long as you name it honestly rather than exaggerating it into fear.

title: Write Versions for Different Places
promptText: Help me write versions of my value proposition sized for different places for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My core proposition is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], and the places I need it are [WHERE, E.G. HOMEPAGE, SOCIAL BIO, ELEVATOR PITCH, EMAIL SIGNATURE]. Give me a version for each: a full one, a one line one, and a few word one, all saying the same thing at different lengths. Note that the same proposition has to work as a headline, a bio, and a spoken line, so having sized versions ready keeps the message consistent everywhere instead of me improvising a different description each time, and consistency across places is part of what makes a proposition stick. Give me the sized versions.
description: Create full, one line, and few word versions of your proposition.
useCase: Use this when you describe your business differently in every place. The same proposition has to work as a headline, a bio, and a spoken line, so having sized versions ready keeps the message consistent instead of improvising each time, and that consistency is part of what makes it stick.
variables: WHERE, E.G. HOMEPAGE, SOCIAL BIO, ELEVATOR PITCH, EMAIL SIGNATURE

title: Test If Your Proposition Is Clear
promptText: Help me test whether my value proposition is actually clear for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here it is: [PASTE IT]. Read it as a first time visitor who knows nothing about me and tell me honestly: can you tell what I do, who it is for, and why it matters, in a few seconds. Point out anything confusing, ambiguous, or that made you pause. Note that I am too close to my own business to judge my proposition, since what is obvious to me is often unclear to a stranger, so reading it cold as an outsider catches the gaps I cannot see, and if a newcomer has to work to understand it that is a problem worth fixing. Give me the honest first read.
description: Stress test your value proposition by reading it cold as a stranger.
useCase: Use this before you commit to a value proposition. You are too close to your business to judge it, and what is obvious to you is often unclear to a stranger, so a cold read as a first time visitor catches the gaps you cannot see, and any confusion a newcomer hits is worth fixing.

title: Adjust the Proposition for Your Buyer Type
promptText: Help me adjust my value proposition for the kind of buyer I sell to for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My buyer is [A BUSINESS OR A CONSUMER], what I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], and what they care about most in a decision is [THEIR MAIN CONCERN]. Shape the proposition to speak to how this type of buyer actually decides. Note that a business buyer often weighs return, risk, and time saved while a consumer often weighs how something makes them feel or look, so the same offer needs a different emphasis for each, and matching the proposition to what my specific buyer values beats a generic version that half fits both. Give me the adjusted proposition.
description: Shape your value proposition to how your specific buyer type decides.
useCase: Use this when you are not sure your proposition fits your buyer. A business buyer often weighs return, risk, and time saved while a consumer weighs how something feels, so the same offer needs a different emphasis for each, and matching to what your buyer values beats a version that half fits both.

title: Justify a Premium Price in Your Proposition
promptText: Help me build a value proposition that justifies charging more than cheaper competitors for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I offer is [WHAT YOU DO], why I cost more is [WHAT JUSTIFIES THE PRICE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me make the case for the value that supports my price without badmouthing cheaper options. Note that competing on being the cheapest is a race I usually cannot win, so the stronger move is making the higher value clear enough that the price feels fair, and this only works if the extra value is real, since a premium price with no substance behind it just loses the sale. Give me the value justified proposition.
description: Build a proposition that makes a higher price feel worth it.
useCase: Use this when you cost more than competitors and need to justify it. Competing on being cheapest is a race you usually cannot win, so making the higher value clear enough that the price feels fair is the stronger move, and it only works when the extra value is genuinely real.

title: Fix a Generic Value Proposition
promptText: Help me fix my value proposition, which sounds like every other business in my field, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here it is: [PASTE IT], my competitors are [WHO THEY ARE], and what is actually true and specific about me is [YOUR REAL SPECIFICS]. Tell me which parts are interchangeable filler and rebuild it around what only I can honestly say. Note that a good test is whether a competitor could put their name on my exact proposition, and if they could, it is not really mine, so the fix is trading generic claims for specific true ones, and specificity is usually what separates a proposition that works from one that blends in. Give me the sharpened version.
description: Rebuild a generic value proposition around what only you can say.
useCase: Use this when your proposition could belong to any competitor. A good test is whether a rival could put their name on it unchanged, and if they could it is not really yours, so trading generic claims for specific true ones is the fix, and that specificity is usually what separates a proposition that works.

title: Turn Your Proposition Into a Spoken Pitch
promptText: Help me turn my value proposition into something natural to say when someone asks what I do for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My written proposition is [PASTE IT], and the setting is [WHERE, E.G. NETWORKING, A PARTY, A NEW CLIENT CALL]. Give me a spoken version that sounds like a real person talking, not a memorized marketing line. Note that a proposition written for a page often sounds stiff or salesy said out loud, so the spoken version needs to feel like natural conversation while still landing the value, and something I can actually say comfortably beats a polished line I would feel awkward delivering. Give me the spoken version.
description: Turn your written proposition into a natural spoken answer.
useCase: Use this when your written proposition sounds stiff said aloud. A line written for a page often comes across as salesy in conversation, so the spoken version needs to feel natural while still landing the value, and something you can say comfortably beats a polished line you would feel awkward delivering.
variables: WHERE, E.G. NETWORKING, A PARTY, A NEW CLIENT CALL

title: Find the Value Proposition Across Offers
promptText: Help me find one clear value proposition that ties together the different things I offer for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The offers I have are [LIST WHAT YOU SELL], and who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE]. Help me find the common thread so I have one overarching proposition rather than a confusing list of unrelated services. Note that a business offering many things can leave customers unsure what it really does, so finding the through line that connects the offers gives people one clear idea to remember, and if the offers genuinely do not connect that is useful to know too, since it may point to a focus problem worth addressing. Give me the unifying proposition.
description: Find one value proposition that ties your different offers together.
useCase: Use this when you offer several things and the message feels scattered. A business offering many things can leave customers unsure what it really does, so finding the through line gives people one clear idea to remember, and offers that genuinely do not connect may point to a focus problem worth knowing about.

title: Frame the Before and After You Deliver
promptText: Help me frame my value proposition as the before and after my customer goes through for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Where the customer starts is [THEIR SITUATION BEFORE], where they end up after working with me is [THEIR SITUATION AFTER], and what I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER]. Turn that shift into a proposition that shows the transformation clearly. Note that the value of what I do is clearest in the gap between before and after, so showing that shift communicates worth better than describing my service in the abstract, though the after has to be an honest outcome I can deliver rather than a dream state, since an inflated after undermines trust. Give me the before and after proposition.
description: Frame your proposition as the honest before and after you deliver.
useCase: Use this when the worth of what you do is hard to convey. The value is clearest in the gap between where a customer starts and where they end up, so showing that shift communicates worth better than describing your service in the abstract, as long as the after is an honest outcome you can deliver.

title: Audit Your Current Value Proposition
promptText: Help me audit the value proposition I am currently using for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is what I have across my site and profiles: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Go through it and tell me what is working, what is vague, whether it leads with benefit or feature, whether it is specific to me, and the one or two changes that would improve it most. Note that most propositions are not broken so much as fuzzy, and small fixes like leading with the outcome or cutting one buzzword often do more than a full rewrite, so an honest audit that finds the highest value fixes beats starting over from a blank page. Give me the audit and the priority fixes.
description: Audit your existing value proposition and find the highest value fixes.
useCase: Use this when your proposition is fine but not sharp. Most are not broken so much as fuzzy, and small fixes like leading with the outcome or cutting a buzzword often do more than a rewrite, so an audit that finds the highest value changes beats starting over from a blank page.

title: Generate Tagline Options
promptText: Help me come up with tagline options for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], who I serve is [WHO THEY ARE], and the feeling or idea I want to leave people with is [THE IMPRESSION]. Give me a range of tagline options in different directions: some clear and descriptive, some benefit led, some with a little personality, each short enough to remember. Note that a tagline has to be short and stick, so a clear line people remember beats a clever one they do not understand, and it is worth generating many options because the first idea is rarely the best and the strong one often emerges a few tries in. Give me the options grouped by direction.
description: Generate a range of tagline options across clear, benefit led, and personality directions.
useCase: Use this when you need a tagline and want real choices. A tagline has to be short and stick, so generating many options across different directions beats settling on the first idea, since the first is rarely the best and the strong one usually emerges a few tries in.

title: Turn Your Value Proposition Into a Tagline
promptText: Help me distill my value proposition into a short tagline for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My value proposition is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Pull out the single most important idea and turn it into a few words that capture the heart of it. Note that a tagline cannot carry the whole proposition, it can only point at the one thing that matters most, so the job is choosing what to drop as much as what to keep, and a focused line about one clear benefit beats a crammed one trying to say everything at once. Give me the tagline options.
description: Distill your value proposition down to a short tagline built on one idea.
useCase: Use this when you have a value proposition but need a short line from it. A tagline cannot carry the whole proposition, only the one thing that matters most, so the job is choosing what to drop, and a focused line about one clear benefit beats a crammed one trying to say everything.

title: Get Quick Tagline Ideas
promptText: I need some quick tagline ideas to react to. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the vibe I want is [THE FEELING]. Give me a short list of tagline options, a mix of clear and characterful, no explanation, just the lines. Give me the list.
description: Get a quick list of tagline options to react to.
useCase: Use this when you want a fast batch of lines to spark something. A quick mix of clear and characterful options gives you material to react to, and seeing a range of directions at once often surfaces the angle worth developing faster than staring at a blank page.

title: Choose Between Clear and Clever
promptText: Help me decide between a clear tagline and a clever one for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My clear option is [THE STRAIGHTFORWARD LINE], my clever option is [THE WORDPLAY LINE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Weigh them honestly for my situation and tell me which serves me better. Note that clever wordplay is satisfying to land but often makes people work to get it, and a tagline that needs explaining has already failed, so for a business people do not know yet, clear usually wins, while a clever line only earns its place if the meaning lands instantly. Give me the honest call and why.
description: Weigh a clear tagline against a clever one and pick the right fit.
useCase: Use this when torn between a plain line and a witty one. Clever wordplay is satisfying but often makes people work to get it, and a tagline that needs explaining has failed, so for a business people do not know yet clear usually wins unless the clever meaning lands instantly.

title: Write a Benefit Led Tagline
promptText: Help me write a tagline built around the benefit my customer gets for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], and the main benefit is [THE RESULT THEY GET]. Give me several short tagline options that put that benefit front and center rather than describing what I do. Note that a tagline naming what the customer gets tends to connect faster than one describing my process, since people care about the result more than the method, though the benefit has to be real and specific, because a vague promise like better results feels as empty in a tagline as anywhere else. Give me the benefit led options.
description: Write tagline options centered on the benefit the customer gets.
useCase: Use this when you want the tagline to sell the result. A line naming what the customer gets connects faster than one describing your process, since people care about the result more than the method, as long as the benefit is real and specific rather than a vague promise.

title: Test If a Tagline Is Memorable
promptText: Help me test whether my tagline is actually memorable for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline is [PASTE IT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Tell me honestly whether it is easy to say, easy to recall, and whether it sticks or slides right out of the head, and what specifically helps or hurts its memorability. Note that a tagline only works if people remember it, and length, rhythm, and how easily it rolls off the tongue matter as much as the meaning, so a line that is accurate but clunky to say will be forgotten, and testing this before committing saves putting a forgettable line everywhere. Give me the honest read.
description: Test whether a tagline is easy to say, recall, and actually sticks.
useCase: Use this before committing to a tagline. A tagline only works if people remember it, and rhythm and how easily it rolls off the tongue matter as much as meaning, so a line that is accurate but clunky gets forgotten, and testing this first saves putting a forgettable line everywhere.

title: Focus a Tagline on One Idea
promptText: Help me fix a tagline that is trying to say too much for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current line is [PASTE IT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Point out how many ideas it is juggling, help me pick the single strongest one, and rewrite it around that alone. Note that a tagline crammed with two or three ideas dilutes all of them and becomes a mouthful nobody remembers, so cutting down to the one idea that matters most makes the line sharper and more memorable, and the hard part is usually letting go of the good ideas that do not make the cut. Give me the focused rewrites.
description: Cut a crowded tagline down to its single strongest idea.
useCase: Use this when your tagline tries to say everything. A line juggling two or three ideas dilutes all of them and becomes a mouthful nobody remembers, so cutting to the one idea that matters most makes it sharper, and the hard part is letting go of the good ideas that do not make the cut.

title: Add Personality to a Flat Tagline
promptText: Help me add some personality to my tagline, which is accurate but flat, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current line is [PASTE IT], my brand tone is [YOUR TONE, E.G. WARM, BOLD, PLAYFUL, NO NONSENSE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me versions that keep the meaning but carry more of my brand character. Note that a technically correct tagline with no personality is forgettable, but personality has to match the brand, since a jokey line on a serious service or a stiff line on a fun brand both feel wrong, so the goal is character that fits rather than character for its own sake. Give me the versions with more personality.
description: Inject brand appropriate personality into a flat but accurate tagline.
useCase: Use this when your tagline is correct but forgettable. A technically fine line with no personality slides out of the head, but the character has to match the brand, since a jokey line on a serious service feels as wrong as a stiff line on a fun one, so the goal is character that fits.
variables: YOUR TONE, E.G. WARM, BOLD, PLAYFUL, NO NONSENSE

title: Shorten a Tagline That Is Too Long
promptText: Help me shorten my tagline, which runs too long, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current line is [PASTE IT], and the idea I need to keep is [THE CORE MEANING]. Cut it down to something tight and punchy without losing the point, and show me a few lengths so I can pick. Note that most taglines are stronger with fewer words, and every word that does not earn its place weakens the line and makes it harder to remember, so ruthless trimming usually improves a tagline, and the shortest version that still carries the meaning is almost always the best one. Give me the shorter versions.
description: Trim an overlong tagline to something tight and punchy.
useCase: Use this when your tagline is a sentence, not a tagline. Most are stronger with fewer words, and every word that does not earn its place weakens the line and makes it harder to recall, so ruthless trimming improves it, and the shortest version that still carries the meaning is usually best.

title: Match Your Tagline to Your Brand Voice
promptText: Help me make sure my tagline matches the rest of my brand voice for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline options are [PASTE THEM], the tone I use across my brand is [YOUR TONE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Tell me which options fit my voice and which feel like a different brand wrote them. Note that a tagline sits next to everything else I say, so a line in a tone that clashes with my website and posts creates a jarring mismatch, and consistency matters more than picking the objectively cleverest line, so the best tagline is the strong one that also sounds like the rest of me. Give me which fit and why.
description: Check which tagline options fit your brand voice and which clash.
useCase: Use this when choosing among tagline options. A tagline sits next to everything else you say, so a line whose tone clashes with your site and posts creates a jarring mismatch, and consistency matters more than picking the cleverest line, so the best is the strong one that sounds like the rest of you.

title: Check How a Tagline Sounds Out Loud
promptText: Help me check how my tagline sounds when said out loud for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline is [PASTE IT]. Read it for rhythm and flow: does it trip on any words, have an awkward mouthful in the middle, or land cleanly, and are there any accidental double meanings or unfortunate sounds when spoken. Note that taglines get said aloud far more than people expect, in ads, introductions, and word of mouth, so a line that looks fine written but stumbles when spoken causes trouble, and reading it out loud catches clunky rhythm and unlucky word combinations that the eye misses. Give me the sound and rhythm read.
description: Check a tagline for rhythm, flow, and awkward sounds when spoken aloud.
useCase: Use this before finalizing a tagline. Taglines get said aloud more than people expect, so a line that looks fine written but stumbles when spoken causes trouble, and reading it out loud catches clunky rhythm and unlucky word combinations the eye misses on the page.

title: Check a Tagline for Clichés
promptText: Help me check whether my tagline is a tired cliché for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline is [PASTE IT], and my field is [YOUR INDUSTRY]. Tell me honestly if it uses overused phrasing, a formula every business in my space already uses, or words so common they say nothing, and suggest fresher directions. Note that lines built on your success, our passion, or where quality meets service feel meaningful to write but are so worn that customers glaze over them, so a cliché tagline actively signals a generic business, and catching this before committing keeps me from blending into every competitor who used the same tired formula. Give me the honest verdict and fresher angles.
description: Catch whether a tagline leans on worn out clichés and find fresher angles.
useCase: Use this before you commit a tagline. Lines like your success, our passion feel meaningful to write but are so worn that customers glaze over them, so a cliche tagline signals a generic business, and catching it early keeps you from blending into every competitor using the same formula.

title: Make a Tagline That Stands Apart
promptText: Help me write a tagline that sets me apart from competitors for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What competitors tend to say is [THEIR TYPICAL TAGLINES OR CLAIMS], what is genuinely different about me is [YOUR DIFFERENCE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me tagline options that lean on my difference so I do not sound like everyone else. Note that if my tagline could sit on a competitor's site unchanged it is not doing its job, so the useful test is whether the line is true specifically for me, and a tagline built on a real difference stands out where a generic quality claim disappears into the crowd. Give me the distinctive options.
description: Write tagline options built on a real difference so you stand apart.
useCase: Use this when your tagline could belong to any competitor. If a line could sit on a rival's site unchanged it is not doing its job, so the test is whether it is true specifically for you, and a tagline built on a real difference stands out where a generic quality claim disappears into the crowd.

title: Write a Slogan for a Campaign
promptText: Help me write a slogan for a specific campaign or promotion for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The campaign is about [WHAT IT IS], the audience is [WHO IT IS FOR], and the action I want is [WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO]. Give me slogan options that fit this campaign, punchier and more time bound than my permanent tagline. Note that a campaign slogan is different from a brand tagline, it can be bolder and more specific because it does not have to last forever, so it should push the particular offer or moment rather than sum up the whole business, and it is fine for it to be disposable since the campaign is too. Give me the campaign slogan options.
description: Write punchy campaign slogan options distinct from your permanent tagline.
useCase: Use this for a specific promotion or campaign. A campaign slogan is different from a brand tagline, it can be bolder and more specific because it does not have to last forever, so it should push the particular offer rather than sum up the whole business, and being disposable is fine.
variables: WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO

title: Pick the Best From Your Shortlist
promptText: Help me choose the best tagline from my shortlist for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My finalists are [PASTE THE OPTIONS], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the impression I want to leave is [THE FEELING]. Compare them on clarity, memorability, fit with my brand, and how well they stand apart, and tell me which one you would pick and why. Note that at the shortlist stage the options are usually all decent, so the decision is about tradeoffs rather than right or wrong, and a clear rundown of what each one gains and gives up helps me commit instead of endlessly second guessing, since agonizing between good options wastes more than picking a solid one and moving on. Give me the comparison and your pick.
description: Compare your tagline finalists and get a clear recommended pick.
useCase: Use this when you have a few taglines you like and cannot decide. At the shortlist stage the options are all usually decent, so it is about tradeoffs not right or wrong, and a clear rundown of what each gains and gives up helps you commit rather than endlessly second guessing good options.

title: Rework a Tagline That Is Not Landing
promptText: Help me rework my current tagline, which is not landing, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline is [PASTE IT], what I think is wrong with it is [YOUR HUNCH, OR WRITE NOT SURE], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Diagnose why it is falling flat, whether it is unclear, generic, clunky, or off tone, then give me reworked versions that fix the actual problem. Note that a tagline can be near miss rather than a total failure, where a small change in one word or the order fixes it, so the diagnosis matters, and I should not throw out a line that just needs a tune up any more than I should keep polishing one that is fundamentally wrong. Give me the diagnosis and reworks.
description: Diagnose why a tagline falls flat and rework it to fix the real problem.
useCase: Use this when your tagline is not working but you are not sure why. A tagline can be a near miss where changing one word fixes it, so the diagnosis matters, and you should not scrap a line that just needs a tune up any more than keep polishing one that is fundamentally wrong.
variables: YOUR HUNCH, OR WRITE NOT SURE

title: Decide Where and How to Use a Tagline
promptText: Help me figure out where and how to actually use my new tagline for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tagline is [PASTE IT], and the places I show up are [WHERE, E.G. WEBSITE, SOCIAL BIOS, SIGNAGE, EMAIL]. Tell me where a tagline helps, where it just adds clutter, and how to place it so it reinforces the brand without being repeated to the point of annoyance. Note that a tagline works through consistent repetition in the right places, but slapping it onto everything can make it feel forced, so knowing where it earns its place versus where it is noise matters, and a tagline used well in a few key spots beats one crammed everywhere. Give me the usage guide.
description: Decide where a tagline earns its place and where it just adds clutter.
useCase: Use this once you have a tagline you like. A tagline works through consistent repetition in the right places, but slapping it on everything makes it feel forced, so knowing where it earns its place versus where it is noise matters, and a tagline used well in a few key spots beats one crammed everywhere.
variables: WHERE, E.G. WEBSITE, SOCIAL BIOS, SIGNAGE, EMAIL

title: Decide If You Even Need a Tagline
promptText: Help me decide whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] actually needs a tagline right now. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], where I show up is [YOUR MAIN PLACES], and why I think I might need one is [YOUR REASON]. Tell me honestly whether a tagline would help me now or whether a clear description of what I do would serve me better at this stage. Note that plenty of small businesses do fine with a clear plain description and no tagline, and a forced mediocre tagline is worse than none, so it is worth checking whether I actually need one before spending effort on it, since chasing a clever line can be a distraction from clearer work that matters more. Give me the honest verdict.
description: Check honestly whether you need a tagline or a clear description serves better.
useCase: Use this before pouring effort into a tagline. Plenty of small businesses do fine with a clear description and no tagline, and a forced mediocre one is worse than none, so it is worth checking whether you actually need one, since chasing a clever line can distract from work that matters more.

title: Write the Same Tagline in Different Tones
promptText: Help me see my tagline idea written in a few different tones so I can feel which fits my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The core idea is [THE MEANING YOU WANT], and my customer is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me the same underlying message as a warm version, a bold version, a playful version, and a straight professional version, so I can compare. Note that the right tone for a tagline is hard to judge in the abstract, and seeing the same idea in several tones side by side often makes the fit obvious in a way that describing the tone I want does not, so this is about feeling the options rather than reasoning them out. Give me the tonal variations.
description: See one tagline idea rendered in several tones to feel the right fit.
useCase: Use this when you know the message but not the tone. The right tone is hard to judge in the abstract, and seeing the same idea as warm, bold, playful, and professional side by side often makes the fit obvious in a way that describing the tone you want does not, so you feel it rather than reason it.

title: Build Your Tone of Voice Guide
promptText: Help me build a tone of voice guide for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and how I want to come across is [THE IMPRESSION YOU WANT]. Give me a simple guide covering three or four voice traits, a short description of each, and how they show up in writing, in plain terms I can actually apply. Note that a voice guide only helps if it is specific enough to guide real decisions, so friendly and professional are too vague to be useful on their own, and the useful version names traits distinct enough that two people writing from them would sound alike. Give me the tone of voice guide.
description: Build a simple, specific tone of voice guide with a few distinct traits.
useCase: Use this when your writing sounds different every time and you want a standard. A voice guide only helps if it is specific enough to guide real decisions, since friendly and professional are too vague alone, so naming a few distinct traits gives you something two people could write from and still sound alike.

title: Define Your Three Voice Traits
promptText: Help me pin down three voice traits that define how my [BUSINESS TYPE] should sound. What I do is [WHAT YOU OFFER], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and words I would use to describe my ideal vibe are [YOUR ROUGH WORDS]. Turn my rough words into three clear traits, each with a short definition, and steer me away from generic ones everyone claims. Note that three traits is usually enough to guide writing without being impossible to hold in mind, and traits that everyone picks like professional and approachable do little work, so the useful set is specific to me, and a trait that would surprise a competitor is often the one that actually shapes my voice. Give me the three traits defined.
description: Turn rough vibe words into three specific, distinctive voice traits.
useCase: Use this when you know the feeling you want but not how to name it. Three traits is enough to guide writing without overwhelming, and generic ones like professional do little work, so a set specific to you, including a trait a competitor would not claim, is what actually shapes your voice.

title: Get a Quick Voice Guide
promptText: I need a quick tone of voice guide to work from. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the vibe I want is [THE FEELING]. Give me three voice traits with a one line description each and one quick dos and don'ts pair, no long theory, just the guide. Give me the quick guide.
description: Get a quick three trait voice guide with dos and don'ts to start from.
useCase: Use this when you want a usable voice guide fast. Three traits with a one line description and a dos and don'ts pair covers enough to start writing consistently, and a quick draft you can refine beats having no shared standard while you post day to day.

title: Build a Voice Guide From Your Best Writing
promptText: Help me build a voice guide by studying writing of mine that already sounds right for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here are a few pieces I feel good about: [PASTE SAMPLES]. Read them and tell me the voice traits, word choices, and patterns that make them sound like me, then turn that into a guide I can follow deliberately. Note that my best natural writing already contains my real voice, so pulling the guide out of what I have actually written beats inventing a voice from scratch, and this captures how I genuinely sound rather than an aspirational voice I would struggle to keep up. Give me the guide drawn from my samples.
description: Reverse engineer a voice guide from writing that already sounds like you.
useCase: Use this when some of your writing already feels right.
