title: Build a Set of Differentiation Messages
promptText: Help me turn my point of difference into a set of ready messages I can use for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My main difference is [WHAT SETS YOU APART], my customer is [WHO THEY ARE], and the places I need it are [WHERE, E.G. HOMEPAGE, SALES CALL, SOCIAL, EMAIL]. Give me a version of my differentiation message for each place, all pointing at the same core difference. Note that a difference only sticks through consistent repetition across everywhere a customer meets me, so having it phrased for each context keeps the message unified instead of me describing my edge differently every time, and consistent differentiation is what makes the difference actually register in a customer's mind over time. Give me the differentiation messages.
description: Turn your difference into a consistent set of messages for each context.
useCase: Use this to say your difference the same way everywhere. A difference only sticks through consistent repetition across every place a customer meets you, so having it phrased for each context keeps the message unified rather than described differently each time, which is what makes it actually register over time.
variables: WHERE, E.G. HOMEPAGE, SALES CALL, SOCIAL, EMAIL

title: Check If Your Difference Will Last
promptText: Help me check whether my point of difference is durable or easy to copy for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My main differentiator is [WHAT SETS YOU APART], and my competitors are [WHO THEY ARE]. Tell me honestly how hard it would be for a competitor to match this, and whether I should be building toward a more defensible difference. Note that some differences are easy to copy, like a feature or a price, while others are hard to copy, like a reputation, a community, deep expertise, or a genuine relationship with customers, so a differentiator anyone could match in a week is weaker than one built over years, and knowing which kind I have tells me whether to lean on it or build something more durable underneath. Give me the durability read.
description: Assess whether your differentiator is durable or easy for competitors to copy.
useCase: Use this to judge how defensible your difference is. Some differences are easy to copy, like a feature or price, while others are hard, like reputation, community, or deep expertise, so a differentiator anyone could match in a week is weaker than one built over years, and knowing which you have tells you whether to build something more durable.

title: Write Your Rebrand Announcement
promptText: Help me write the announcement for my rebrand for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What is changing is [NAME, LOOK, FOCUS, OR ALL OF THESE], why we are changing is [THE REAL REASON], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Write an announcement that leads with what it means for them, explains the change plainly, and tells them what stays the same. Note that customers care less about my new logo than about whether anything they rely on is changing, so the announcement should answer that first, and a rebrand framed as an exciting new chapter with no real reason given tends to read as cosmetic or as hiding something. Give me the announcement.
description: Write a rebrand announcement that leads with what it means for customers.
useCase: Use this when you are ready to tell people about a rebrand. Customers care less about the new logo than whether anything they rely on is changing, so answering that first and giving a real reason keeps the change from reading as cosmetic or evasive.
variables: NAME, LOOK, FOCUS, OR ALL OF THESE

title: Explain Why You Are Rebranding
promptText: Help me explain honestly why my [BUSINESS TYPE] is rebranding. The real reason is [WHAT ACTUALLY DROVE IT, E.G. OUTGREW THE NAME, NEW FOCUS, CONFUSION, A CONFLICT], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Turn that into a short clear explanation I can use in announcements and conversations. Note that people accept change much more easily when they understand the reason, and a vague answer like evolving our brand invites guessing, so a plain true reason, even an unglamorous one like the old name confused people, builds more trust than polished corporate language. Give me the explanation.
description: Turn the real reason for your rebrand into a short, honest explanation.
useCase: Use this when people ask why you are changing. A plain true reason builds more trust than vague talk of evolving the brand, which invites guessing, and even an unglamorous reason like the old name confused people lands better than polished corporate language.
variables: WHAT ACTUALLY DROVE IT, E.G. OUTGREW THE NAME, NEW FOCUS, CONFUSION, A CONFLICT

title: Get a Quick Rebrand Announcement
promptText: I need a quick rebrand announcement I can post. My old name or look was [WHAT IT WAS], the new one is [WHAT IT IS NOW], and the short reason is [WHY]. Give me a short announcement that says what changed, why, and that customers do not need to do anything different, no long explanation, just the post. Give me the announcement.
description: Get a short, ready to post rebrand announcement.
useCase: Use this when you need to announce a rebrand fast. A short post covering what changed, why, and that customers need do nothing different handles most of what people want to know, and getting a clear message out beats a polished one that sits in drafts.

title: Reassure Customers About What Stays the Same
promptText: Help me reassure existing customers about what is not changing in my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [THE CHANGES], what stays the same is [PEOPLE, PRICES, SERVICE, ACCOUNTS, CONTACT DETAILS], and my customers are [WHO THEY ARE]. Write clear reassurance that answers their likely worries directly. Note that the first reaction to any rebrand is often worry about what customers might lose, like their account, their pricing, or the person they deal with, so spelling out exactly what stays the same does more to keep loyal customers calm than describing everything that is new. Give me the reassurance message.
description: Reassure existing customers clearly about what the rebrand does not change.
useCase: Use this to keep loyal customers calm through a rebrand. The first reaction is often worry about losing an account, pricing, or a familiar contact, so spelling out exactly what stays the same does more than describing everything new.
variables: PEOPLE, PRICES, SERVICE, ACCOUNTS, CONTACT DETAILS

title: Email Existing Customers About the Rebrand
promptText: Help me write an email to my existing customers about my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [THE CHANGES], the reason is [WHY], what they need to do, if anything, is [ACTIONS, OR NOTHING], and when it takes effect is [THE DATE]. Write a short personal email that tells them before they see it elsewhere and makes any practical steps obvious. Note that existing customers should hear about a rebrand directly from me rather than stumble on a new logo or a changed sender name, which can look like a scam or a takeover, so a heads up email with the practical details, like a new email address to whitelist, protects trust and prevents confusion. Give me the email.
description: Write a heads up email that tells existing customers about the rebrand first.
useCase: Use this before the rebrand goes public. Customers who stumble on a new logo or a changed sender name can mistake it for a scam or a takeover, so telling them directly first, with any practical steps like a new address to whitelist, protects trust.

title: Plan Rebrand Posts for Social Media
promptText: Help me plan a short series of social posts to roll out my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [THE CHANGES], my platform is [WHERE YOU POST], and my audience is [WHO THEY ARE]. Give me a few posts across the rollout: a teaser if it fits, the reveal, a post explaining the why, and a follow up that settles into normal posting under the new brand. Note that a single announcement post is easy to miss, so a short sequence helps followers notice and connect the old brand to the new one, but dragging out a reveal for weeks mostly tests patience, so a tight sequence works better than a long campaign for a small business. Give me the post series.
description: Plan a tight series of social posts to roll out a rebrand.
useCase: Use this to make sure followers actually notice the change. A single post is easy to miss, so a short sequence helps people connect the old brand to the new one, while a weeks long reveal mostly tests patience for a small business.

title: Bridge an Old Name to a New One
promptText: Help me connect my old business name to my new one so people do not lose track of me for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The old name is [OLD NAME], the new name is [NEW NAME], and the places people find me are [WHERE, E.G. GOOGLE, SOCIAL, SIGNAGE, REFERRALS]. Give me bridging language like formerly or now called, and tell me where and for how long to use it. Note that people search for and recommend the name they remember, so dropping the old name overnight can make me hard to find, and a period of saying new name, formerly old name, keeps word of mouth and search traffic flowing to the right place until the new name sticks. Give me the bridging plan.
description: Use formerly and now called messaging so people can still find you after a name change.
useCase: Use this when your business name is changing. People search for and recommend the name they remember, so dropping the old one overnight can make you hard to find, and a period of new name, formerly old name keeps word of mouth and search traffic flowing.
variables: WHERE, E.G. GOOGLE, SOCIAL, SIGNAGE, REFERRALS

title: Decide Whether You Actually Need a Rebrand
promptText: Help me decide honestly whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] needs a rebrand or something smaller. What feels wrong with my current brand is [THE PROBLEM], how long I have used it is [HOW LONG], and the recognition I have built is [ROUGHLY HOW KNOWN YOU ARE]. Tell me whether a full rebrand, a refresh, or simply clearer messaging would solve the actual problem. Note that a rebrand costs time, money, and some of the recognition I have built, and many brand problems are really messaging or offer problems that a new logo will not fix, so it is worth being sure the brand is the real issue before throwing away what people already know. Give me the honest recommendation.
description: Check whether a rebrand, a refresh, or clearer messaging fits the real problem.
useCase: Use this before committing to a rebrand. A rebrand costs time, money, and recognition you have built, and many brand problems are really messaging or offer problems a new logo will not fix, so confirming the brand is the real issue first can save a costly reset.

title: Choose Between a Refresh and a Full Rebrand
promptText: Help me choose between refreshing my brand and fully rebranding my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current brand is [NAME, LOOK, AND MESSAGE], what I want to fix is [THE GOAL], and my budget and time are [WHAT YOU HAVE]. Lay out what each option would change, what it would cost me in effort and recognition, and which fits my goal. Note that a refresh keeps the name and core identity while updating the look and message, which keeps recognition, while a full rebrand starts over and is only worth it when the old identity is actively holding me back, so the smaller change is often the smarter one. Give me the comparison and recommendation.
description: Compare a brand refresh with a full rebrand and pick the right scope.
useCase: Use this when you know something needs to change but not how much. A refresh updates the look and message while keeping recognition, while a full rebrand starts over and only pays off when the old identity actively holds you back, so the smaller change is often smarter.

title: Keep What People Already Love About Your Brand
promptText: Help me identify what to keep from my current brand as I rebrand my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What customers know me for is [WHAT PEOPLE RECOGNIZE OR SAY ABOUT YOU], elements I am attached to are [COLORS, PHRASES, SYMBOLS, YOUR STORY], and what is driving the change is [THE REASON]. Help me sort what carries real recognition and should survive from what can safely go. Note that years of recognition sit in small things like a color, a phrase, or the way I talk, and a rebrand that throws all of it away makes loyal customers feel they are dealing with a stranger, so carrying a few recognizable threads into the new brand protects the trust I have already earned. Give me what to keep and what to let go.
description: Sort which parts of your current brand carry recognition worth keeping.
useCase: Use this so a rebrand does not erase earned trust. Recognition sits in small things like a color, a phrase, or the way you talk, and throwing all of it away makes loyal customers feel they are dealing with a stranger, so carrying a few threads forward protects that trust.
variables: WHAT PEOPLE RECOGNIZE OR SAY ABOUT YOU

title: Message a Change in Focus or Audience
promptText: Help me message a rebrand that changes who my [BUSINESS TYPE] serves or what it focuses on. I used to focus on [OLD FOCUS OR AUDIENCE], I now focus on [NEW FOCUS OR AUDIENCE], and the customers who may no longer fit are [WHO]. Help me explain the shift clearly to the new audience while treating the old one with respect. Note that a repositioning rebrand will leave some existing customers outside the new focus, and pretending nothing changed confuses everyone, so it is better to say plainly who I now serve and, where it is true, how past customers will still be looked after or where they can go. Give me the repositioning message.
description: Explain a shift in focus or audience clearly while respecting past customers.
useCase: Use this when a rebrand changes who you serve. A repositioning leaves some customers outside the new focus, and pretending nothing changed confuses everyone, so saying plainly who you now serve and how past customers will be looked after keeps the shift honest.

title: Respond to Customers Who Dislike the Rebrand
promptText: Help me respond to customers who are unhappy about my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. The complaints I am getting are [PASTE OR DESCRIBE THEM], the reason for the change is [WHY], and my tone is [YOUR TONE]. Give me replies that acknowledge their feelings, explain without getting defensive, and stay firm where the decision is final. Note that some pushback is normal with any change, since people get attached to what they know, and most of it fades once the new brand becomes familiar, so calm, appreciative replies work better than arguing or instantly reversing course, though repeated specific complaints about something practical are worth taking seriously. Give me the replies.
description: Answer rebrand complaints calmly without getting defensive or caving.
useCase: Use this when the rebrand gets negative reactions. Pushback is normal since people get attached to what they know, and most of it fades as the new brand becomes familiar, so calm appreciative replies beat arguing or reversing course, while repeated practical complaints deserve a real look.

title: Build a Rebrand FAQ
promptText: Help me build a short FAQ for my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [THE CHANGES], what stays the same is [WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE], and practical details customers might need are [NEW WEBSITE, EMAIL, PAYMENT NAME, ACCOUNTS]. Anticipate the questions customers will actually ask and give clear short answers. Note that the same handful of questions tends to come in again and again after a rebrand, like is this still the same company, do my accounts still work, and why does my bank statement look different, so answering them once in a FAQ saves a lot of repeated replies and quietly prevents confusion. Give me the FAQ.
description: Answer the questions customers will ask about a rebrand in one FAQ.
useCase: Use this to stop answering the same rebrand questions over and over. The same few come up repeatedly, like is this still the same company or why does my statement look different, so answering them once in a FAQ saves replies and prevents confusion.
variables: NEW WEBSITE, EMAIL, PAYMENT NAME, ACCOUNTS

title: List Every Place Your Brand Needs Updating
promptText: Help me list every place my brand appears so nothing is missed in my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [NAME, LOGO, COLORS, MESSAGE], and the main places I show up are [WHAT YOU KNOW OF, E.G. WEBSITE, SOCIAL, INVOICES, SIGNAGE]. Give me a thorough checklist of touchpoints, including the easy to forget ones, grouped by priority. Note that the obvious places get updated and the forgotten ones linger for months, like an email signature, a payment processor name, an old directory listing, or a templates folder, and a mix of old and new names in the wild looks careless and confuses customers, so a full checklist up front is what makes a rebrand feel clean. Give me the checklist.
description: Build a full checklist of every touchpoint a rebrand needs to reach.
useCase: Use this so the old brand does not linger in forgotten places. Email signatures, payment processor names, old directory listings, and templates are easy to miss, and a mix of old and new names looks careless, so a full checklist up front makes the rebrand feel clean.
variables: WHAT YOU KNOW OF, E.G. WEBSITE, SOCIAL, INVOICES, SIGNAGE

title: Plan the Rebrand Rollout Order
promptText: Help me plan the order of my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand rollout. The changes are [WHAT IS CHANGING], my audiences are [CUSTOMERS, PARTNERS, SUPPLIERS, THE PUBLIC], and my target date is [WHEN]. Give me a simple sequence of who hears first, what goes live when, and how long to keep both brands visible. Note that the order matters, since customers and partners who hear about it from me first feel respected while those who discover it by surprise can feel blindsided, and switching everything in one day is rarely realistic for a small business, so a planned sequence with a short overlap keeps the transition calm. Give me the rollout plan.
description: Sequence who hears about the rebrand first and what goes live when.
useCase: Use this to keep the transition calm. People who hear about the change from you first feel respected while those who discover it by surprise can feel blindsided, and switching everything in one day is rarely realistic, so a planned sequence with a short overlap works better.

title: Notify Partners and Suppliers of a Rebrand
promptText: Help me write a notice to partners, suppliers, and other businesses I work with about my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand. What is changing is [THE CHANGES], the practical updates they need are [NEW LEGAL NAME, INVOICE DETAILS, EMAIL, LOGO FILES], and the effective date is [THE DATE]. Write a short professional notice that makes the practical changes impossible to miss. Note that partners and suppliers mostly care about the practical side, like which name goes on invoices, where payments go, and which logo to use, and unclear details here cause real problems like rejected payments or outdated co branding, so the notice should be specific and easy to act on rather than promotional. Give me the notice.
description: Write a practical rebrand notice for partners and suppliers.
useCase: Use this to tell the businesses you work with. Partners and suppliers care about which name goes on invoices, where payments go, and which logo to use, and unclear details cause rejected payments or outdated co branding, so a specific practical notice beats a promotional one.
variables: NEW LEGAL NAME, INVOICE DETAILS, EMAIL, LOGO FILES

title: Update Your Website Copy for the Rebrand
promptText: Help me update my website copy so it fits my new brand for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My new brand direction is [NEW NAME, FOCUS, AND VOICE], and here is my current homepage or key page copy: [PASTE IT]. Rewrite it to match the new brand, and suggest a small note or banner explaining the change for returning visitors. Note that a new logo on top of old copy feels half finished, since the words still describe the old business, and returning visitors who land on an unfamiliar site may think they are in the wrong place, so matching the copy to the new brand and briefly acknowledging the change keeps both new and returning visitors oriented. Give me the updated copy and the note.
description: Rewrite key website copy to match the new brand and orient returning visitors.
useCase: Use this when the site still sounds like the old business. A new logo on old copy feels half finished, and returning visitors may think they landed in the wrong place, so matching the words to the new brand and adding a brief note keeps everyone oriented.

title: Check How the Rebrand Landed
promptText: Help me check how my [BUSINESS TYPE] rebrand has landed a few weeks or months in. What I changed was [THE CHANGES], what I have noticed since is [FEEDBACK, ENQUIRIES, SALES, CONFUSION, SEARCH TRAFFIC], and what I hoped it would achieve is [YOUR GOAL]. Help me read the signals honestly and decide what to adjust. Note that early reactions to a rebrand are noisy, since some dip in recognition is normal while people adjust, so it is worth separating short term confusion that will fade from real problems like customers who cannot find me, and judging the rebrand against the goal I set rather than how it feels day to day. Give me the honest read and adjustments.
description: Read the signals after a rebrand and decide what to adjust.
useCase: Use this a few weeks or months after the change. Early reactions are noisy and some dip in recognition is normal, so separating short term confusion that will fade from real problems like customers who cannot find you, and judging against your goal, gives an honest read.
variables: FEEDBACK, ENQUIRIES, SALES, CONFUSION, SEARCH TRAFFIC

title: Build a Complete Job Description
promptText: Help me write a complete job description for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The main work this person will do is [WHAT THEY WILL ACTUALLY DO], the skills that truly matter are [KEY SKILLS], and the arrangement is [FULL TIME, PART TIME, CONTRACT, REMOTE, LOCATION]. Give me a clear description with a short summary, responsibilities, must have requirements, nice to haves, and how we work. Note that a job description is the document both of us will measure the role against later, so it should describe the real day to day work rather than an idealized version, and a description that oversells the role attracts people who leave once they see what the job actually is. Give me the job description.
description: Write a full job description built around the real day to day work.
useCase: Use this when you need the core document for a new role. A job description is what you and the hire will measure the role against later, so describing the real work rather than an idealized version attracts people who stay once they see what the job actually is.
variables: FULL TIME, PART TIME, CONTRACT, REMOTE, LOCATION

title: Turn Your Task List Into Responsibilities
promptText: Help me turn a messy list of tasks into clear responsibilities for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here are the tasks I want to hand off: [LIST THE TASKS], and roughly how my week splits across them is [TIME ESTIMATES IF YOU HAVE THEM]. Group them into a handful of clear responsibility areas, ordered by how much of the job each takes. Note that a raw task list makes a role look either trivial or chaotic, while grouped responsibilities show a candidate what the job really is, and ordering them by time spent stops a minor task listed first from giving a misleading picture of the role. Give me the responsibilities.
description: Group a raw task list into clear responsibility areas ordered by time spent.
useCase: Use this when you know what you want off your plate but not how to describe the role. A raw task list looks trivial or chaotic, while grouped responsibilities ordered by time spent show candidates what the job really is and stop a minor task from defining it.
variables: TIME ESTIMATES IF YOU HAVE THEM

title: Separate Must Haves From Nice to Haves
promptText: Help me separate the true requirements from the nice to haves for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is everything I think I want in a candidate: [YOUR FULL WISH LIST], and the work they will do is [THE CORE WORK]. Go through it and tell me which items someone genuinely cannot do the job without and which are preferences. Note that long requirement lists scare off capable people, especially those who only apply when they meet every line, while barely affecting people who apply to everything, so cutting the must haves to what the work truly demands widens the good pool without lowering the bar. Give me the sorted requirements.
description: Cut a wish list down to genuine requirements and separate the preferences.
useCase: Use this when your requirements list keeps growing. Long lists scare off capable people who only apply when they meet every line while barely affecting those who apply to everything, so trimming must haves to what the work demands widens the good pool without lowering the bar.

title: Get a Quick Job Description Draft
promptText: I need a quick job description draft to edit. The role is [ROLE TITLE], the main work is [WHAT THEY WILL DO], and the arrangement is [FULL TIME, PART TIME, CONTRACT, REMOTE]. Give me a short draft with a summary, five responsibilities, and a short requirements list, no explanation, just the draft. Give me the job description.
description: Get a short job description draft you can edit right away.
useCase: Use this when you need something on the page fast. A short draft with a summary, a handful of responsibilities, and core requirements gives you a structure to correct, and fixing a rough draft is much quicker than starting a job description from a blank page.
variables: FULL TIME, PART TIME, CONTRACT, REMOTE

title: Write an Outcomes Based Job Description
promptText: Help me describe a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE] by the results I need rather than just the tasks. What I need this person to achieve in their first six to twelve months is [THE OUTCOMES], and the work involved is [THE MAIN TASKS]. Rewrite the role around a few clear outcomes, each with the work that drives it. Note that tasks tell a candidate what they will do while outcomes tell them what success looks like, and a role defined by outcomes makes it far easier to judge candidates, set expectations, and later know whether the hire is working out, though the outcomes need to be realistic for someone new to my business. Give me the outcomes based description.
description: Define a role by the results you need, not just the tasks.
useCase: Use this when you want the role tied to results. Tasks say what someone will do while outcomes say what success looks like, which makes judging candidates, setting expectations, and later knowing if the hire is working out far easier, as long as the outcomes are realistic for a newcomer.

title: Create a Scorecard for the Role
promptText: Help me create a simple scorecard for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE] that I can use when hiring and after. The role's main outcomes are [WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE], and the skills and traits that matter are [KEY SKILLS AND TRAITS]. Give me a short scorecard with a few measurable outcomes and the competencies behind them, written so I can rate candidates against it. Note that without a scorecard hiring decisions drift toward whoever was most likeable in the interview, so writing down what good looks like before meeting anyone keeps the decision tied to the job, and the same scorecard becomes the starting point for reviewing the hire later. Give me the scorecard.
description: Build a role scorecard to rate candidates against and review the hire later.
useCase: Use this before you start interviewing. Without a scorecard decisions drift toward whoever was most likeable, so writing down what good looks like first keeps the choice tied to the job, and the same scorecard becomes the basis for reviewing the hire later.

title: Check If You Are Describing an Impossible Hire
promptText: Help me check whether my job description asks for a person who does not exist. Here is my draft: [PASTE THE JOB DESCRIPTION], and my budget for the role is [PAY RANGE]. Tell me honestly whether the skills I am asking for normally live in one person, whether the experience matches the pay, and whether this is really two roles combined. Note that small businesses often bundle several jobs into one description, like a designer who also does ads, writes copy, and manages the books, and the result is either no good applicants or a hire who is mediocre at most of it, so it is worth splitting the role or picking the priority before posting. Give me the honest check and how to fix it.
description: Check whether your job description bundles several jobs into one impossible hire.
useCase: Use this when a role keeps growing as you write it. Small businesses often bundle several jobs into one description, which brings either no good applicants or a hire mediocre at most of it, so splitting the role or picking the priority before posting saves a failed hire.

title: Set and Present the Pay Range
promptText: Help me think through the pay range for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE] and how to present it in the job description. Where the person will be based is [COUNTRY OR CITY, OR REMOTE FROM ANYWHERE], what I can afford is [YOUR BUDGET], and the experience level I need is [LEVEL]. Help me sanity check my number against the level I am asking for and word it clearly, including whether pay is hourly, monthly, or per project. Note that local pay norms differ hugely by country and market, so I should check current rates for where the person actually is rather than assume, and pay transparency rules apply in some places, while a clear range saves both sides time by filtering out mismatches before anyone invests in interviews. Give me the pay guidance and wording.
description: Sanity check your pay against the level you want and word it clearly.
useCase: Use this before posting a role with pay. Pay norms differ hugely by country and market, so checking current local rates beats assuming, some places require pay transparency, and a clear range filters out mismatches before anyone spends time interviewing.
variables: COUNTRY OR CITY, OR REMOTE FROM ANYWHERE

title: Pin Down the Right Seniority Level
promptText: Help me decide what seniority level I actually need for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The work involves [THE WORK], how much direction I can give is [HOW MUCH TIME YOU HAVE TO MANAGE OR TRAIN], and my budget is [PAY RANGE]. Tell me whether I need someone junior I can train, a mid level person who can run with it, or a senior person who can set direction, and adjust the description to match. Note that hiring junior saves money only if I have time to teach, while hiring senior to do routine work wastes money and bores them, so the right level depends as much on how much support I can give as on the work itself. Give me the recommended level and adjusted wording.
description: Match the seniority level to the work and the support you can actually give.
useCase: Use this when you are unsure how experienced the hire should be. Hiring junior saves money only if you have time to teach, while hiring senior for routine work wastes money and bores them, so the right level depends on the support you can give as much as on the work.
variables: HOW MUCH TIME YOU HAVE TO MANAGE OR TRAIN

title: Write the Description for Your First Hire
promptText: Help me write the job description for the first person I am ever hiring for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I need help with most is [WHAT IS OVERWHELMING YOU], what I can realistically pay is [BUDGET], and how I work day to day is [HOW YOU OPERATE, E.G. MESSAGING, NO FIXED HOURS, ON SITE]. Write a description that is honest about what working for a very small business is like, both the upsides and the rough edges. Note that a first hire works without the systems, colleagues, and structure a bigger company has, so candidates need to know they will help build processes as they go, and being upfront about that attracts people who enjoy it while saving everyone from a mismatch. Give me the first hire job description.
description: Write an honest job description for your very first hire.
useCase: Use this when hiring your first person ever. A first hire works without systems, colleagues, or structure, so being upfront that they will help build processes as they go attracts people who enjoy that and avoids a mismatch with people expecting a settled company.
variables: HOW YOU OPERATE, E.G. MESSAGING, NO FIXED HOURS, ON SITE

title: Scope a Part Time or Fractional Role
promptText: Help me write a job description for a part time or fractional [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The hours or days available are [HOURS PER WEEK OR MONTH], the work I need is [THE WORK], and the priorities are [WHAT MATTERS MOST]. Scope the role so the responsibilities genuinely fit the hours and say clearly what is out of scope. Note that part time roles often get loaded with full time expectations, which burns out the hire or leaves important work half done, so the description should prioritize ruthlessly and state the limits, since a clear small scope done well beats a vague large one done badly. Give me the scoped description.
description: Scope a part time or fractional role so the work truly fits the hours.
useCase: Use this when you can only afford limited hours. Part time roles often get loaded with full time expectations, burning out the hire or leaving work half done, so prioritizing ruthlessly and stating what is out of scope keeps the role doable.

title: Describe a Contract or Freelance Role
promptText: Help me write a role description for a contractor or freelancer for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The work is [WHAT YOU NEED DONE], the expected volume or duration is [HOW MUCH AND FOR HOW LONG], and how I want to pay is [HOURLY, PER PROJECT, RETAINER]. Frame it around deliverables and results rather than how they spend their time. Note that a contractor role written like an employee job, with set hours and close supervision, can blur the line between contractor and employee in ways that create legal and tax issues in some countries, so focusing on what gets delivered rather than how and when they work keeps the arrangement clear, and I should check the rules where I and they are based. Give me the contractor role description.
description: Describe a contract role around deliverables, not hours and supervision.
useCase: Use this when hiring a freelancer or contractor. A contract role written like an employee job can blur the line in ways that create legal and tax issues in some countries, so framing it around deliverables keeps the arrangement clear, while checking the rules where you both are based.
variables: HOW MUCH AND FOR HOW LONG

title: Spell Out Remote, Location, and Time Zone Needs
promptText: Help me write the location and working hours section of a job description for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Where I am based is [YOUR LOCATION AND TIME ZONE], whether the role is [ON SITE, HYBRID, REMOTE], how much real time overlap I need is [HOURS OF OVERLAP], and any country limits are [WHERE THEY CAN OR CANNOT BE BASED]. Write it so candidates know exactly what is expected before applying. Note that remote roles cause the most mismatches on time zones and availability, like a candidate twelve hours away who cannot join any live calls, so stating the overlap and any location limits plainly filters people correctly and avoids wasted interviews. Give me the location and hours section.
description: State location, remote setup, and time zone overlap clearly up front.
useCase: Use this for any remote or distributed role. Most remote mismatches come from time zones and availability, like a candidate twelve hours away who cannot join live calls, so stating overlap and location limits plainly filters candidates correctly before interviews.
variables: WHERE THEY CAN OR CANNOT BE BASED

title: Adapt a Job Description to a Local Market
promptText: Help me adapt a job description for hiring in a specific country or local market for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The market I am hiring in is [COUNTRY OR CITY], here is my current draft: [PASTE THE JOB DESCRIPTION], and the language candidates will read it in is [LANGUAGE]. Point out anything that assumes a different market, like titles, benefits, qualifications, or working norms that do not fit there, and suggest adjustments I should verify locally. Note that job descriptions copied from another country often use titles, benefits, and requirements that mean little or something different locally, and candidates notice, so adapting to how roles are actually described and valued in that market gets better applicants, though I should confirm specifics like legal requirements with a local source. Give me the adjustments.
description: Adapt a job description to how roles work in a specific country or market.
useCase: Use this when hiring outside the market your template came from. Titles, benefits, and requirements copied from another country often mean little or something different locally, so adapting to local norms gets better applicants, while confirming legal specifics with a local source.

title: Check Your Job Description for Off Putting Language
promptText: Help me check my job description for language that might turn good candidates away for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is the draft: [PASTE THE JOB DESCRIPTION], and the kind of candidates I hope to reach are [WHO]. Flag wording that is needlessly exclusionary, like rockstar or ninja, young and energetic, native speaker when fluency is what matters, or requirements unrelated to the work, and suggest plainer alternatives. Note that small wording choices quietly signal who is welcome, and phrases meant as fun or casual can put off strong candidates or even raise discrimination concerns in some places, so plain descriptions of the work and real requirements reach the widest good pool. Give me the flags and rewrites.
description: Flag wording in a job description that quietly turns good candidates away.
useCase: Use this before posting. Small wording choices signal who is welcome, and phrases like rockstar, young and energetic, or native speaker when fluency is what matters can put off strong candidates or raise discrimination concerns, so plain language reaches the widest good pool.

title: Focus Requirements on Skills Over Credentials
promptText: Help me rewrite the requirements in my job description to focus on what a candidate can do rather than their credentials for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current requirements are [PASTE THEM], and the work is [THE CORE WORK]. For each degree, certificate, or years of experience requirement, tell me whether it is truly needed or can be replaced by a demonstrable skill, and show me how to ask for evidence of that skill instead. Note that degrees and year counts are rough stand ins for ability, and some of the best candidates are self taught or changed careers, so asking for the skill itself, ideally shown through a portfolio or small paid test, finds capable people credentials would screen out, though some roles do legally require a qualification. Give me the skills based requirements.
description: Replace credential requirements with demonstrable skills where the role allows.
useCase: Use this when requirements lean on degrees and years of experience. Those are rough stand ins for ability and screen out capable self taught or career changing candidates, so asking for the skill itself, shown through a portfolio or paid test, finds them, unless a qualification is legally required.

title: Be Honest About the Hard Parts of the Role
promptText: Help me write an honest section about the challenging parts of a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The hard or less glamorous parts are [WHAT IS TOUGH, E.G. EARLY MORNINGS, REPETITIVE TASKS, DIFFICULT CUSTOMERS, SEASONAL CRUNCH], and what makes it worth it is [THE GENUINE UPSIDES]. Write it in a straightforward way that does not scare off good people but does not hide the reality. Note that every job has parts people will not love, and hiding them only means the hire discovers them in week two and starts looking elsewhere, while naming them upfront lets candidates self select and makes the people who still apply far more likely to stay. Give me the honest role section.
description: Name the hard parts of a role upfront so the right people self select.
useCase: Use this to reduce early turnover. Every job has parts people will not love, and hiding them means the hire finds out in week two and starts looking elsewhere, while naming them upfront lets candidates self select and makes those who still apply far more likely to stay.
variables: WHAT IS TOUGH, E.G. EARLY MORNINGS, REPETITIVE TASKS, DIFFICULT CUSTOMERS, SEASONAL CRUNCH

title: Write a Genuine Why Work Here Section
promptText: Help me write the section of my job description that explains why someone would want to work at my small [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I can genuinely offer is [FLEXIBILITY, LEARNING, IMPACT, PAY, TEAM, MISSION], what I cannot offer compared to bigger employers is [WHAT YOU LACK], and the kind of person who thrives here is [WHO]. Write it honestly around the real advantages of a small business. Note that a small business usually cannot win on salary or benefits against large companies, but can offer real ownership, direct access to the founder, flexibility, and visible impact, and claiming perks I do not really have backfires fast, so leaning on the true advantages attracts people who value exactly what I can give. Give me the why work here section.
description: Explain honestly why someone would want to work at your small business.
useCase: Use this when you cannot compete on salary or benefits. A small business can offer real ownership, direct founder access, flexibility, and visible impact, and claiming perks you do not have backfires fast, so leaning on the true advantages attracts people who value what you can give.
variables: FLEXIBILITY, LEARNING, IMPACT, PAY, TEAM, MISSION

title: Write Application Instructions That Filter Well
promptText: Help me write the how to apply section of a job description for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I need to see from applicants is [CV, PORTFOLIO, SHORT ANSWER, SAMPLE WORK], how I want them to apply is [EMAIL, FORM, PLATFORM], and my timeline is [WHEN YOU WILL DECIDE]. Write clear instructions, including one small specific request that shows who actually read the description. Note that a simple instruction like answer one short question about the role filters out mass applicants who did not read it, but asking for heavy unpaid work at this stage drives good people away, so the request should be quick and relevant, and stating my timeline sets expectations and cuts follow up messages. Give me the application instructions.
description: Write how to apply instructions that filter out applicants who did not read the role.
useCase: Use this to cut down on careless applications. One small specific request filters out mass applicants who did not read the description, while heavy unpaid work drives good people away, so a quick relevant request plus a stated timeline keeps the pool strong and the follow ups down.
variables: CV, PORTFOLIO, SHORT ANSWER, SAMPLE WORK

title: Review a Job Description for Clarity
promptText: Help me review my job description as a candidate would read it for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is the draft: [PASTE THE JOB DESCRIPTION]. Read it cold and tell me honestly whether you could explain what this person does all day, how success is judged, what it pays, and whether you would be a fit, and point out anything vague, contradictory, or full of jargon. Note that I know the role so well that gaps are invisible to me, and vague phrases like various duties as needed or fast paced environment tell a candidate nothing, so a cold read catches what a real applicant would be confused by before it costs me good applications. Give me the review and fixes.
description: Read your job description cold as a candidate and fix what is vague.
useCase: Use this before posting any role. You know the role too well to see the gaps, and phrases like various duties as needed or fast paced environment tell a candidate nothing, so a cold read catches the confusion a real applicant would hit before it costs you good applications.

title: Refresh an Outdated Job Description
promptText: Help me update an old job description for my [BUSINESS TYPE] so it matches the role as it really is now. Here is the old description: [PASTE IT], and what the role actually involves today is [WHAT HAS CHANGED, OR WHAT THE CURRENT PERSON REALLY DOES]. Rewrite it to reflect the current reality, and flag anything from the old version that no longer belongs. Note that roles drift over time as a business changes, so rehiring from an old description often brings in someone suited to a job that no longer exists, and if someone currently does the role, asking them what the job really involves is the fastest way to get it right. Give me the refreshed description.
description: Update an old job description to match the role as it really is today.
useCase: Use this before rehiring for an existing role. Roles drift as a business changes, so hiring from an old description brings someone suited to a job that no longer exists, and asking the current person what the job really involves is the fastest way to get it right.
variables: WHAT HAS CHANGED, OR WHAT THE CURRENT PERSON REALLY DOES

title: Build a Structured Interview Question Set
promptText: Help me build a structured set of interview questions for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What success in the role looks like is [THE OUTCOMES OR SCORECARD], the skills that matter most are [KEY SKILLS], and the interview length is [HOW LONG]. Give me a fixed set of questions I will ask every candidate in the same order, each tied to a skill or outcome, with a note on what a strong answer includes. Note that asking every candidate the same questions makes answers comparable, while a free flowing chat mostly measures who I clicked with, so a structured set is one of the most reliable ways a small business can hire well without an HR team. Give me the structured question set.
description: Build a fixed interview question set tied to the role so candidates are comparable.
useCase: Use this before your first interview for a role. Asking every candidate the same questions makes their answers comparable, while a free flowing chat mostly measures who you clicked with, so a structured set is one of the most reliable ways to hire well without an HR team.

title: Write Behavioral Interview Questions
promptText: Help me write behavioral interview questions for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The situations this person will face are [REAL SITUATIONS IN THE ROLE, E.G. AN ANGRY CUSTOMER, A MISSED DEADLINE, UNCLEAR INSTRUCTIONS], and the qualities I need are [THE TRAITS]. Write questions that ask about real past experiences, like tell me about a time when, each with a couple of follow ups that dig for specifics. Note that what someone actually did before is a better predictor than what they say they would do, since hypothetical answers are easy to polish, and the follow ups matter most because rehearsed answers fall apart when asked what exactly they did and what happened next. Give me the behavioral questions.
description: Write past experience questions with follow ups that get past rehearsed answers.
useCase: Use this to learn how a candidate actually behaves at work. What someone did before predicts better than what they say they would do, and the follow ups matter most, since rehearsed answers fall apart when asked exactly what they did and what happened next.
variables: REAL SITUATIONS IN THE ROLE, E.G. AN ANGRY CUSTOMER, A MISSED DEADLINE, UNCLEAR INSTRUCTIONS

title: Get Quick Interview Questions for a Role
promptText: I have an interview soon and need questions fast. The role is [ROLE TITLE], the main work is [WHAT THEY WILL DO], and the one thing I most need to find out is [YOUR BIGGEST CONCERN]. Give me eight solid interview questions with one line on what a good answer sounds like, no long explanation, just the list. Give me the questions.
description: Get eight solid interview questions with good answer cues, fast.
useCase: Use this when an interview is coming up and you have not prepared. Eight questions focused on the role and your biggest concern, each with a cue for a good answer, beat improvising, and a quick prepared list keeps the interview on the things that matter.

title: Write Questions That Test Real Skill
promptText: Help me write interview questions that test whether a candidate can actually do the work of a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The core skills are [THE SKILLS], and a typical piece of work in the role is [AN EXAMPLE TASK]. Give me questions that make them explain how they would approach real work, walk through something they built or did, or reason through a small problem live. Note that people can describe skills they do not really have, so questions that require showing the thinking, like walk me through how you would handle this exact task, reveal real ability far better than asking whether they know a tool, and for some roles a small paid test says more than any question. Give me the skill questions.
description: Write interview questions that make candidates show real skill, not claim it.
useCase: Use this to check ability, not just claims. People can describe skills they do not have, so questions that require showing the thinking, like walking through how they would handle a real task, reveal ability far better than asking whether they know a tool.

title: Write Situational Questions From Real Scenarios
promptText: Help me turn real situations from my [BUSINESS TYPE] into interview questions for a [ROLE TITLE]. Here are a few things that actually happen here: [REAL SCENARIOS, E.G. TWO URGENT REQUESTS AT ONCE, A SUPPLIER LETS US DOWN, A CLIENT CHANGES SCOPE]. Write each as a short scenario question and describe what a strong, average, and weak answer would look like. Note that scenarios drawn from my real business test judgment in the exact conditions the person will face, which generic questions cannot, and writing down what strong looks like beforehand stops me from rating a confident answer higher than a sound one. Give me the scenario questions and answer guides.
description: Turn real situations from your business into scenario questions with answer guides.
useCase: Use this to test judgment in your actual conditions. Scenarios drawn from your real business show how someone would handle what they will actually face, and writing strong, average, and weak answers beforehand stops you rating a confident answer above a sound one.
variables: REAL SCENARIOS, E.G. TWO URGENT REQUESTS AT ONCE, A SUPPLIER LETS US DOWN, A CLIENT CHANGES SCOPE

title: Prepare Follow Up Probes for Vague Answers
promptText: Help me prepare follow up probes for when a candidate gives vague or rehearsed answers in an interview for a [ROLE TITLE]. My main questions are [PASTE YOUR QUESTIONS], and the kinds of vague answers I tend to get are [E.G. WE DID THIS AS A TEAM, I ALWAYS GIVE 110 PERCENT]. Give me a set of follow ups that politely push for specifics, like what was your part exactly, what would you do differently, and how did you measure that. Note that the first answer is often the prepared one, and the real information comes from the second and third question, so having follow ups ready lets me get past polish without being aggressive, and a candidate who cannot give any specifics at all is telling me something too. Give me the follow up probes.
description: Prepare polite follow ups that push vague answers toward specifics.
useCase: Use this when interviews feel full of polished but empty answers. The first answer is often the prepared one and the real information comes from the second and third question, so ready follow ups get past polish politely, and an inability to give any specifics is itself useful information.
variables: E.G. WE DID THIS AS A TEAM, I ALWAYS GIVE 110 PERCENT

title: Create a Scoring Rubric for Answers
promptText: Help me create a simple scoring rubric for my interview questions for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My questions are [PASTE YOUR QUESTIONS], and what matters most in the role is [THE PRIORITIES]. For each question, give me a one to four scale with a short description of what each score looks like, and tell me how to weight the questions. Note that scoring right after each interview, before comparing candidates, keeps my memory from blurring and stops the most recent or most charming candidate from winning by default, and a written rubric also makes it easier to explain a decision to myself later. Give me the rubric.
description: Create a one to four scoring rubric for each interview question.
useCase: Use this to compare candidates fairly. Scoring against a written rubric right after each interview keeps memory from blurring and stops the most recent or most charming candidate from winning by default, and it makes the final decision easier to justify.

title: Plan a Short Screening Call
promptText: Help me plan a short screening call of about [HOW MANY MINUTES] for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The dealbreakers I need to check are [PAY EXPECTATIONS, AVAILABILITY, TIME ZONE, LANGUAGE, CORE SKILL], and what I want to sense about the person is [WHAT ELSE]. Give me a tight script with a few questions in order and a clear way to end the call either way. Note that a short screen exists to catch dealbreakers early, so checking pay, availability, and basic fit first saves both sides from a long interview that was never going to work, and keeping it short and consistent respects candidates' time. Give me the screening call plan.
description: Plan a short screening call that catches dealbreakers before full interviews.
useCase: Use this before booking longer interviews. A short screen catches dealbreakers like pay, availability, and time zone early, which saves both sides from a long interview that was never going to work, and keeping it consistent respects everyone's time.
variables: PAY EXPECTATIONS, AVAILABILITY, TIME ZONE, LANGUAGE, CORE SKILL

title: Ask Candidates to Walk Through Past Work
promptText: Help me plan a walkthrough of a candidate's past work for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What they are bringing is [PORTFOLIO, SAMPLE, PAST PROJECT, CODE, CASE STUDY], and what I need to judge is [QUALITY, PROCESS, OWNERSHIP, DECISIONS]. Give me questions that uncover what they personally did, why they made the choices they made, and what they would change. Note that portfolios show finished results, often from team efforts, so the walkthrough is where I find out their actual contribution and thinking, and a candidate who can clearly explain their decisions and mistakes is usually more reliable than one with prettier samples and vague explanations. Give me the walkthrough questions.
description: Plan questions that reveal what a candidate personally did in their past work.
useCase: Use this when a candidate brings a portfolio or past project. Portfolios show finished results, often from teams, so a walkthrough reveals their actual contribution and thinking, and someone who explains their decisions and mistakes clearly is usually more reliable than one with prettier samples.
variables: PORTFOLIO, SAMPLE, PAST PROJECT, CODE, CASE STUDY

title: Ask About Values Without Hiring Clones
promptText: Help me write interview questions about how a candidate works and what they value for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The working values that really matter here are [YOUR VALUES, E.G. OWNERSHIP, DIRECT FEEDBACK, RELIABILITY], and how we actually work day to day is [YOUR WORKING STYLE]. Write questions that test for those values through past behavior, and warn me where culture fit could slide into hiring people just like me. Note that culture fit questions easily turn into checking whether someone shares my background, hobbies, or personality, which narrows the team and can be unfair, so the useful version tests shared working values like reliability and honesty while welcoming different backgrounds and styles. Give me the values questions.
description: Test for working values through behavior without screening for sameness.
useCase: Use this when fit matters but you want a fair process. Culture fit questions easily slide into checking whether someone shares your background or personality, which narrows the team and can be unfair, so testing shared working values while welcoming different styles is the useful version.
variables: YOUR VALUES, E.G. OWNERSHIP, DIRECT FEEDBACK, RELIABILITY

title: Check for Questions You Should Not Ask
promptText: Help me check my interview questions for anything inappropriate or legally risky for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My questions are [PASTE YOUR QUESTIONS], and I am hiring in [COUNTRY OR REGION]. Flag questions that touch on age, marital status, pregnancy or family plans, religion, health, nationality, or similar personal areas, and suggest job related alternatives where there is a real need behind them. Note that many casual questions, like do you have kids or where are you originally from, can be unlawful or discriminatory in many places and are rarely relevant to the work anyway, and rules differ by country, so I should confirm the specifics for my location, while the safe rule is to ask only about the job and the ability to do it. Give me the flags and alternatives.
description: Flag interview questions that touch personal or legally risky areas.
useCase: Use this before any interview. Casual questions like do you have kids or where are you from can be unlawful or discriminatory in many places and are rarely relevant to the work, so flagging them and asking only about the job is safer, while confirming the rules for your country.

title: Probe Gently on Possible Red Flags
promptText: Help me ask about possible concerns in a candidate's background fairly, for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I noticed is [E.G. SHORT JOB STINTS, A GAP, A VAGUE ROLE, A SKILL CLAIM THAT SEEMS STRETCHED], and why it matters for this role is [YOUR CONCERN]. Give me neutral, non accusing questions that let the candidate explain. Note that many apparent red flags have ordinary explanations like caring for family, a company closing, or contract work, so asking openly gives them a fair chance and often resolves the worry, while assuming the worst quietly rules out good people, and the real signal is usually how honestly and clearly they explain it. Give me the questions.
description: Ask neutral questions about background concerns so candidates can explain.
useCase: Use this when something in a candidate's history gives you pause. Gaps and short stints often have ordinary explanations like family care or a company closing, so asking openly gives them a fair chance and often resolves the worry, and how honestly they explain it is usually the real signal.
variables: E.G. SHORT JOB STINTS, A GAP, A VAGUE ROLE, A SKILL CLAIM THAT SEEMS STRETCHED

title: Write Questions for a Remote Role
promptText: Help me write interview questions for a remote [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. How we work remotely is [YOUR SETUP, E.G. ASYNC MESSAGING, DAILY CALLS, TIME ZONE OVERLAP], and the hardest parts of remote work here are [WHAT TRIPS PEOPLE UP]. Write questions that reveal how they manage their own time, communicate in writing, handle unclear instructions without someone nearby, and stay reachable. Note that remote work exposes self management and written communication far more than office work does, and a strong performer in an office can struggle without structure, so questions about how they actually worked remotely before, plus how clearly they write to me during the process, tell me more than any claim that they are self motivated. Give me the remote role questions.
description: Write questions that test self management and written communication for remote work.
useCase: Use this when hiring someone you will rarely see. Remote work exposes self management and written communication far more than office work, so asking how they actually worked remotely before, and noticing how clearly they write to you during hiring, beats a claim of being self motivated.
variables: YOUR SETUP, E.G. ASYNC MESSAGING, DAILY CALLS, TIME ZONE OVERLAP

title: Interview Fairly Across a Language Gap
promptText: Help me interview candidates fairly when we are working in a language that is not the first language for one or both of us, for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The interview language is [LANGUAGE], the level of that language the job truly needs is [WHAT THE ROLE REQUIRES, E.G. CUSTOMER FACING, INTERNAL ONLY, WRITTEN ONLY], and the candidates are mostly [WHO]. Help me phrase questions plainly, test the language level the role actually needs, and avoid confusing fluency with competence. Note that a candidate can be excellent at the work but slower or less polished in an interview language, and a smooth talker can be weak at the job, so I should test the language level the role really requires separately and judge the skills on their own, using simple wording and allowing written follow ups where it helps. Give me the approach and adjusted questions.
description: Run interviews across a language gap without mistaking fluency for skill.
useCase: Use this when hiring across languages. A strong worker can be less polished in an interview language while a smooth talker can be weak at the job, so testing the language level the role truly needs separately and judging skills on their own gives a fairer and more accurate result.
variables: WHAT THE ROLE REQUIRES, E.G. CUSTOMER FACING, INTERNAL ONLY, WRITTEN ONLY

title: Write Questions for Your First Hire
promptText: Help me write interview questions for the first person I am hiring at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The role is [WHAT THEY WILL DO], how things run right now is [HOW CHAOTIC OR STRUCTURED IT IS], and what I worry about most is [YOUR BIGGEST WORRY]. Write questions that test whether they can work with little structure, figure things out alone, and handle a role that will change. Note that a first hire in a tiny business needs different strengths from someone joining an established team, like comfort with ambiguity and building their own systems, and someone who thrived with clear processes and a manager nearby may struggle, so the questions should test for that reality rather than general competence. Give me the first hire questions.
description: Test whether a first hire can thrive with little structure and a changing role.
useCase: Use this when hiring your first person. A first hire needs comfort with ambiguity and building their own systems, and someone who thrived with clear processes and a manager nearby may struggle, so questions should test for that reality rather than general competence.
variables: HOW CHAOTIC OR STRUCTURED IT IS

title: Prepare for the Questions Candidates Ask You
promptText: Help me prepare honest answers to the questions good candidates will ask me about my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The role is [ROLE TITLE], the things I am a little nervous about being asked are [E.G. HOW STABLE THE BUSINESS IS, GROWTH, PAY REVIEWS, WHY THE LAST PERSON LEFT], and the honest answers are [THE TRUTH]. Give me a list of likely questions and clear, honest ways to answer them. Note that strong candidates are interviewing me too and will often ask about stability, growth, and why the role is open, and evasive answers make good people walk away while honest answers, even imperfect ones, build trust and set the right expectations from day one. Give me the questions and answers.
description: Prepare honest answers to the hard questions strong candidates ask you.
useCase: Use this before interviewing strong candidates. They interview you too and often ask about stability, growth, and why the role is open, and evasive answers make good people walk away while honest ones, even imperfect, build trust and set the right expectations.
variables: E.G. HOW STABLE THE BUSINESS IS, GROWTH, PAY REVIEWS, WHY THE LAST PERSON LEFT

title: Close an Interview Well
promptText: Help me plan how to close interviews for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My next steps after the interview are [WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, E.G. A PAID TEST, A SECOND CALL, A DECISION], and my timeline is [WHEN YOU WILL DECIDE]. Give me a short closing script that invites their questions, checks anything I still need, like notice period or start date, and tells them exactly what happens next and when. Note that candidates judge my business partly by how the interview ends, and leaving them with no idea of next steps or timing is one of the most common complaints about hiring, so a clear close, followed through, keeps good candidates interested even if they have other offers. Give me the closing script.
description: End interviews with clear next steps, timing, and room for their questions.
useCase: Use this so good candidates stay interested. Candidates judge your business by how the interview ends, and leaving them unsure of next steps is one of the most common hiring complaints, so a clear close that you then follow through on keeps strong people engaged.
variables: WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, E.G. A PAID TEST, A SECOND CALL, A DECISION

title: Capture Interview Notes While They Are Fresh
promptText: Help me turn my rough notes from an interview into a clear record for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My notes are [PASTE YOUR NOTES], and my scoring rubric or priorities are [YOUR RUBRIC OR PRIORITIES]. Organize them by question or skill, separate what the candidate actually said from my impressions, and suggest a score for each area with the evidence behind it. Note that memory of an interview fades and blends within a day, especially across several candidates, so writing up evidence right away, and keeping facts apart from gut feelings, makes the final comparison fairer and stops one memorable moment from outweighing everything else. Give me the organized record.
description: Turn rough interview notes into an evidence based record with scores.
useCase: Use this right after each interview. Memory of interviews fades and blends within a day, especially across several candidates, so writing up evidence immediately and keeping facts apart from gut feelings makes the final comparison fairer and stops one memorable moment dominating.

title: Improve Questions That Are Not Working
promptText: Help me improve interview questions that are not telling me enough for a [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current questions are [PASTE THEM], and the problem is [E.G. EVERYONE GIVES SIMILAR ANSWERS, A HIRE STRUGGLED WITH SOMETHING I NEVER ASKED ABOUT, THEY ARE TOO EASY TO REHEARSE]. Tell me which questions are weak, why, and give me sharper replacements. Note that questions everyone answers well do not separate candidates, and if a past hire struggled with something, that gap is a clue about what the interview missed, so the best improvements come from asking what went wrong after previous hires and adding a question that would have caught it. Give me the improved questions.
description: Sharpen interview questions that fail to separate candidates.
useCase: Use this when your interviews are not predicting how hires turn out. Questions everyone answers well do not separate candidates, and a past hire's struggle points to what the interview missed, so adding a question that would have caught it is usually the best improvement.
variables: E.G. EVERYONE GIVES SIMILAR ANSWERS, A HIRE STRUGGLED WITH SOMETHING I NEVER ASKED ABOUT, THEY ARE TOO EASY TO REHEARSE

title: Build a 30 60 90 Day Onboarding Plan
promptText: Help me build a 30, 60, and 90 day onboarding plan for a new [ROLE TITLE] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What they need to learn is [SYSTEMS, PRODUCTS, CUSTOMERS, PROCESSES], what I want them handling independently by day 90 is [THE GOAL], and how much time I can give them each week is [YOUR REAL AVAILABILITY]. Give me a plan with learning goals, small wins, and checkpoints for each stage. Note that most new hires in small businesses are thrown in and left to figure it out, which slows them down and drives early quitting, but a plan that is too ambitious for the support I can actually give fails just as badly, so the plan has to match my real time, and a few clear milestones beat a long list nobody follows. Give me the 30 60 90 plan.
description: Build a realistic 30, 60, and 90 day plan matched to the time you can give.
useCase: Use this before a new hire starts. Being thrown in to figure it out slows people down and drives early quitting, but an over ambitious plan fails just as badly if you cannot support it, so a few clear milestones matched to your real time are what make onboarding work.

title: Prepare Everything Before Day One
promptText: Help me make a checklist of everything to set up before a new [ROLE TITLE] starts at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tools and accounts they will need are [E.G. useCase: Use this when freelance work misses the mark. Contractor feedback works best tied to what the brief agreed rather than general preferences, since they deliver against a scope, and owning any unclear parts of the brief keeps good freelancers willing to work with you again.

title: Ask Your Team for Feedback on You
promptText: Help me ask the people who work for me at my [BUSINESS TYPE] for honest feedback on how I manage them. My team is [WHO], things I suspect I could do better are [YOUR GUESSES], and how I plan to ask is [IN PERSON, ANONYMOUS FORM, ONE ON ONE]. Give me a few specific questions and a way of asking that makes honest answers feel safe. Note that people rarely give the boss honest criticism, especially in a very small team where anonymity is hard, so specific questions like what is one thing I should stop doing work better than are you happy, and how I react to the first piece of criticism decides whether I ever get honest feedback again. Give me the questions and approach.
description: Ask your team for honest feedback on how you manage them.
useCase: Use this to find your own blind spots as a manager. People rarely criticize the boss honestly, especially in tiny teams where anonymity is hard, so specific questions work better than asking if they are happy, and how you react to the first criticism decides whether you hear more.
variables: IN PERSON, ANONYMOUS FORM, ONE ON ONE

title: Have a Career Growth Conversation
promptText: Help me have a career growth conversation with a good team member at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Their role is [ROLE TITLE], what they seem interested in is [THEIR INTERESTS OR AMBITIONS], and what growth I can realistically offer is [MORE RESPONSIBILITY, NEW SKILLS, PAY, TITLE, OR LIMITED]. Help me plan the conversation, including being honest if the growth they want is not possible here. Note that small businesses often cannot offer the promotion ladder a large company can, but can offer new responsibility, skills, and closer involvement, and being honest about the limits builds more trust than vague promises that never happen, since a good person who feels stuck will leave either way. Give me the growth conversation plan.
description: Talk about growth honestly, including what your small business can and cannot offer.
useCase: Use this to keep good people engaged. Small businesses rarely have a promotion ladder but can offer new responsibility, skills, and involvement, and honesty about the limits builds more trust than vague promises, since a good person who feels stuck will leave either way.
variables: MORE RESPONSIBILITY, NEW SKILLS, PAY, TITLE, OR LIMITED

title: Handle a Pay Raise Conversation
promptText: Help me handle a conversation about pay with a team member at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. They have asked for or I am considering [THE RAISE OR CHANGE], their performance is [YOUR HONEST VIEW], what the business can afford is [YOUR REAL LIMITS], and local pay for similar roles is [WHAT YOU KNOW, OR UNSURE]. Help me prepare whether the answer is yes, not yet, or no, with honest reasoning and, if not now, what would change it. Note that a vague maybe later without criteria feels like a no and damages trust, so tying pay to clear expectations and a timeline is fairer, and I should check current local market rates rather than guess, since underpaying a strong person usually costs more in turnover than the raise would. Give me the conversation plan.
description: Prepare an honest yes, not yet, or no answer to a pay discussion.
useCase: Use this when pay comes up. A vague maybe later feels like a no and damages trust, so tying pay to clear expectations and a timeline is fairer, and checking local market rates rather than guessing matters, since underpaying a strong person often costs more in turnover than the raise.

title: Follow Up After Giving Feedback
promptText: Help me follow up after giving a team member feedback at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The feedback was about [THE ISSUE], what we agreed was [THE ACTIONS], and what I have seen since is [IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, OR MIXED]. Help me plan what to say at the follow up, including recognizing progress and addressing anything that has not changed. Note that feedback without follow up quietly signals it did not matter, so a short check in a week or two later shows I meant it, and noticing real improvement out loud is as important as raising what is still missing, since people who change and get no acknowledgment tend to stop trying. Give me the follow up plan.
description: Follow up on feedback to recognize progress or address what has not changed.
useCase: Use this a week or two after giving feedback. Feedback without follow up signals it did not matter, so a short check in shows you meant it, and noticing real improvement out loud matters as much as raising what is missing, since people who change unnoticed tend to stop trying.

title: Adapt Feedback Across Cultures
promptText: Help me adapt how I give feedback to a team member from a different cultural background at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My usual feedback style is [YOUR STYLE, E.G. VERY DIRECT, INFORMAL], their background or where they are based is [COUNTRY OR CONTEXT], and what I have noticed so far is [E.G. THEY NEVER DISAGREE, THEY SEEM HURT BY CRITICISM, THEY MISS HINTS]. Help me adjust my approach so the message lands without being lost or causing offense. Note that norms around direct criticism, saving face, disagreeing with a boss, and public versus private feedback vary widely between cultures, so feedback that feels normal to me can feel harsh or be missed entirely, but I should treat cultural patterns as a starting point and ask the person directly how they prefer to receive feedback rather than stereotype them. Give me the adjusted approach.
description: Adjust how you give feedback so it lands across cultural differences.
useCase: Use this when feedback is not landing with someone from a different background. Norms around direct criticism, saving face, and disagreeing with a boss vary widely, so your normal style can feel harsh or be missed, but asking the person how they prefer feedback beats relying on stereotypes.
