title: Build a Complete Project Brief for a Contractor
promptText: Help me build a complete project brief for a contractor working with my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The project is [WHAT YOU NEED DONE], why I need it and who it is for is [THE GOAL AND AUDIENCE], my budget and deadline are [BUDGET AND DATE], and what I already have is [FILES, EXAMPLES, ACCESS]. Give me a brief with background, goal, deliverables, what is out of scope, deadline, budget, how work will be reviewed, and who to contact. Note that most contractor problems come from briefs that seemed clear to me but left key decisions unstated, so the brief should answer the questions a good contractor would otherwise have to ask, and a contractor guessing at what I want usually means paying for a second round. Give me the project brief.
description: Build a full contractor brief that answers the questions a good contractor would ask.
useCase: Use this before hiring anyone for a project. Most contractor problems come from briefs that seemed clear but left key decisions unstated, so answering the questions a good contractor would ask up front saves paying for a second round of guesswork.

title: Define What Is In and Out of Scope
promptText: Help me define the scope of a contractor project for my [BUSINESS TYPE] so it does not grow out of control. The project is [THE WORK], the deliverables I need are [THE DELIVERABLES], and the extras I might be tempted to add later are [LIKELY ADD ONS]. Give me a clear in scope list, an out of scope list, and a sentence on how extra requests will be handled and priced. Note that scope creep usually comes from me, not the contractor, as one more small thing gets added mid project, which causes delays, frustration, and disputes about price, so naming what is out of scope up front protects the relationship and the budget, and it makes it easy to say that is a separate job when ideas come up. Give me the scope section.
description: Set clear in scope and out of scope lists to prevent scope creep.
useCase: Use this before a project starts. Scope creep usually comes from the client adding one more small thing mid project, causing delays and price disputes, so naming what is out of scope up front protects the budget and the relationship and makes new ideas easy to treat as separate jobs.

title: Get a Quick Contractor Brief
promptText: I need a short brief for a contractor right now. The job is [WHAT YOU NEED], the deadline is [DATE], the budget is [AMOUNT], and the one thing they must get right is [THE PRIORITY]. Give me a short clear brief I can paste into a message, no explanation, just the brief. Give me the brief.
description: Get a short paste ready contractor brief for a quick job.
useCase: Use this for small, quick jobs. A short brief covering the task, deadline, budget, and the one thing that must be right is enough for simple work, and sending something clear now beats either no brief or a long one that delays a small job.

title: Define What Done Looks Like
promptText: Help me write clear acceptance criteria for a contractor project for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The deliverable is [WHAT THEY WILL HAND OVER], what it needs to do or achieve is [THE REQUIREMENTS], and the format I need it in is [FILE TYPES, PLATFORMS, SIZES]. Give me a short checklist that defines when the work counts as finished and accepted. Note that disagreements about whether work is done are one of the most common contractor disputes, especially when payment depends on it, so a checklist agreed at the start turns a subjective argument into a simple check, though it should cover what genuinely matters rather than every personal preference. Give me the acceptance criteria.
description: Define a checklist for when contractor work counts as finished.
useCase: Use this when payment depends on the work being done. Disagreements over whether work is finished are one of the most common contractor disputes, so a checklist agreed at the start turns an argument into a simple check, as long as it covers what genuinely matters.

title: Set Revision Rounds in the Brief
promptText: Help me set the revision terms for a contractor project for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The type of work is [DESIGN, WRITING, VIDEO, CODE, OTHER], how many rounds of changes I expect to need is [YOUR GUESS], and how I will give feedback is [HOW]. Give me a short revisions section stating how many rounds are included, what counts as a revision versus new work, and how extra rounds are handled. Note that unlimited revisions sound good for me but often lead to slower, defensive work and strained relationships, while clear limits push me to give complete feedback each round, and the difference between a revision and a new request is worth stating plainly to avoid surprise bills. Give me the revisions section.
description: Set clear revision rounds and separate revisions from new work.
useCase: Use this for creative or technical work that may need changes. Unlimited revisions often lead to slower, defensive work and strained relationships, while clear limits push you to give complete feedback each round, and stating what counts as new work avoids surprise bills.

title: Structure Payment Milestones
promptText: Help me structure payment for a contractor project for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The total budget is [AMOUNT AND CURRENCY], the project length is [DURATION], how I will pay is [BANK TRANSFER, PLATFORM, WALLET, OTHER], and the natural stages of the work are [STAGES]. Suggest a milestone payment plan tied to deliverables, with clear triggers for each payment. Note that paying everything up front puts all the risk on me while paying only at the end puts it on them, so milestones tied to finished stages share the risk fairly, and paying on time as agreed is one of the main reasons good freelancers keep choosing to work with a client, while cross border payments can carry fees and delays worth agreeing on in advance. Give me the payment plan.
description: Split contractor payments into milestones tied to finished deliverables.
useCase: Use this for projects larger than a quick job. Paying all up front puts the risk on you and paying only at the end puts it on them, so milestones tied to finished stages share risk fairly, and agreeing on cross border fees and timing in advance avoids friction.

title: Explain Your Taste With Reference Examples
promptText: Help me explain the style or quality I want to a contractor using reference examples for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The work is [WHAT THEY ARE MAKING], examples I like are [LINKS OR DESCRIPTIONS], what I like about each is [WHAT SPECIFICALLY], and examples I dislike are [WHAT TO AVOID AND WHY]. Turn this into a clear references section that tells the contractor what to take from each example and what not to copy. Note that words like modern, clean, or professional mean different things to different people, so concrete examples communicate taste far better, but only if I say what specifically I like in each, since a contractor shown a reference without explanation may copy the wrong thing, and examples I dislike are often just as useful. Give me the references section.
description: Turn reference examples into clear guidance on the style you want.
useCase: Use this for creative work where taste matters. Words like modern or clean mean different things to different people, so concrete examples communicate far better, but only if you say what you like in each, and examples you dislike are often just as useful.

title: Write a Brief for a Freelance Writer
promptText: Help me write a brief for a freelance writer creating content for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The piece is [TYPE, E.G. BLOG POST, WEBSITE COPY, EMAIL SERIES], the audience is [WHO WILL READ IT], the goal is [WHAT IT SHOULD ACHIEVE], key points or sources to use are [WHAT TO INCLUDE], and the length and tone are [LENGTH AND VOICE]. Give me a writer brief including keywords if relevant, what to avoid, and how I will review it. Note that a writer can only be as accurate as the information I give, so sharing my real expertise, examples, and opinions makes the result sound like my business rather than generic filler, and being clear about facts that must be checked or claims I cannot make saves risky edits later. Give me the writer brief.
description: Brief a freelance writer with the audience, goal, voice, and facts to use.
useCase: Use this when hiring someone to write for you. A writer can only be as accurate as what you give them, so sharing your expertise, examples, and opinions makes the piece sound like your business rather than filler, and flagging claims you cannot make saves risky edits later.
variables: TYPE, E.G. BLOG POST, WEBSITE COPY, EMAIL SERIES

title: Write a Brief for a Freelance Designer
promptText: Help me write a brief for a freelance designer working on [WHAT THEY ARE DESIGNING, E.G. SOCIAL GRAPHICS, PACKAGING, A FLYER, A WEBSITE PAGE] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Who it is for is [THE AUDIENCE], my existing brand assets are [LOGO, COLORS, FONTS, OR NONE], where it will be used and in what sizes is [FORMATS], and the text or content that must appear is [THE CONTENT]. Give me a design brief covering purpose, audience, assets, formats, required content, and the files I need back. Note that designers lose a lot of time waiting for final text and missing assets, and getting a beautiful design in the wrong size or without editable source files is a common frustration, so the brief should supply the content up front and state exactly which files and formats I need delivered. Give me the design brief.
description: Brief a designer with content, assets, formats, and the files you need back.
useCase: Use this when hiring a designer for non logo work. Designers lose time waiting on final text and missing assets, and getting a great design in the wrong size or without editable files is a common frustration, so supplying content up front and naming the files you need back avoids both.

title: Write a Brief for a Video Editor
promptText: Help me write a brief for a video editor for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The footage I have is [WHAT AND HOW MUCH], the finished video should be [LENGTH, PLATFORM, ASPECT RATIO], the goal is [WHAT THE VIDEO SHOULD DO], and the style I want is [PACE, MUSIC, CAPTIONS, BRANDING]. Give me an editing brief with the story or structure, must include moments, style notes, captions and branding, and delivery formats. Note that editors cannot read my mind about which moments matter, so marking timestamps for the key parts and stating the target length and platform saves rounds of back and forth, and I should confirm I have the rights to any music or footage I hand over, since licensing problems fall on my business. Give me the video editing brief.
description: Brief a video editor with structure, key moments, style, and delivery formats.
useCase: Use this when handing footage to an editor. Editors cannot guess which moments matter, so marking timestamps and stating the target length and platform saves rounds of revisions, and confirming you have rights to any music or footage avoids licensing problems that fall on you.

title: Brief a Virtual Assistant on Recurring Tasks
promptText: Help me brief a virtual assistant on recurring tasks for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tasks are [WHAT THEY WILL DO REGULARLY], how often each happens is [DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY], the tools involved are [APPS AND ACCOUNTS], and the decisions they can make alone versus check with me are [YOUR LIMITS]. Give me a task brief with a short step by step for each task, how to report back, and what to do when something unusual comes up. Note that a virtual assistant works from instructions rather than context, so steps that seem obvious to me need writing down, and a clear rule for when to stop and ask prevents both endless questions and costly guesses, while giving access only to what each task needs protects my accounts. Give me the VA task brief.
description: Brief a virtual assistant with step by step tasks and clear decision limits.
useCase: Use this when handing routine work to a VA. A VA works from instructions rather than context, so obvious seeming steps need writing down, a clear rule for when to ask prevents both endless questions and costly guesses, and limited access protects your accounts.

title: Write a Brief for Ongoing Retainer Work
promptText: Help me write a brief for an ongoing retainer with a contractor for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The ongoing work is [WHAT THEY WILL DO EACH MONTH], the monthly amount or hours is [THE RETAINER], how requests will come in is [HOW YOU WILL ASSIGN WORK], and how often we will review it is [FREQUENCY]. Give me a retainer brief covering what is included each month, turnaround times, how unused or extra hours are handled, reporting, and how either side can end it. Note that retainers work well for steady needs but go wrong when the monthly scope is vague, leaving one side feeling short changed, so stating what a month covers and how overflow is handled keeps it fair, and a regular review lets us adjust before frustration builds. Give me the retainer brief.
description: Brief an ongoing retainer with monthly scope, turnaround, and overflow rules.
useCase: Use this for steady, ongoing contractor work. Retainers go wrong when monthly scope is vague and one side feels short changed, so stating what a month covers, how unused or extra hours work, and reviewing regularly keeps the arrangement fair before frustration builds.

title: Plan What Access a Contractor Gets
promptText: Help me plan what access a contractor needs for a project with my [BUSINESS TYPE] and how to give it safely. The work is [THE PROJECT], the systems involved are [WEBSITE, HOSTING, SOCIAL ACCOUNTS, DRIVE, PAYMENT TOOLS, CUSTOMER DATA], and the project length is [DURATION]. Give me a list of what access they need, the safest way to grant each, like a separate user or limited role instead of my own login, and a checklist for removing access when the work ends. Note that handing a contractor my main password is convenient but means they can do anything and I cannot easily take it back, so limited, individual access is much safer, and forgotten access after a project ends is a common security gap for small businesses. Give me the access plan.
description: Give a contractor only the access they need and plan to remove it afterward.
useCase: Use this before sharing any logins with a contractor. Handing over your main password means they can do anything and you cannot easily take it back, so limited individual access is safer, and forgotten access after a project ends is a common small business security gap.

title: State File Delivery and Ownership in the Brief
promptText: Help me write the delivery and ownership section of a contractor brief for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The work produced will be [WHAT THEY CREATE], the files I need at the end are [FINAL FILES, SOURCE FILES, EDITABLE VERSIONS, CODE REPOSITORY], and how I plan to use it is [WHERE AND HOW LONG]. Give me a clear section stating what files get delivered, where, and who owns the work once paid, plus questions to confirm with the contractor. Note that many small businesses discover too late that they only received a flattened image or that the contractor still owns the code or source files, which makes future edits costly, so ownership and source files should be agreed in writing up front, and ownership rules vary by country, so a proper contract matters for anything important. Give me the delivery and ownership section.
description: Agree up front on which files you receive and who owns the work.
useCase: Use this for any work you will want to edit or reuse later. Many businesses discover too late they only got a flattened image or the contractor still owns the source files or code, so agreeing files and ownership in writing up front matters, along with a proper contract for important work.

title: Check a Brief for Missing Information
promptText: Help me check my contractor brief for gaps before I send it for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is the brief: [PASTE THE BRIEF], and the type of contractor is [WHO THEY ARE]. Read it as that contractor would and list the questions they would need to ask before starting, plus anything vague, contradictory, or missing like budget, deadline, formats, or how work is approved. Note that a contractor who must email ten questions before starting loses momentum and may quote higher to cover the uncertainty, while some will simply guess, so catching gaps before sending is faster for both sides, and if I cannot answer a question myself, that is a decision I need to make first. Give me the gaps and questions.
description: Read your brief as the contractor would and find the missing answers.
useCase: Use this before sending any brief. A contractor facing many unanswered questions loses momentum, may quote higher to cover uncertainty, or simply guesses, so catching gaps first is faster for both sides, and a question you cannot answer is a decision you need to make first.

title: Give Feedback on a Contractor's First Draft
promptText: Help me give clear, consolidated feedback on a contractor's first draft for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The brief asked for [WHAT WAS AGREED], the draft I received is [DESCRIBE IT], what works is [THE GOOD PARTS], and what needs changing is [THE CHANGES]. Turn this into one organized feedback message with specific changes, priorities, and anything that is a change from the original brief. Note that scattered feedback sent in several messages, or vague notes like make it pop, cost revision rounds and frustrate good contractors, so one complete, specific message tied to the brief gets better results, and being honest when I changed my mind rather than presenting it as their mistake keeps the relationship fair. Give me the feedback message.
description: Turn reactions to a draft into one clear, consolidated feedback message.
useCase: Use this when a contractor sends a draft. Scattered feedback across several messages or vague notes like make it pop waste revision rounds, so one complete, specific message tied to the brief gets better results, and owning changes of mind keeps the relationship fair.

title: Request a Change to Agreed Scope
promptText: Help me ask a contractor for a change to the agreed work for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The original scope was [WHAT WAS AGREED], what I now want to add or change is [THE CHANGE], why it changed is [THE REASON], and my budget and timing flexibility is [WHAT YOU CAN OFFER]. Write a clear message acknowledging this is new work and asking for their cost and time impact. Note that framing a scope change as a quick tweak when it is really new work damages trust and leads to rushed or resentful work, while openly asking what it will cost and how it affects the deadline treats the contractor fairly and keeps quality up, and getting the change confirmed in writing avoids disputes at payment time. Give me the change request message.
description: Ask openly for a scope change and its cost and timing impact.
useCase: Use this when you need more than was agreed. Framing new work as a quick tweak damages trust and leads to rushed or resentful work, while openly asking about cost and deadline impact treats the contractor fairly, and confirming the change in writing avoids disputes at payment time.

title: Wrap Up a Contractor Project Cleanly
promptText: Help me wrap up a finished contractor project for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The project was [WHAT THEY DID], what still needs handing over is [FILES, PASSWORDS, DOCUMENTATION, INSTRUCTIONS], and whether I want to work with them again is [YES, MAYBE, NO]. Give me an end of project checklist and a short closing message covering final payment, file handover, access removal, and, if deserved, thanks and a review or referral. Note that projects often fizzle out with loose ends, like missing source files, unpaid final invoices, or contractors still holding access, so a clean wrap up protects my business, and a genuine thank you or a public review costs nothing and makes a good contractor much more likely to prioritize me next time. Give me the checklist and closing message.
description: Close a contractor project with handover, payment, access removal, and thanks.
useCase: Use this when a contractor finishes. Projects often fizzle with missing source files, unpaid invoices, or contractors still holding access, so a clean wrap up protects your business, and a genuine thank you or review makes a good contractor more likely to prioritize you next time.

title: Define Your Team's Working Values
promptText: Help me define the working values for my small team at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. How we actually work at our best is [EXAMPLES OF GOOD WORK HABITS], what frustrates me or the team is [BEHAVIORS YOU DO NOT WANT], and the size of the team is [HOW MANY PEOPLE]. Turn this into three to five values, each with a plain explanation and one example of what it looks like in practice. Note that values like integrity and excellence sound right but guide nobody because everyone already claims them, while values written as real behaviors, like we reply to customers within a day or we flag problems early instead of hiding them, actually shape how people act, and values only mean something if I follow them too. Give me the working values.
description: Turn how your team actually works into a few values written as real behaviors.
useCase: Use this when you want shared standards for your team. Values like integrity sound right but guide nobody, while values written as behaviors, like flagging problems early, actually shape how people act, and they only mean something if you follow them too.

title: Write a How We Work Document
promptText: Help me write a short how we work document for my team at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Our tools are [WHAT WE USE], our working hours and availability are [HOURS AND TIME ZONES], how work is assigned and tracked is [YOUR SYSTEM], and the unwritten rules people usually learn the hard way are [THINGS NEW PEOPLE GET WRONG]. Turn this into a practical document covering tools, hours, communication, how tasks move, and the unwritten rules. Note that most friction in small teams comes from unwritten expectations that everyone assumes others know, so writing down how things actually work, rather than how I wish they worked, saves new people weeks of guessing and settles small disagreements before they start. Give me the how we work document.
description: Write down how your team actually works, including the unwritten rules.
useCase: Use this when people keep learning the rules the hard way. Most small team friction comes from unwritten expectations everyone assumes others know, so writing down how things actually work saves new people weeks of guessing and settles small disagreements early.

title: Get a Quick Team Culture Doc Draft
promptText: I need a quick team culture doc draft to edit. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], the team is [SIZE AND SETUP], and the three things that matter most in how we work are [YOUR TOP THREE]. Give me a short one page draft covering values, how we communicate, and what we expect from each other, no explanation, just the draft. Give me the culture doc.
description: Get a short one page team culture draft to edit.

title: Create a Starter Team Handbook
promptText: Help me create a short starter handbook for my team at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The team is [WHO, INCLUDING EMPLOYEES OR CONTRACTORS], where we are based is [COUNTRY OR COUNTRIES], and topics people keep asking about are [E.G. TIME OFF, PAY DATES, EXPENSES, SICK DAYS, EQUIPMENT]. Give me a handbook outline with a short plain section for each topic. Note that a small business handbook should answer the questions people actually ask rather than copy a corporate template, and anything touching pay, leave, termination, or legal rights must follow local employment law, which varies a lot by country, so those sections should be checked locally before sharing, while being clear that a handbook is guidance rather than a promise I cannot keep. Give me the starter handbook.
description: Create a short handbook that answers the questions your team actually asks.
useCase: Use this when the same practical questions keep coming up. A small business handbook should answer real questions rather than copy a corporate template, and sections on pay, leave, and termination must follow local employment law, which varies by country, so check those locally first.

title: Write a Team Communication Guide

title: Write Norms for a Remote or Mixed Team
promptText: Help me write working norms for a remote or partly remote team at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. promptText: Help me review my partnership pitch before I send it, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is the pitch: [PASTE IT], and the partner is [WHO]. Read it as the busy owner receiving it and tell me honestly whether it is clear within a few seconds, whether the benefit to them is obvious, whether it is too long, and whether the ask is easy to say yes to. Note that most partnership pitches talk too much about the sender and too little about the receiver, run long, and end without a clear ask, so a quick read from their point of view catches the problems that cause pitches to be ignored, and cutting the pitch in half often improves it. Give me the review and a tightened version.
description: Read your pitch as the busy recipient and tighten it before sending.
useCase: Use this before sending any partnership pitch. Most pitches talk too much about the sender, run long, and end without a clear ask, so reading it from the recipient's side catches what gets pitches ignored, and cutting it in half often improves it.

title: Write a Full Collaboration Proposal
promptText: Help me write a full collaboration proposal between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The collaboration is [WHAT WE WILL DO TOGETHER], what we discussed so far is [KEY POINTS FROM CONVERSATIONS], what each side contributes is [WHO DOES WHAT], and how money or benefits are shared is [THE SPLIT]. Give me a proposal with the goal, scope, roles, timeline, costs and revenue split, how success is measured, and how either side can end it. Note that a proposal should capture what both sides already agreed in conversation rather than introduce surprises, since new terms appearing in writing feel like a bait and switch, and spelling out the uncomfortable parts like money and exit now prevents far bigger arguments later. Give me the collaboration proposal.
description: Turn agreed points into a full proposal covering roles, money, timeline, and exit.
useCase: Use this once a partner is interested. A proposal should capture what both sides already agreed rather than introduce surprises, which feel like a bait and switch, and spelling out money and exit terms now prevents far bigger arguments later.

title: Define Who Does What in a Collaboration
promptText: Help me define roles and responsibilities for a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The tasks involved are [ALL THE WORK, E.G. CREATING, PROMOTING, SELLING, DELIVERING, SUPPORTING CUSTOMERS], what each side is good at is [STRENGTHS], and the time each can give is [AVAILABILITY]. Give me a clear table of who owns each task, who helps, and the deadlines. Note that collaborations most often fall apart over unclear ownership, where each side assumes the other is handling something, and resentment builds when one partner ends up doing most of the work, so naming a single owner for every task, including dull ones like customer support, keeps the effort fair and visible. Give me the roles and responsibilities.
description: Assign a single owner to every collaboration task, including the dull ones.
useCase: Use this before any joint work starts. Collaborations most often fall apart over unclear ownership, where each side assumes the other is handling something, so naming one owner for every task, including dull ones like support, keeps effort fair and visible.
variables: ALL THE WORK, E.G. CREATING, PROMOTING, SELLING, DELIVERING, SUPPORTING CUSTOMERS

title: Get a Quick Collaboration Proposal Outline
promptText: I need a quick outline for a collaboration proposal. My business is [WHAT YOU DO], the partner is [WHO], and the collaboration is [THE IDEA]. Give me a short outline with goal, who does what, timeline, money split, and next step, no explanation, just the outline. Give me the proposal outline.
description: Get a short collaboration proposal outline to fill in.
useCase: Use this when you need a proposal structure fast. A short outline covering goal, roles, timeline, money, and next step gives you the skeleton to fill in, and sending a clear outline soon after a good conversation keeps momentum that a long delay would lose.

title: Agree on a Fair Revenue or Cost Split
promptText: Help me work out a fair way to split costs and revenue in a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The expected costs are [WHAT IT COSTS AND WHO PAYS], what each side contributes is [MONEY, AUDIENCE, PRODUCT, TIME, SKILLS], and how revenue will come in is [HOW CUSTOMERS PAY AND TO WHOM]. Suggest a few split options with the reasoning, and how payments between us will be tracked and settled. Note that an even split sounds fair but often is not when contributions differ, while a split nobody can explain causes resentment later, so tying the split to what each side actually puts in, deciding who collects the money, and setting when and how we settle up, including any fees or currency differences, avoids the most common collaboration fights. Give me the split options.
description: Work out a fair cost and revenue split tied to what each side contributes.
useCase: Use this before money changes hands in a collaboration. An even split sounds fair but often is not when contributions differ, so tying the split to what each side puts in, deciding who collects the money, and agreeing when and how you settle up avoids the most common fights.
variables: WHAT IT COSTS AND WHO PAYS
HOW CUSTOMERS PAY AND TO WHOM

title: Build a Collaboration Timeline
promptText: Help me build a realistic timeline for a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The final goal or launch is [WHAT AND WHEN], the main stages are [STEPS IN THE WORK], and the busy periods or constraints for each side are [HOLIDAYS, PEAK SEASONS, OTHER COMMITMENTS]. Give me a timeline with milestones, owners, and buffer time, plus the decision points where we check progress. Note that collaborations move slower than solo projects because every step waits on two schedules, so a timeline that looks fine for one business usually runs late with two, and building in buffer and naming the dates where we decide whether to continue keeps a slipping project from quietly dying. Give me the collaboration timeline.
description: Build a collaboration timeline with buffer for two schedules.
useCase: Use this when planning joint work with a deadline. Collaborations move slower because every step waits on two schedules, so a timeline that works for one business usually runs late with two, and buffer time plus clear decision points keep a slipping project from quietly dying.

title: Agree How You Will Measure Success
promptText: Help me agree on how to measure the success of a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. What each side hopes to get is [YOUR GOAL AND THEIR GOAL], and the data we can realistically track is [E.G. SALES, SIGN UPS, CODES, CLICKS, ATTENDANCE]. Give me a short set of agreed measures, how each will be tracked and shared, and what result would make us repeat, adjust, or stop. Note that partners often want different things from the same collaboration, like one wanting sales and the other wanting audience growth, so agreeing measures for both prevents one side declaring success while the other feels it failed, and the tracking has to be set up before launch, since results that cannot be measured cannot be split or judged. Give me the success measures.
description: Agree on measures for both partners and set up tracking before launch.
useCase: Use this before a collaboration launches. Partners often want different things, like sales versus audience growth, so agreeing measures for both prevents one side calling it a success while the other feels it failed, and tracking must be set up before launch.
variables: E.G. SALES, SIGN UPS, CODES, CLICKS, ATTENDANCE

title: Clarify Who Owns What You Create Together
promptText: Help me clarify ownership of what my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER] create together. What we will create is [E.G. A PRODUCT, A COURSE, CONTENT, A BRAND NAME, AN EMAIL LIST, PHOTOS], what each side brings in that they already own is [EXISTING ASSETS], and how we each want to use the result later is [FUTURE USE]. Give me clear proposal language on who owns what, who can use it and how, and what happens to it if the collaboration ends. Note that ownership feels unimportant while a collaboration is going well and becomes the main fight when it ends, especially over shared customer lists, content, and names, so agreeing in writing up front matters, and for anything valuable a proper written contract is worth it since ownership rules vary by country. Give me the ownership terms.
description: Agree who owns and can use what you create together, including after it ends.
useCase: Use this before creating anything jointly. Ownership feels unimportant while things go well and becomes the main fight when they end, especially over shared customer lists, content, and names, so agree in writing up front and use a proper contract for anything valuable.
variables: E.G. A PRODUCT, A COURSE, CONTENT, A BRAND NAME, AN EMAIL LIST, PHOTOS

title: Plan How a Collaboration Ends
promptText: Help me write the ending terms for a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The collaboration is [WHAT IT IS], how long it is meant to run is [FIXED END DATE OR ONGOING], and the things that would need sorting out at the end are [E.G. SHARED CUSTOMERS, STOCK, MONEY OWED, CONTENT, ACCESS]. Give me terms covering the end date or notice period, what happens to shared assets and customers, final payments, and how to part on good terms. Note that discussing how a collaboration ends feels negative at the start, but agreeing it while everyone is friendly is far easier than negotiating it after something has gone wrong, and a clear notice period protects both sides from being left with commitments they cannot meet. Give me the exit terms.
description: Agree how a collaboration ends while everyone is still friendly.
useCase: Use this in any collaboration proposal. Discussing the ending feels negative at the start, but agreeing it while everyone is friendly is far easier than after something goes wrong, and a clear notice period protects both sides from commitments they cannot meet.
variables: E.G. SHARED CUSTOMERS, STOCK, MONEY OWED, CONTENT, ACCESS

title: Propose a Joint Product or Bundle
promptText: Help me write a proposal for a joint product or bundle between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. What I offer is [YOUR PRODUCT OR SERVICE], what they offer is [THEIRS], the combined offer would be [THE BUNDLE OR JOINT PRODUCT], and the target customer is [WHO]. Give me a proposal covering the offer, pricing, who sells it and delivers each part, how customer support works, and how revenue is split. Note that a bundle sounds simple but raises practical questions, like who takes payment, who handles a refund, and who the customer contacts when something goes wrong, so answering those in the proposal prevents confused customers and finger pointing, and the bundle should be genuinely better for the customer than buying separately. Give me the joint product proposal.
description: Propose a joint product or bundle with clear sales, support, and refund roles.
useCase: Use this when combining offers with a partner. Bundles raise practical questions like who takes payment, who handles refunds, and who customers contact, so answering them up front prevents confused customers and finger pointing, and the bundle must be genuinely better than buying separately.

title: Propose a Co Hosted Event or Workshop
promptText: Help me write a proposal to co host an event or workshop with [THE PARTNER] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The event idea is [THE EVENT], whether it is [IN PERSON OR ONLINE], the expected audience is [WHO AND HOW MANY], and the costs involved are [VENUE, PLATFORM, FOOD, MATERIALS]. Give me a proposal covering format, who presents what, who promotes and to which audience, costs and income, attendee data, and follow up. Note that co hosted events often go wrong over who gets the attendee list and who does the promotion work, so agreeing how sign up details are shared and used, respecting attendee privacy and any local data rules, and splitting promotion fairly matters as much as the event content. Give me the event proposal.
description: Propose a co hosted event with clear roles, costs, and attendee data terms.
useCase: Use this when planning a joint event or workshop. Co hosted events often go wrong over who gets the attendee list and who does the promotion, so agreeing how sign up details are shared, respecting attendee privacy, and splitting promotion fairly matters as much as the content.

title: Propose a Content Collaboration
promptText: Help me propose a content collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER OR CREATOR]. The content idea is [E.G. A JOINT VIDEO SERIES, GUEST POSTS, A SHARED GUIDE, A LIVE SESSION], our platforms and audiences are [WHERE EACH OF YOU PUBLISHES], and what each side would create is [WHO MAKES WHAT]. Give me a proposal covering the content plan, publishing schedule, approval process, credit and tagging, and who can reuse the content afterwards. Note that content collaborations break down over approval and reuse, like one side posting something the other did not sign off on, or using the content in ads later without asking, so agreeing approval steps and future use up front keeps both brands comfortable. Give me the content collaboration proposal.
description: Propose a content collaboration with clear approval, credit, and reuse terms.
useCase: Use this for joint videos, posts, or guides. Content collaborations break down over approval and reuse, like one side posting without sign off or reusing content in ads later without asking, so agreeing approval steps and future use up front keeps both brands comfortable.
variables: E.G. A JOINT VIDEO SERIES, GUEST POSTS, A SHARED GUIDE, A LIVE SESSION

title: Propose a Collaboration With a Creator
promptText: Help me write a collaboration proposal for a content creator or influencer working with my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The creator is [WHO, PLATFORM, AND AUDIENCE SIZE], what I want is [E.G. A REVIEW, A SERIES, AN AFFILIATE DEAL, PRODUCT FEATURE], my budget or offer is [FEE, FREE PRODUCT, COMMISSION], and the creator's style is [WHAT THEIR CONTENT IS LIKE]. Give me a proposal covering deliverables, creative freedom, payment, disclosure, timeline, and usage rights. Note that creators know their audience better than I do, so heavy scripting usually produces content that flops, and paid or gifted posts generally need clear disclosure under advertising rules in many countries, so leaving room for their voice while being clear on deliverables, disclosure, and how long I can reuse the content keeps it honest and effective. Give me the creator proposal.
description: Propose a creator collaboration with clear deliverables, disclosure, and usage rights.
useCase: Use this when working with an influencer or creator. Heavy scripting usually produces content that flops since creators know their audience, and paid or gifted posts generally need clear disclosure in many countries, so leave room for their voice while being clear on deliverables and reuse rights.
variables: E.G. A REVIEW, A SERIES, AN AFFILIATE DEAL, PRODUCT FEATURE

title: Respond to a Partner's Counter Proposal
promptText: Help me respond to changes a partner wants to my collaboration proposal for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My original proposal was [WHAT YOU PROPOSED], what they want to change is [THEIR CHANGES], what matters most to me is [YOUR MUST HAVES], and where I am flexible is [WHAT YOU COULD GIVE]. Help me sort which changes are fine, which need a trade, and which are dealbreakers, and write a reply that keeps things moving. Note that a counter proposal is usually a sign of real interest rather than a problem, and treating it as a negotiation where each side gives something tends to land better than accepting everything or refusing everything, while being clear about my genuine dealbreakers early avoids wasting time on a deal that will not work. Give me the analysis and reply.
description: Sort a partner's requested changes and reply with fair trades.
useCase: Use this when a partner pushes back on your proposal. A counter proposal usually signals real interest, so trading where each side gives something lands better than accepting or refusing everything, and naming genuine dealbreakers early avoids wasting time on a deal that cannot work.

title: Summarize the Agreed Terms in Writing
promptText: Help me write a plain summary of everything agreed for a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The agreed points are [ROLES, MONEY, TIMELINE, OWNERSHIP, EXIT, AND ANYTHING ELSE], and how we agreed it was [CALLS, MESSAGES, MEETINGS]. Turn this into a clear written summary for both sides to confirm, and flag anything that seems unclear or missing. Note that many small collaborations run on verbal agreement, which works until memories differ, so a written summary both sides confirm, even by a simple reply, prevents most disputes, though for collaborations involving significant money, shared ownership, or long commitments a proper contract reviewed by someone who knows local law is worth the cost. Give me the written summary.
description: Turn verbal agreements into a written summary both sides confirm.
useCase: Use this once terms are agreed. Many small collaborations run on verbal agreement, which works until memories differ, so a written summary both sides confirm prevents most disputes, while significant money or shared ownership deserves a proper contract checked against local law.
variables: ROLES, MONEY, TIMELINE, OWNERSHIP, EXIT, AND ANYTHING ELSE

title: Review a Collaboration Proposal for Risks
promptText: Help me review a collaboration proposal for my [BUSINESS TYPE] before I send or sign it. Here is the proposal: [PASTE IT], and whether I wrote it or the partner did is [WHO WROTE IT]. Tell me honestly where it is vague, where the effort or money looks unbalanced, what happens if things go wrong, and which questions are left unanswered. Note that a proposal written in an excited early stage tends to describe the best case and skip what happens if sales are poor, someone drops out, or the partners disagree, so checking the downside cases now is the cheapest protection I have, and if the partner wrote it, terms that favor them are normal and worth questioning politely rather than assuming bad intent. Give me the risk review.
description: Check a collaboration proposal for vague terms, imbalance, and downside gaps.
useCase: Use this before sending or signing a proposal. Proposals written in excitement describe the best case and skip poor sales, dropouts, or disagreements, so checking downside cases now is the cheapest protection, and terms favoring the partner who wrote it are normal and worth questioning politely.

title: Plan Check Ins During a Collaboration
promptText: Help me plan regular check ins during a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. The collaboration runs for [DURATION], the key measures are [WHAT YOU TRACK], and how we communicate is [CALLS, MESSAGES, SHARED DOC]. Give me a check in schedule and a short agenda covering progress, numbers, problems, and whether to continue as planned. Note that collaborations rarely fail in one dramatic moment, they drift as each side gets busy with its own business, so short scheduled check ins catch slipping tasks and small frustrations while they are easy to fix, and they give both sides a natural moment to adjust or end things without awkwardness. Give me the check in plan.
description: Schedule short check ins that catch drift before a collaboration fades.
useCase: Use this once a collaboration is under way. Collaborations rarely fail dramatically, they drift as each side gets busy, so short scheduled check ins catch slipping tasks and small frustrations while they are easy to fix, and give a natural moment to adjust or end things.

title: Report Collaboration Results to a Partner
promptText: Help me write a results report for a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER]. What we agreed to measure was [THE MEASURES], the actual results are [THE NUMBERS], what worked and what did not is [YOUR OBSERVATIONS], and what I would suggest next is [REPEAT, ADJUST, OR STOP]. Give me a short, honest report with the numbers, lessons, and a recommendation. Note that sharing results openly, including disappointing ones, builds the trust that leads to a second and better collaboration, while quietly letting a project end without reporting back damages the relationship, and comparing results against what we agreed beforehand keeps the conversation about facts rather than feelings. Give me the results report.
description: Share honest collaboration results with lessons and a recommendation.
useCase: Use this when a collaboration or pilot finishes. Sharing results openly, even disappointing ones, builds the trust that leads to a better second collaboration, while letting it quietly end damages the relationship, and comparing against agreed measures keeps it about facts.

title: End a Collaboration on Good Terms
promptText: Help me end a collaboration between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [THE PARTNER] on good terms. Why it is ending is [THE HONEST REASON], what still needs wrapping up is [MONEY, CUSTOMERS, CONTENT, STOCK, ACCESS], and what the exit terms say is [WHAT YOU AGREED, OR NOTHING]. Write a respectful message that explains the decision, proposes how to settle the remaining items, and thanks them. Note that how a collaboration ends shapes my reputation in a small network far more than how it started, since partners talk, so ending clearly, honestly, and with loose ends handled, rather than just going quiet, keeps the door open and protects my name, even when the collaboration itself did not work out. Give me the ending message.
description: End a collaboration honestly with loose ends settled and the door left open.
useCase: Use this when a collaboration needs to stop. How it ends shapes your reputation in a small network more than how it started, since partners talk, so ending clearly and honestly with loose ends handled, rather than going quiet, keeps the door open and protects your name.

title: Find Podcasts Worth Pitching
promptText: Help me find the right podcasts to pitch myself as a guest for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My expertise is [WHAT YOU CAN TALK ABOUT], my ideal customers are [WHO THEY ARE], and the languages and regions I can work in are [LANGUAGES AND MARKETS]. Help me define the types of shows whose listeners match my customers, how to search for them, and how to judge which are worth pitching. Note that a small show whose listeners are exactly my customers usually does more for my business than a huge general show, and big shows are flooded with pitches, so starting with niche and mid sized podcasts that are still actively publishing gets more yeses and more relevant listeners. Give me the target show types and how to find them.
description: Find podcasts whose listeners match your customers, not just the biggest shows.
useCase: Use this before pitching any podcast. A small show whose listeners are exactly your customers usually does more for your business than a huge general one, and big shows are flooded with pitches, so niche and mid sized active shows get more yeses and more relevant listeners.

title: Research a Podcast Before Pitching
promptText: Help me prepare to pitch a specific podcast as a guest for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The show is [SHOW NAME AND HOST], what I have seen of it is [RECENT EPISODES, FORMAT, TYPICAL GUESTS], and my expertise is [YOUR TOPIC]. Help me note what the host cares about, what topics they have already covered, and the gap my episode could fill. Note that hosts can tell immediately whether a guest has actually listened, and a pitch that references a specific episode and proposes something they have not covered stands out from the many generic pitches they get, but I should only mention episodes I have genuinely heard rather than guess from titles. Give me the research notes and angle.
description: Research a show's past episodes so your pitch fills a real gap.
useCase: Use this before pitching a specific show. Hosts can tell immediately whether a guest has listened, and referencing a real episode while proposing something not yet covered stands out from generic pitches, as long as you only mention episodes you have genuinely heard.

title: Get a Quick Podcast Guest Pitch
promptText: I want to pitch myself as a podcast guest quickly. The show is [SHOW NAME], my topic is [WHAT YOU WOULD TALK ABOUT], and why I am credible is [YOUR EXPERIENCE]. Give me a short pitch email with a subject line and two or three episode ideas, no explanation, just the pitch. Give me the pitch.
description: Get a short podcast guest pitch with episode ideas, fast.
useCase: Use this when you want to send a pitch today. A short email with a clear subject line, your credibility, and two or three episode ideas covers what most hosts need to decide, and sending a focused pitch now beats perfecting one you never send.

title: Find Episode Angles Hosts Will Want
promptText: Help me turn my expertise into episode ideas a podcast host would want for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I know and have done is [YOUR EXPERIENCE AND STORIES], the show's audience is [WHO LISTENS], and topics I am tired of hearing in my field are [OVERUSED TOPICS]. Give me several specific episode angles with a working title and the main takeaway for listeners. Note that hosts are not looking for a guest to talk about their business, they want an episode their listeners will value, so specific angles like a surprising lesson, a contrarian view, or a step by step story work far better than broad topics like marketing tips, and my own real experience is what makes an angle different from every other guest. Give me the episode angles.
description: Turn your expertise into specific episode angles built for the listener.
useCase: Use this before writing any pitch. Hosts want episodes their listeners will value, not a guest promoting their business, so specific angles like a surprising lesson or a step by step story beat broad topics, and your own real experience is what makes an angle stand out.

title: Write a Podcast Guest Pitch Email
promptText: Help me write a pitch email to be a guest on [SHOW NAME] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The host is [HOST NAME], an episode of theirs I genuinely listened to is [EPISODE AND WHAT YOU LIKED], my proposed topics are [YOUR EPISODE ANGLES], and why I am credible is [YOUR EXPERIENCE OR RESULTS]. Write a short email with a clear subject line that opens with their show, proposes the topics as listener benefits, gives brief credibility, and makes saying yes easy. Note that hosts receive many pitches that are clearly mass sent and all about the guest, so a short, specific email focused on what their listeners get, with links to a bio or past interviews instead of long attachments, has a far better chance of being read and answered. Give me the pitch email.
description: Write a short, specific guest pitch focused on what the listeners get.
useCase: Use this when pitching a show you want to appear on. Hosts get many mass sent pitches all about the guest, so a short specific email focused on what their listeners get, with links rather than long attachments, has a far better chance of being read and answered.

title: Create a Podcast Guest One Sheet
promptText: Help me create a one page guest sheet hosts can look at when deciding whether to book me for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My background is [YOUR EXPERIENCE], topics I can speak on are [YOUR TOPICS], past interviews or talks are [LINKS OR NONE YET], and how to contact me is [CONTACT DETAILS]. Give me the content for a one sheet with a short bio, topic list with sample questions, credibility points, past appearances, and contact info. Note that a one sheet saves busy hosts from researching me and makes it easy for them to prepare, but it should be honest, since listing credentials or audience numbers I cannot back up is easy to check and costs credibility, and if I have no past interviews yet, it is better to say so and offer a sample than to pad it. Give me the one sheet content.
description: Create an honest one page guest sheet that makes booking you easy.
useCase: Use this to make your pitches easier to say yes to. A one sheet saves hosts from researching you and helps them prepare, but it must be honest, since padded credentials are easy to check, and with no past interviews it is better to say so and offer a sample.

title: Write a Bio for Hosts to Read on Air
promptText: Help me write a short guest bio that podcast hosts can read aloud to introduce me, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Who I am and what I do is [YOUR BACKGROUND], the one thing I want listeners to remember is [THE KEY POINT], and how to pronounce my name or business if needed is [PRONUNCIATION]. Give me a spoken style bio of about thirty seconds and a shorter one line version. Note that a written bio full of titles and long sentences sounds awkward read aloud, so a spoken bio with short sentences and one memorable detail works better for audio, and including pronunciation for my name or business saves the host an uncomfortable moment on air. Give me the on air bios.
description: Write a short bio built to be read aloud, with pronunciation help.
useCase: Use this when a host asks how to introduce you. A written bio full of titles sounds awkward read aloud, so short sentences and one memorable detail work better for audio, and adding pronunciation for your name or business saves the host an uncomfortable moment.

title: Follow Up on a Podcast Pitch
promptText: Help me follow up on a podcast guest pitch that has not had a reply, for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The show is [SHOW NAME], what I pitched and when was [THE ORIGINAL PITCH], and something new I could offer is [E.G. A FRESH ANGLE, A TIMELY HOOK, A NEW RESULT, NOTHING]. Write one short follow up and a polite final note. Note that podcast hosts are often small teams or one person running the show around other work, so silence usually means busy rather than no, but booking calendars fill months ahead, so one follow up with something new and then moving on to other shows is a better use of my time than repeated chasing. Give me the follow up messages.
description: Follow up once with something new, then move on to other shows.
useCase: Use this when a host has not replied. Podcasts are often one person or a small team, so silence usually means busy, but calendars fill months ahead, so one follow up with something new and then moving on is a better use of time than repeated chasing.
variables: E.G. A FRESH ANGLE, A TIMELY HOOK, A NEW RESULT, NOTHING

title: Get Booked With No Podcast Experience Yet
promptText: Help me land my first podcast guest appearances for my [BUSINESS TYPE] when I have never been interviewed before. My expertise is [WHAT YOU KNOW], my network includes [PEOPLE OR COMMUNITIES YOU ARE PART OF], and what I could share to show I can speak well is [E.G. A SHORT VIDEO, A TALK, A LIVE STREAM, NOTHING YET]. Give me a plan for starting with smaller shows, building samples, and working up. Note that hosts worry about booking a guest who freezes or rambles, so a short clip of me speaking clearly does more than any credential, and newer and community shows are often happy to book a first time guest with a good topic, so starting there builds both confidence and links to show bigger hosts later. Give me the first appearances plan.
description: Land first podcast appearances by starting small and building samples.
useCase: Use this if you have never been on a podcast. Hosts worry about guests who freeze or ramble, so a short clip of you speaking clearly does more than credentials, and newer or community shows often book first time guests with good topics, building confidence and links for bigger shows.
variables: PEOPLE OR COMMUNITIES YOU ARE PART OF
E.G. A SHORT VIDEO, A TALK, A LIVE STREAM, NOTHING YET

title: Prepare for a Podcast Interview
promptText: Help me prepare for an upcoming podcast interview for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The show is [SHOW NAME AND FORMAT], the agreed topic is [THE TOPIC], the questions the host sent, if any, are [QUESTIONS OR NONE], and the length is [HOW LONG]. Help me prepare likely questions, short answers built around stories, the key points I want to land, and how to handle a question I cannot answer. Note that guests who memorize scripts sound stiff while guests who prepare nothing ramble, so the sweet spot is knowing three key points and a few short stories that illustrate them, and saying honestly that something is outside my expertise sounds far better on audio than bluffing. Give me the interview prep.
description: Prepare key points and short stories instead of a stiff script.
useCase: Use this in the days before a recording. Memorized scripts sound stiff and no preparation leads to rambling, so knowing three key points and a few short stories is the sweet spot, and admitting something is outside your expertise sounds far better on audio than bluffing.

title: Turn Expertise Into Stories for Audio
promptText: Help me turn my main points into short stories and examples that work well on a podcast for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My key points are [WHAT YOU WANT LISTENERS TO LEARN], and real experiences I could draw from are [CLIENT STORIES, MISTAKES, TURNING POINTS]. For each point, give me a short story with a clear lesson, kept under about a minute to tell. Note that listeners cannot see slides or skim, so abstract advice slides past them while a concrete story with a clear lesson sticks, and stories involving clients should be anonymized or shared with permission, since a podcast is public and permanent. Give me the stories and lessons.
description: Turn key points into short stories that stick with listeners.
useCase: Use this to make your interview memorable. Listeners cannot see slides or skim, so abstract advice slides past them while a concrete story with a clear lesson sticks, and client stories should be anonymized or shared with permission since a podcast is public and permanent.
variables: WHAT YOU WANT LISTENERS TO LEARN

title: Create a Listener Offer or Next Step
promptText: Help me create a simple next step for listeners after my podcast appearance for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I offer is [YOUR PRODUCT OR SERVICE], the episode topic is [THE TOPIC], and what I could give listeners is [E.G. A FREE GUIDE, A CHECKLIST, A DISCOUNT, A RESOURCE PAGE]. Give me a short, easy to say call to action and an idea for a simple page or link that matches the episode. Note that listeners are usually driving, walking, or working while they listen, so a long website address or complicated offer gets forgotten, while one short, memorable link and a free resource tied to the episode topic gets far more people to follow through, and it should be agreed with the host rather than turning the episode into an ad. Note that fears behind avoidance often feel much bigger than the realistic outcome, and avoiding them usually has its own quiet cost, like lost income or growing stress, so naming the realistic worst case and a plan for it often shrinks the fear enough to act, while a small test is gentler than forcing a giant leap. Give me the fear check and first step.
description: Size up the fear behind avoidance and test it with a smaller step.
useCase: Use this when fear is keeping you from an important task. Fears behind avoidance often feel bigger than the realistic outcome, and avoiding them has its own quiet cost like lost income, so naming the realistic worst case with a plan often shrinks the fear enough to act, starting with a small test.
variables: E.G. RAISING PRICES, LAUNCHING, POSTING PUBLICLY, CALLING A CLIENT, SENDING A PROPOSAL

title: Plan a Time Boxed Work Session
promptText: Help me plan a short, time boxed work session to make progress on something I have been avoiding. The task is [THE TASK], the time I can give is [MINUTES OR HOURS], when my energy is usually best is [YOUR BEST TIME OF DAY], and what usually distracts me is [YOUR DISTRACTIONS]. Give me a session plan with a clear goal for the time box, how to remove distractions, and how to stop and note where to pick up next time. Note that committing to work on something for a fixed short time, rather than until it is done, makes starting far less daunting, and stopping with a note about the next step makes the following session much easier to begin, while scheduling hard tasks for my best energy hours beats fighting them when I am drained. Give me the session plan.
description: Plan a short time boxed session with a clear goal and a note for next time.
useCase: Use this to make progress on dreaded work. Committing to a fixed short time rather than until done makes starting far less daunting, stopping with a note on the next step makes the next session easier, and putting hard tasks in your best energy hours beats fighting them when drained.

title: Reduce the Distractions You Escape Into
promptText: Help me reduce the distractions I escape into when I should be working. My usual escapes are [E.G. SOCIAL MEDIA, NEWS, EMAIL, MESSAGES, CLEANING, BUSYWORK], when it happens most is [TIMES OR SITUATIONS], and the tools and devices I use are [YOUR SETUP]. Suggest practical changes to make distractions harder and focus easier, without relying on willpower alone. Note that distractions are often the visible symptom of avoiding a harder task, and blocking them helps but does not fix the reason I am escaping, so combining friction like moving apps off my phone with a clearer first step for the real task works better than either alone, and busywork like tidying the inbox is a sneaky form of procrastination that feels productive. Give me the distraction plan.
description: Add friction to your usual escapes while fixing the task you are avoiding.
useCase: Use this when you keep drifting into distractions. Distractions are often a symptom of avoiding a harder task, so blocking them helps but does not fix the cause, and combining friction with a clearer first step works best, while busywork like inbox tidying is a sneaky procrastination that feels productive.

title: Spot Busywork Disguised as Progress
promptText: Help me check whether I am filling my days with busywork instead of the work that matters in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I did this week is [YOUR TASKS AND ROUGH TIME SPENT], and the work that would actually move my business forward is [THE HIGH VALUE WORK]. Sort my week into important work and busywork, and point out what I am likely avoiding behind the busy tasks. Note that a full, tiring week can still be procrastination when the time goes to easy, comfortable tasks like tweaking a logo, reorganizing files, or answering every message instantly, while the one uncomfortable task that matters stays untouched, so seeing where the time actually went is often the wake up call that makes it easier to protect time for the real work. Give me the busywork check.
description: Sort your week into real progress and comfortable busywork.
useCase: Use this when you feel busy but nothing important moves. A full tiring week can still be procrastination when time goes to comfortable tasks like tweaking a logo while the one uncomfortable task that matters stays untouched, so seeing where time actually went makes it easier to protect the real work.
variables: YOUR TASKS AND ROUGH TIME SPENT

title: Find the Decision Hiding Behind a Stuck Task
promptText: Help me find whether a stuck task is really an unmade decision. The task is [THE STUCK TASK], what I keep circling around is [WHAT YOU KEEP THINKING ABOUT], and the options I can see are [THE CHOICES]. Help me name the decision underneath, the information I actually need to make it, and a deadline for deciding. Note that many tasks stall not because the work is hard but because a decision has not been made, like which price to charge or which client to focus on, and no amount of willpower moves a task forward until that decision is made, so naming it, gathering only the information that matters, and setting a date to decide usually unblocks the work. Give me the decision and plan.
description: Name the unmade decision behind a stuck task and set a date to decide.
useCase: Use this when a task stalls for no obvious reason. Many tasks stall because a decision has not been made, like which price to charge, and no willpower moves the task until it is, so naming the decision, gathering only the information that matters, and setting a date to decide usually unblocks it.

title: Decide Whether to Do, Delegate, or Drop It
promptText: Help me decide what to do with tasks that have sat on my list for weeks. The tasks are [YOUR LONG STANDING TASKS], what each would actually achieve is [YOUR BEST GUESS], and who else could do them is [ANYONE OR NOBODY]. Sort them into do now, schedule, delegate, or drop, with a short reason for each. Note that a list full of tasks I keep postponing drains energy every time I look at it, and some of those tasks quietly stopped mattering, so deliberately dropping them is healthier than carrying them forever, while tasks I avoid because they are not my strength may be worth paying someone else to do. Give me the sorted list.
description: Sort long postponed tasks into do, schedule, delegate, or drop.
useCase: Use this when your to do list is full of old tasks. A list of things you keep postponing drains energy every time you look at it, and some tasks quietly stopped mattering, so dropping them deliberately is healthier, while tasks you avoid because they are not your strength may be worth paying someone to do.

title: Finish Projects That Stall Near the End
promptText: Help me finish a project that is almost done but has stalled. The project is [THE PROJECT], what is left is [THE REMAINING WORK], and why I think I keep not finishing it is [YOUR GUESS, E.G. FEAR OF LAUNCHING, BORING DETAILS, LOST INTEREST]. Give me a finishing list of every remaining task, the minimum needed to call it done, and a finish date. Note that the last part of a project is often the least exciting and the most exposing, since finishing means it can be judged, so many owners have several almost done projects sitting idle, and listing the remaining tasks usually shows there is less left than it feels, while one finished project is worth more than several nearly finished ones. Give me the finishing plan.
description: List what is left on an almost done project and set a finish date.
useCase: Use this for projects stuck at nearly done. The last part is often the least exciting and most exposing since finishing means it can be judged, and listing remaining tasks usually shows less is left than it feels, while one finished project is worth more than several nearly finished ones.
variables: YOUR GUESS, E.G. FEAR OF LAUNCHING, BORING DETAILS, LOST INTEREST

title: Tackle Dreaded Admin Tasks
promptText: Help me tackle the admin tasks I keep putting off for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tasks are [E.G. BOOKKEEPING, INVOICES, TAX PAPERS, CONTRACTS, EMAIL BACKLOG], how far behind I am is [HOW BACKLOGGED], and why they feel so heavy is [YOUR REASON]. Give me a catch up plan in small sessions, a simple routine to stay current afterwards, and which tasks might be worth outsourcing. Note that admin left to pile up becomes much harder than doing it regularly, and some of it carries real consequences like late payment, penalties, or missed deadlines, so a short regular routine is far easier than a dreaded catch up marathon, and getting help with the parts I hate is often cheaper than the cost of neglecting them. Give me the admin plan.
description: Catch up on dreaded admin in small sessions and set a routine to stay current.
useCase: Use this when bookkeeping, invoices, or paperwork pile up. Admin left to pile up gets much harder and can carry real consequences like late payment or penalties, so a short regular routine beats a dreaded catch up marathon, and outsourcing the parts you hate is often cheaper than neglecting them.
variables: E.G. BOOKKEEPING, INVOICES, TAX PAPERS, CONTRACTS, EMAIL BACKLOG

title: Pair Dreaded Tasks With Something You Enjoy
promptText: Help me make dreaded tasks more bearable by pairing them with things I enjoy. The tasks I dread are [THE TASKS], things I enjoy are [E.G. A GOOD COFFEE, MUSIC, A CAFE, A WALK, A FAVORITE SNACK, A SHOW], and when I usually do these tasks is [WHEN]. Suggest pairings and small rewards that make starting easier without becoming a reason to avoid work. Note that pairing a dull task with something pleasant, like only listening to a favorite podcast while doing admin, can make it easier to start, and small rewards after finishing help build the habit, but rewards should be small and immediate rather than big promises to myself, since those tend to be ignored. Give me the pairing ideas.
description: Pair dreaded tasks with small pleasures to make them easier to start.
useCase: Use this for dull work you keep avoiding. Pairing a dull task with something pleasant, like a favorite podcast only during admin, makes starting easier, and small immediate rewards after finishing build the habit, while big promises to yourself tend to be ignored.
variables: E.G. A GOOD COFFEE, MUSIC, A CAFE, A WALK, A FAVORITE SNACK, A SHOW

title: Use Body Doubling or a Work Buddy
promptText: Help me use a work buddy or body doubling to get through tasks I avoid. The tasks are [WHAT YOU AVOID], people who might join me are [E.G. A FRIEND, ANOTHER FOUNDER, AN ONLINE COWORKING GROUP, NOBODY YET], and whether I prefer [IN PERSON OR ONLINE]. Suggest a simple setup, like working alongside someone on a video call or meeting at a cafe, and how to structure the session. Note that simply working in the presence of someone else, even silently, helps many people start and stay on task, and sharing a short goal at the start and checking in at the end adds gentle accountability, while for solo owners working alone all day it also reduces isolation, which can itself be a cause of stalled work. Give me the work buddy setup.
description: Work alongside someone, in person or online, to start avoided tasks.
useCase: Use this if you work alone and struggle to start. Working in someone's presence, even silently, helps many people start and stay on task, sharing a goal at the start and checking in at the end adds gentle accountability, and for solo owners it also reduces the isolation that can stall work.
variables: E.G. A FRIEND, ANOTHER FOUNDER, AN ONLINE COWORKING GROUP, NOBODY YET

title: Stop the Guilt Spiral About Procrastinating
promptText: Help me break the guilt spiral that comes after I procrastinate. What I put off is [THE TASK], how I talk to myself about it is [YOUR SELF TALK], and what happens next is [E.G. MORE AVOIDANCE, STAYING UP LATE, FEELING STUCK]. Help me reframe the self talk into something kind but honest, and plan one small step to get back on track. Note that beating myself up after procrastinating usually leads to more avoidance, because the task now carries guilt as well as the original discomfort, while treating a slip with the understanding I would give a friend makes it easier to start again, and this is not about excusing everything, it is about getting back to work faster. Give me the reframe and next step.
description: Replace harsh self talk after procrastinating with a kind, honest restart.
useCase: Use this when guilt about procrastinating keeps you stuck. Beating yourself up usually leads to more avoidance since the task now carries guilt too, while treating a slip as you would a friend's makes it easier to restart, which is about getting back to work faster, not excusing everything.
variables: E.G. MORE AVOIDANCE, STAYING UP LATE, FEELING STUCK

title: Spot Your Procrastination Patterns
promptText: Help me spot patterns in when and what I procrastinate on. The tasks I usually avoid are [EXAMPLES], the times or situations it happens most are [E.G. AFTERNOONS, AFTER BAD NEWS, WHEN TIRED, WHEN A TASK INVOLVES PEOPLE], and what has worked before is [ANYTHING THAT HELPED]. Find the common threads and suggest two or three systems that address my specific patterns. Note that procrastination tends to follow personal patterns, like always avoiding tasks that involve selling, or always stalling in the afternoon, and once I see the pattern I can design around it, like scheduling those tasks in my best hours or pairing them with support, which works much better than generic productivity tips. Give me the pattern review and systems.
description: Find your personal procrastination patterns and design systems around them.
useCase: Use this when generic productivity tips do not stick. Procrastination follows personal patterns, like always avoiding sales tasks or stalling in the afternoon, and once you see yours you can design around it, like scheduling those tasks in your best hours, which beats generic advice.

title: Check Whether It Is More Than Procrastination
promptText: Help me think about whether my ongoing avoidance might be about something bigger than procrastination. What I have noticed is [E.G. AVOIDING ALMOST EVERYTHING, LOW ENERGY FOR WEEKS, DREADING THE BUSINESS ITSELF, TROUBLE FOCUSING FOR YEARS], how long it has been going on is [DURATION], and what else is happening in my life is [CONTEXT]. Help me reflect on whether this looks like a temporary slump, burnout, a business that no longer fits me, or something worth talking to a professional about. Note that persistent avoidance across most of my work, especially with low mood, exhaustion, or long running focus difficulties, can be a sign of burnout, depression, or attention differences rather than a lack of discipline, and productivity tricks will not fix those, so talking to a doctor, counselor, or someone I trust is a sensible step, while sometimes it simply means the work itself needs to change. Give me the reflection.
description: Reflect on whether ongoing avoidance points to burnout or something bigger.
useCase: Use this when avoidance has lasted a long time or spread to everything. Persistent avoidance with low mood, exhaustion, or long running focus problems can signal burnout, depression, or attention differences rather than lack of discipline, which tricks will not fix, so talking to a professional or someone you trust is sensible.
variables: E.G. AVOIDING ALMOST EVERYTHING, LOW ENERGY FOR WEEKS, DREADING THE BUSINESS ITSELF, TROUBLE FOCUSING FOR YEARS

title: Check Whether a Decision Is Reversible
promptText: Help me figure out how carefully I need to make a decision for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The decision is [THE DECISION], the options are [YOUR OPTIONS], and what it would take to undo each one is [COST, TIME, OR DAMAGE OF REVERSING]. Tell me whether this is an easily reversible decision I should make quickly or a hard to reverse one that deserves more time, and how to approach it either way. Note that many decisions feel heavy but are easy to reverse, like trying a new price or tool, and these are best made quickly and adjusted, while truly hard to undo decisions, like signing a long lease or a major hire, deserve slower thinking, so sorting the decision first stops me agonizing over small choices and rushing big ones. Give me the reversibility check.
description: Sort a decision by how reversible it is to know how carefully to decide.
useCase: Use this first on any decision you are stuck on. Many decisions feel heavy but are easy to reverse and are best made quickly and adjusted, while hard to undo ones deserve slower thinking, so sorting them stops you agonizing over small choices and rushing big ones.
