title: Compare Options With a Weighted Decision Matrix
promptText: Help me compare my options using a weighted decision matrix. The decision is [THE DECISION], the options are [YOUR OPTIONS], and the factors that matter to me are [E.G. COST, TIME, RISK, INCOME, ENJOYMENT, FIT WITH GOALS]. Help me weight each factor by importance, score each option, and show the totals, then tell me whether the result matches my gut and what that might mean. Note that a matrix makes tradeoffs visible and stops one vivid factor from dominating, but the numbers are only as good as my weights, so if the winner feels wrong, that usually means I have left out a factor that matters to me, which is useful information rather than a reason to ignore the result. Give me the decision matrix.
description: Weight your factors and score options to see the tradeoffs clearly.
useCase: Use this when comparing several options on many factors. A matrix makes tradeoffs visible and stops one vivid factor dominating, but it is only as good as your weights, so if the winner feels wrong you have likely left out a factor that matters, which is useful information.
variables: E.G. COST, TIME, RISK, INCOME, ENJOYMENT, FIT WITH GOALS

title: Get a Quick Decision Gut Check
promptText: I need to make a decision quickly. The choice is between [OPTION A] and [OPTION B], what matters most to me is [YOUR TOP PRIORITY], and I need to decide by [WHEN]. Give me a short comparison and the option you would lean toward with one reason, no long analysis, just the call. Give me the quick take.
description: Get a short comparison and a lean between two options, fast.
useCase: Use this for decisions that do not deserve hours. A short comparison and a lean based on your top priority helps you move on a small or reversible choice, and a quick decent decision usually beats a slow perfect one when the stakes are low.

title: Run a Pre Mortem Before Deciding
promptText: Help me run a pre mortem on a decision for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The decision I am leaning toward is [THE DECISION], and my plan is [HOW YOU WILL CARRY IT OUT]. Imagine it is a year from now and this decision went badly, list the most likely reasons it failed, and for each, a way to prevent it or an early warning sign to watch. Note that people tend to see only the reasons a favored plan will work, and imagining it has already failed makes it much easier to spot risks I am ignoring, while the goal is not to talk myself out of the decision but to make it stronger, since most risks can be reduced once named. Give me the pre mortem.
description: Imagine a decision failed to find and fix its risks in advance.
useCase: Use this before committing to a big decision. People see mainly the reasons a favored plan will work, and imagining it already failed makes overlooked risks easier to spot, which is about strengthening the decision rather than talking yourself out of it, since most risks shrink once named.
variables: HOW YOU WILL CARRY IT OUT

title: Think Through Second Order Effects
promptText: Help me think beyond the immediate result of a decision for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The decision is [THE DECISION], the immediate effect I expect is [THE FIRST RESULT], and the people affected are [CUSTOMERS, TEAM, FAMILY, PARTNERS]. Walk me through what happens next, and then after that, for each option, including effects on my time, cash, relationships, and reputation. Note that many decisions look good at first and cause problems later, like a discount that brings sales but trains customers to wait for deals, or a big client that brings revenue but takes over my calendar, so asking and then what a couple of times often reveals the real cost or benefit. Give me the second order effects.
description: Ask and then what to see the later effects of a decision.
useCase: Use this when an option looks great at first glance. Many decisions look good initially and cause problems later, like a discount that trains customers to wait, so asking and then what a couple of times often reveals the real cost or benefit before you commit.

title: Use the 10 10 10 Test
promptText: Help me apply the 10 10 10 test to a decision I am stuck on. The decision is [THE DECISION], the options are [YOUR OPTIONS], and what I feel strongly about right now is [YOUR CURRENT FEELINGS]. For each option, help me think through how I will likely feel about it in ten minutes, ten months, and ten years. Note that strong feelings in the moment, like fear of an awkward conversation or excitement about a shiny opportunity, can dominate a decision even when they will barely matter in a few months, so stepping through different time frames helps me separate short term discomfort from long term consequences. Give me the 10 10 10 view.
description: Weigh how a decision will feel in ten minutes, ten months, and ten years.
useCase: Use this when emotions in the moment are driving a choice. Fear of an awkward conversation or excitement about a shiny opportunity can dominate even when it barely matters later, so stepping through different time frames separates short term discomfort from long term consequences.

title: Use Regret Minimization for a Big Choice
promptText: Help me think through a big life or business choice using regret minimization. The choice is [THE BIG DECISION, E.G. STARTING A BUSINESS, MOVING, CHANGING DIRECTION], what scares me about each option is [YOUR FEARS], and what I would hope my life looks like later is [YOUR LONG TERM HOPES]. Help me imagine looking back from much later and ask which choice I would most regret not making. Note that people often regret the chances they did not take more than the ones that did not work out, but this frame works best for big, values driven choices rather than everyday ones, and it should be paired with a realistic plan for the downside, like savings or a fallback, so that following my heart does not mean ignoring real risks. Give me the regret reflection.
description: Ask which choice you would most regret not making, with a downside plan.
useCase: Use this for big, values driven choices like starting or changing direction. People often regret chances not taken more than ones that failed, but this works best for big decisions and should come with a realistic downside plan, so following your heart does not mean ignoring real risks.
variables: THE BIG DECISION, E.G. STARTING A BUSINESS, MOVING, CHANGING DIRECTION

title: Count the Opportunity Cost
promptText: Help me count the opportunity cost of a decision for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The thing I am considering saying yes to is [THE OPPORTUNITY OR PROJECT], the time, money, and energy it would take is [WHAT IT COSTS], and the other things I could do with those same resources are [ALTERNATIVES]. Help me see what I am really giving up by saying yes, and whether it is still worth it. Note that every yes is a no to something else, and small business owners often say yes to good opportunities that quietly crowd out better ones, since the cost of a new project is not just its price but the work I can no longer do, so comparing against my best alternative use of the time is what shows whether it is truly a good deal. Give me the opportunity cost view.
description: See what you give up by saying yes, compared to your best alternative.
useCase: Use this before saying yes to a new project or opportunity. Every yes is a no to something else, and owners often accept good opportunities that crowd out better ones, so comparing against your best alternative use of the time shows whether it is truly a good deal.

title: Check for the Sunk Cost Trap
promptText: Help me check whether I am continuing something only because of what I have already put in. The thing is [THE PROJECT, PRODUCT, TOOL, OR COMMITMENT], what I have already invested is [TIME, MONEY, EFFORT], how it is actually going is [HONEST RESULTS], and what it would take to continue is [FUTURE COST]. Help me judge it as if I were starting fresh today, ignoring what is already spent. Note that money and time already spent are gone whatever I decide, so the only real question is whether the future investment is worth the future return, and the pull to keep going to avoid wasting what I put in is strong and normal, but stopping a losing path early is often the best use of the lesson, though quitting too fast on something just slow to start is also a mistake. Give me the fresh start assessment.
description: Judge whether to continue something as if starting fresh today.
useCase: Use this when you keep going because you have already invested so much. Past time and money are gone either way, so the real question is whether future investment is worth future return, and stopping a losing path early is often wise, though quitting too fast on something merely slow to start is also a mistake.
variables: THE PROJECT, PRODUCT, TOOL, OR COMMITMENT

title: Weigh Your Gut Against the Data
promptText: Help me sort out a decision where my gut and the data disagree. The decision is [THE DECISION], what the numbers or evidence say is [THE DATA], what my gut says is [YOUR INSTINCT], and my experience in this area is [HOW MUCH YOU KNOW THIS FIELD]. Help me explore what my gut might be picking up that the data misses, and what the data shows that my gut might be ignoring. Note that intuition is often reliable in areas where I have lots of experience and quick feedback, and much less reliable in unfamiliar areas, while data can be incomplete or measure the wrong thing, so the useful step is to put my gut feeling into words and test it, rather than blindly following either one. Give me the gut versus data analysis.
description: Put your gut feeling into words and test it against the evidence.
useCase: Use this when instinct and evidence point different ways. Intuition is often reliable where you have lots of experience and fast feedback and much less so in unfamiliar areas, while data can be incomplete, so putting your gut into words and testing it beats blindly following either.
variables: HOW MUCH YOU KNOW THIS FIELD

title: Check a Decision for Common Biases
promptText: Help me check a decision I am about to make for common thinking traps. The decision is [THE DECISION], why I am leaning that way is [YOUR REASONS], and the information I have looked at is [YOUR SOURCES]. Look for signs of confirmation bias, overconfidence, recency bias, following the crowd, anchoring on a first number, and fear of loss, and point out which seem to apply. Note that everyone falls into these traps, and they are hardest to see in my own thinking, especially when I already want a particular answer, so actively looking for evidence against my preferred option, and asking what would change my mind, is one of the simplest ways to make a better decision. Give me the bias check.
description: Look for thinking traps in a decision you are about to make.
useCase: Use this before committing to a decision you are keen on. Everyone falls into thinking traps and they are hardest to see when you already want a particular answer, so actively seeking evidence against your preferred option and asking what would change your mind is a simple way to decide better.

title: Plan for the Realistic Worst Case
promptText: Help me plan for the realistic worst case of a decision I am weighing for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The decision is [THE DECISION], the worst outcome I fear is [YOUR FEAR], and the resources I would have if it happened are [SAVINGS, SKILLS, SUPPORT, OTHER INCOME]. Help me describe the realistic worst case, how likely it is, how I would recover, and what I can set up now to soften it. Note that a vague fear of the worst often feels bigger than the realistic version, and naming exactly what would happen and how I would cope usually makes a decision less frightening, while setting up a cushion in advance, like a cash buffer or a fallback plan, turns a scary risk into a manageable one. Give me the worst case plan.
description: Name the realistic worst case and set up a cushion in advance.
useCase: Use this when fear of failure is blocking a decision. A vague fear of the worst often feels bigger than the realistic version, so naming what would happen and how you would cope usually makes it less frightening, and a cushion set up in advance turns a scary risk into a manageable one.

title: Turn a Decision Into a Small Experiment
promptText: Help me turn a decision I am unsure about into a small, low risk experiment for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The decision is [THE DECISION], what I am uncertain about is [THE KEY UNKNOWN], and the budget and time I can risk on a test are [WHAT YOU CAN SPEND]. Design a small test that answers the key question, with a clear success measure and a date to decide. Note that many decisions do not need to be made in one big leap, since a short test, like selling to five customers before building the full product, gives real evidence instead of guesses, and deciding in advance what result means go, adjust, or stop keeps me from moving the goalposts once I see the results. Give me the experiment.
description: Test an uncertain decision cheaply with a clear success measure.
useCase: Use this when you cannot decide without more information. Many decisions do not need one big leap, since a short test gives real evidence instead of guesses, and deciding in advance what result means go, adjust, or stop keeps you from moving the goalposts once results arrive.

title: Set a Deadline to Stop Overthinking
promptText: Help me stop overthinking a decision by setting a deadline and a process. The decision is [THE DECISION], how long I have been going back and forth is [HOW LONG], what more information I think I need is [WHAT YOU ARE WAITING FOR], and what delaying is costing me is [THE COST OF WAITING]. Help me decide what information is actually worth getting, set a decision date, and choose a simple rule for what I will do if I am still unsure by then. Note that waiting for certainty usually means waiting forever, since most business decisions are made with incomplete information, and the cost of delay, like lost time or missed chances, is often bigger than the risk of choosing imperfectly, so a firm decision date with a default choice breaks the loop. Give me the decision deadline plan.
description: Set a decision date and a default choice to break an overthinking loop.
useCase: Use this when you have been going back and forth too long. Waiting for certainty usually means waiting forever since most decisions use incomplete information, and the cost of delay is often bigger than choosing imperfectly, so a firm date with a default choice breaks the loop.

title: Narrow Down Too Many Options
promptText: Help me narrow down a choice where I have too many options. What I am choosing is [E.G. A TOOL, A SUPPLIER, A NICHE, A PRODUCT IDEA], the options I am considering are [YOUR LIST], and my must haves are [NON NEGOTIABLES]. Help me cut the list using my must haves first, then compare the remaining few on what matters most. Note that having too many options often leads to stalling or regret, and most of the options can usually be removed quickly by checking them against a few must haves, so narrowing to two or three serious choices and then comparing those properly is far easier than trying to weigh everything at once. Give me the narrowed choice.
description: Cut a long list of options down to two or three with your must haves.
useCase: Use this when too many options leave you stalled. Too many choices often lead to stalling or regret, and most can be removed quickly against a few must haves, so narrowing to two or three serious choices and comparing those properly is far easier than weighing everything at once.
variables: E.G. A TOOL, A SUPPLIER, A NICHE, A PRODUCT IDEA

title: Filter a Decision Through Your Values
promptText: Help me check a decision against what matters most to me. The decision is [THE DECISION], the options are [YOUR OPTIONS], and my core values or priorities are [E.G. FREEDOM, FAMILY, HONESTY, SECURITY, CRAFT, GROWTH]. Show me how each option fits or conflicts with my values, and point out any option that looks good on paper but goes against them. Note that a decision can make financial sense and still feel wrong if it conflicts with what I value, like a lucrative client whose practices I disagree with, and those decisions often lead to regret or stress later, so naming my values explicitly makes it easier to choose an option I can live with comfortably. Give me the values filter.
description: Check options against your values to find the one you can live with.
useCase: Use this when an option looks good on paper but feels wrong. promptText: Help me set up a routine to keep my dashboard current for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. title: Set Warning Levels and Color Rules
promptText: Help me set warning levels for the numbers on my [BUSINESS TYPE] dashboard. The numbers are [YOUR KPIS WITH TYPICAL VALUES], levels that would worry me are [YOUR CONCERNS, E.G. CASH BELOW ONE MONTH OF COSTS, NO ORDERS IN TWO DAYS], and what I would do if each crossed the line is [YOUR RESPONSE]. Note that sharing a full dashboard by default can expose sensitive financial or customer information to people who do not need it, and edit access invites accidental changes that break formulas, so giving each person view only access to just what they need protects the business, while customer personal data may also be covered by privacy rules that depend on where I and my customers are. title: Calculate Your Growth Rate Correctly
promptText: Help me calculate my growth rate correctly for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The metric is [E.G. REVENUE, CUSTOMERS, ORDERS], my values over time are [MONTHLY OR YEARLY VALUES], and what I want to know is [E.G. MONTH OVER MONTH, YEAR OVER YEAR, AVERAGE GROWTH OVER SEVERAL YEARS]. Show me the calculation step by step, what the result means in plain terms, and which growth rate is most honest to use for my situation. Note that different growth rates can tell very different stories from the same data, since month over month growth jumps around and can be distorted by seasons, while a simple average of yearly growth rates overstates growth compared with a compound average, so choosing the right method, and showing my working, keeps me from fooling myself or anyone I share it with. Give me the growth calculation.
description: Calculate growth step by step and choose the most honest growth rate.
useCase: Use this when you want to state how fast you are growing. The same data can tell different stories, since month over month growth jumps around with seasons and simple averages of yearly rates overstate compound growth, so the right method with your working shown keeps you from fooling yourself or others.

title: Get a Quick Growth Calculation
promptText: Do a quick growth calculation for me. The metric is [WHAT YOU ARE MEASURING], the starting value was [START], the ending value is [END], and the time between them is [PERIOD]. Give me the total growth, the average monthly or yearly rate, and one sentence on what it means, no long explanation, just the numbers. Give me the calculation.
description: Get total growth, an average rate, and a one line meaning, fast.

title: Break Revenue Growth Into Its Parts
promptText: Help me break my revenue growth into its parts for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My revenue for two periods is [PERIOD ONE AND PERIOD TWO], the number of customers in each is [CUSTOMER COUNTS], the number of orders in each is [ORDER COUNTS], and anything that changed in pricing is [PRICE CHANGES]. Split revenue into number of customers, orders per customer, and average order value, show how each changed, and explain which drove the growth. Note that revenue can grow for very different reasons, like more customers, existing customers buying more often, or higher prices, and each points to a different strategy, so knowing which lever actually moved shows what is working, while growth driven only by price increases may hide a shrinking customer base. Give me the growth breakdown.
description: Split revenue growth into customers, frequency, and order value.
useCase: Use this to see why revenue changed. Revenue can grow from more customers, more frequent buying, or higher prices, and each points to a different strategy, so knowing which lever moved shows what is working, while growth from price alone may hide a shrinking customer base.

title: Calculate Your Customer Acquisition Cost
promptText: Help me calculate how much it costs to win a new customer for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What I spent on marketing and sales over a period is [AD SPEND, TOOLS, CONTENT, FREELANCERS, DISCOUNTS], the hours I spent on marketing and selling is [YOUR TIME], what I value my time at is [HOURLY VALUE], and the number of new customers in that period is [NEW CUSTOMERS]. Calculate acquisition cost with and without my time, by channel if possible, and explain what it tells me. Note that many owners calculate acquisition cost using only ad spend, which makes channels like content, social, or networking look free when they actually consume many hours, so including a value for my time gives a far more honest picture, and acquisition cost only means something when compared with how much a customer is worth. Give me the acquisition cost.
description: Calculate the real cost of winning a customer, including your time.
useCase: Use this to see what new customers really cost. Many owners count only ad spend, making content, social, or networking look free when they consume many hours, so including your time gives an honest picture, and acquisition cost only means something compared with what a customer is worth.

title: Estimate Customer Lifetime Value
promptText: Help me estimate how much a typical customer is worth over time to my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My average order value is [AMOUNT], how often a typical customer buys is [FREQUENCY], how long customers typically keep buying is [ESTIMATED LIFESPAN OR WHAT YOU KNOW], and my gross margin is [MARGIN PERCENT]. Calculate a simple lifetime value based on profit rather than revenue, and give a cautious and an optimistic version. Note that lifetime value is an estimate, not a fact, and newer businesses often overestimate how long customers stay because they have not been open long enough to know, so using gross profit rather than revenue and leaning toward the cautious version prevents spending too much to acquire customers based on an inflated number. Give me the lifetime value estimate.
description: Estimate a cautious, profit based customer lifetime value.
useCase: Use this to know how much a customer is really worth. Lifetime value is an estimate, and newer businesses often overestimate how long customers stay, so basing it on profit rather than revenue and leaning cautious prevents overspending to acquire customers based on an inflated number.

title: Compare What a Customer Is Worth to What It Costs
promptText: Help me compare customer value with acquisition cost for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My estimated lifetime value per customer is [LTV BASED ON PROFIT], my acquisition cost per customer is [CAC, IDEALLY INCLUDING YOUR TIME], and these figures by channel, if I have them, are [CHANNEL BREAKDOWN]. Calculate the ratio, explain what it means for whether my growth is sustainable, and which channels deserve more or less investment. Note that if winning a customer costs close to or more than the profit they bring, growing faster just loses money faster, while a comfortable gap leaves room to invest in growth, though general rules of thumb about a healthy ratio come mostly from venture funded companies and may not fit a small, self funded business, so the trend and the cash available matter as much as any target ratio. Give me the ratio analysis.
description: Compare customer value to acquisition cost to see if growth is sustainable.
useCase: Use this before spending more on growth. If winning a customer costs close to the profit they bring, faster growth just loses money faster, and rules of thumb on healthy ratios mostly come from venture funded companies, so for a self funded business the trend and available cash matter as much as any target.

title: Calculate How Long It Takes to Earn Back a Customer
promptText: Help me calculate how long it takes to earn back the cost of winning a customer for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My acquisition cost per customer is [CAC], the gross profit a customer brings per month or per order is [PROFIT PER PERIOD OR ORDER], and how often they buy is [FREQUENCY]. Calculate the payback period and explain what it means for my cash. Note that a business can be profitable per customer on paper but still run short of cash if it takes many months to earn back acquisition costs, especially while growing fast, so a long payback period means growth needs cash reserves to fund it, while a short one means growth can largely pay for itself, which matters a lot for a self funded small business. Give me the payback calculation.
description: Calculate how many months it takes to earn back a customer's acquisition cost.
useCase: Use this before scaling up marketing. A business can be profitable per customer on paper yet run short of cash if earning back acquisition costs takes months, so a long payback means growth needs cash reserves, while a short one lets growth largely pay for itself.

title: Calculate Customer Retention
promptText: Help me calculate customer retention for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. How customers buy is [ONE OFF, REPEAT, SUBSCRIPTION, CONTRACT], the customers I had at the start of a period are [START COUNT], how many of those were still active or bought again by the end is [RETAINED COUNT], and the period is [TIMEFRAME]. Calculate retention correctly for my model, explain what counts as active for a business like mine, and what the result means. Note that retention is easy to calculate wrongly, for example by counting new customers gained during the period as retained, and the definition of an active customer depends on the business, since a cafe regular may visit weekly while a furniture buyer returns years later, so defining active sensibly for my business matters more than matching anyone else's formula. Give me the retention calculation.

title: Estimate Monthly Task or Operation Usage

Estimate monthly usage for each automation, flag the ones that use the most, and suggest ways to reduce usage, like adding filters early or checking less often. Note that polling triggers, loops over many items, and steps that run even when nothing needs to happen can quietly use far more tasks or operations than expected, and going over a plan limit can pause automations or add charges, so placing filters right after the trigger and reviewing usage in the first week of running is wise. Give me the usage estimate.

promptText: Help me build an inventory of every software tool my [BUSINESS TYPE] uses. The tools I can think of are [LIST TOOLS, INCLUDING FREE ONES, APPS, AND PLUGINS], what each is used for is [PURPOSES IF KNOWN], and how I pay for them is [E.G. CARD, PAYPAL, ANNUAL, MONTHLY]. Organize them into a table with purpose, owner, monthly cost, login owner, what data it holds, what it connects to, and renewal date, and flag overlaps, unused tools, and tools holding important data with no clear owner. Note that most small businesses forget a surprising number of subscriptions and free tools that quietly hold customer data, so checking card statements and email receipts finds what memory misses, and knowing what data lives where is the starting point for any integration plan. Give me the tool inventory.
description: List every tool with its cost, owner, data, and connections.
useCase: Use this before connecting or changing any tools. Most small businesses forget many subscriptions and free tools quietly holding customer data, so check card statements and email receipts, and knowing what data lives where is the starting point for any integration plan.
variables: LIST TOOLS, INCLUDING FREE ONES, APPS, AND PLUGINS

title: Quickly Check Whether Two Tools Connect
promptText: Tell me quickly how [TOOL ONE] and [TOOL TWO] can connect. What I want to happen between them is [GOAL]. List the options, like a native integration, Zapier or Make, an API, or export and import, in order from simplest to hardest, one line each, and say which to try first, no explanation. Give me the options.
description: List the ways two tools can connect, simplest first.
useCase: Use this when you wonder whether two apps can talk to each other. A quick list of options points you to the simplest route, but confirm on each tool's current integrations page, since integrations are added, changed, and retired often.

title: Map How Data Moves Between Your Tools
promptText: Help me map how data moves between the tools in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tools are [TOOLS], the key data is [E.G. CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, PRODUCTS, INVOICES, LEADS, TASKS], and how data moves now is [E.G. NATIVE SYNC, ZAPIER, COPY AND PASTE, EXPORTS, NOT AT ALL]. Create a map showing where each type of data is created, where it is copied, how it moves, which direction, and where it is manually retyped, and flag places where the same data could disagree. Note that problems usually come from the same customer or order being edited in two places that do not fully sync, so knowing which tool is the master for each kind of data matters more than connecting everything, and every manual copy step is both a time cost and a source of errors. Give me the data flow map.
description: Map where each type of data is created, copied, and retyped.
useCase: Use this when data gets out of sync between tools. Problems come from the same customer or order being edited in two places that do not fully sync, so knowing which tool is the master for each kind of data matters more than connecting everything, and every manual copy is a time and error cost.
variables: E.G. CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, PRODUCTS, INVOICES, LEADS, TASKS
E.G. NATIVE SYNC, ZAPIER, COPY AND PASTE, EXPORTS, NOT AT ALL

title: Choose a Source of Truth for Each Kind of Data
promptText: Help me decide which tool should be the single source of truth for each kind of data in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The data types are [E.G. CUSTOMER CONTACTS, PRODUCT INFO AND PRICES, STOCK LEVELS, ORDERS, INVOICES AND PAYMENTS, PROJECT STATUS], the tools that currently hold each are [TOOLS PER DATA TYPE], and the problems we have are [E.G. CONFLICTING PRICES, OUTDATED CONTACTS, STOCK MISMATCHES]. Recommend one master tool per data type, which tools should only read from it, and rules for where changes must be made. Note that when data can be edited in several tools, they drift apart and nobody knows which version is right, so a rule like prices are only changed in the store and flow out from there prevents most conflicts, but the rule only works if everyone follows it, so it should be written down and the other tools set to read only where possible. Give me the source of truth plan.
description: Pick one master tool per data type and set where edits happen.
useCase: Use this when tools disagree about prices, contacts, or stock. Data editable in several tools drifts apart, so a rule like prices are only changed in the store prevents most conflicts, but only if everyone follows it, so write it down and set other tools to read only where possible.
variables: E.G. CUSTOMER CONTACTS, PRODUCT INFO AND PRICES, STOCK LEVELS, ORDERS, INVOICES AND PAYMENTS, PROJECT STATUS
E.G. CONFLICTING PRICES, OUTDATED CONTACTS, STOCK MISMATCHES

title: Check a New Tool Fits Your Existing Stack
promptText: Help me check whether a new tool will fit with the tools my [BUSINESS TYPE] already uses. The new tool is [TOOL NAME AND WHAT I WANT IT FOR], my current stack is [EXISTING TOOLS], the data it must exchange is [DATA AND DIRECTION], and my budget is [BUDGET]. Give me a checklist of integration questions to answer before buying, covering native integrations, Zapier or Make support, API access, data export, plan limits, pricing for the features I need, and availability in my country, plus questions to ask the vendor. Note that tools often advertise integrations that turn out to be one way, limited to higher plans, or missing the specific fields I need, so testing the exact data I care about during a free trial matters more than reading the feature list, and being able to export all my data easily is my protection if the tool does not work out. Give me the fit checklist.
description: Check integrations, exports, and plan limits before buying a new tool.
useCase: Use this before buying any new software. Advertised integrations often turn out one way, limited to higher plans, or missing needed fields, so test your exact data during a free trial, and make sure you can export all your data in case the tool does not work out.
variables: TOOL NAME AND WHAT I WANT IT FOR

title: Choose Native Integration or a Connector Tool
promptText: Help me choose how to connect [TOOL ONE] and [TOOL TWO] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. What needs to flow between them is [DATA, DIRECTION, AND HOW OFTEN], the native integration offers [WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT IT, OR UNKNOWN], and my other options are [E.G. ZAPIER, MAKE, A PLUGIN, CUSTOM CODE, MANUAL EXPORT]. Compare native integration, a connector tool, a plugin, and custom code on cost, reliability, flexibility, setup effort, and who maintains it, and recommend one. Note that native integrations are usually the most reliable and cheapest to run but may sync fewer fields or only in one direction, connector tools are flexible but add monthly costs and another thing that can break, and custom code needs someone able to maintain it, so the simplest option that meets the actual need is usually best. Give me the integration recommendation.
description: Compare native, connector, plugin, and custom options for one link.
useCase: Use this when connecting two specific tools. Native integrations are usually most reliable and cheapest but may sync fewer fields or one way, connectors are flexible but add cost and another failure point, and custom code needs a maintainer, so pick the simplest option that meets the actual need.
variables: WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT IT, OR UNKNOWN
E.G. ZAPIER, MAKE, A PLUGIN, CUSTOM CODE, MANUAL EXPORT

title: Understand an API Well Enough to Plan an Integration
promptText: Help me understand a tool's API well enough to plan an integration for my [BUSINESS TYPE], without being a developer. The tool is [TOOL NAME], here is what its API documentation says: [PASTE KEY PARTS OF THE DOCUMENTATION OR DESCRIBE IT], and what I want to do is [GOAL]. Explain in plain language what the API can and cannot do for my goal, how authentication works, any rate limits or costs, whether webhooks are available, and whether this is a job for a connector tool or a developer, plus what to put in a brief for a freelancer. Note that API documentation often lists capabilities that require a particular plan, partner approval, or developer accounts that are not available in every country, and API keys work like passwords that give full access, so they should never be shared in chat messages or stored in plain documents. Give me the API explanation.
description: Read an API in plain language and decide who should build the link.
useCase: Use this when a tool's API is the only way to connect it. Documented capabilities may require a specific plan, partner approval, or developer accounts unavailable in some countries, and API keys work like passwords with full access, so never share them in chat or plain documents.
variables: PASTE KEY PARTS OF THE DOCUMENTATION OR DESCRIBE IT

title: Write a Brief for a Developer to Build an Integration
promptText: Help me write a clear brief to hire a developer to build an integration for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tools to connect are [TOOLS], what should happen is [TRIGGER, DATA, DIRECTION, AND TIMING], the volume is [E.G. RECORDS PER DAY], what should happen when something fails is [ERROR HANDLING EXPECTATIONS], and my budget and timeline are [BUDGET AND DEADLINE]. Write a brief covering the goal, exact data fields, examples, edge cases, security requirements, who owns the code and hosting, documentation and handover, and how I will test it before paying the final amount. Note that vague briefs lead to integrations that work in a demo but fail on real data, so including real examples and edge cases matters, and I should own the code, accounts, and hosting in my name with documentation, since an integration only one freelancer understands becomes a problem when they move on. Give me the developer brief.
description: Brief a developer with real examples, edge cases, and ownership terms.
useCase: Use this before hiring someone to build an integration. Vague briefs produce integrations that work in a demo but fail on real data, so include real examples and edge cases, and make sure you own the code, accounts, and hosting with documentation, since an integration only one freelancer understands becomes a problem.

title: Plan Sync Direction and Conflict Rules
promptText: Help me plan how two tools should sync data for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tools are [TOOL ONE AND TOOL TWO], the data is [E.G. CONTACTS, PRODUCTS, ORDERS, CALENDAR EVENTS], the fields involved are [FIELDS], and who edits the data in each tool is [WHO EDITS WHERE]. Decide whether the sync should be one way or two way, which tool wins when both change the same record, how deletions are handled, and how often it should sync. Note that two way sync sounds ideal but causes the most problems, like overwrites, loops where each tool keeps updating the other, and deleted records reappearing or disappearing everywhere, so one way sync from a clear master is safer whenever possible, and deletions in particular should not sync automatically until the setup is proven. Give me the sync rules.
description: Set one or two way sync, conflict winners, and deletion rules.
useCase: Use this before syncing data between two tools. Two way sync causes the most problems, like overwrites, update loops, and deleted records reappearing or vanishing everywhere, so one way sync from a clear master is safer, and deletions should not sync automatically until the setup is proven.
variables: E.G. CONTACTS, PRODUCTS, ORDERS, CALENDAR EVENTS

title: Plan a Move From One Tool to Another
promptText: Help me plan moving my [BUSINESS TYPE] from [OLD TOOL] to [NEW TOOL]. The data to move is [E.G. CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, HISTORY, FILES, TEMPLATES, AUTOMATIONS], the integrations connected to the old tool are [CONNECTIONS], who uses it is [PEOPLE], and the deadline or renewal date is [DATE]. Give me a step by step migration plan covering what to export, cleaning data before import, mapping fields, rebuilding integrations and automations, a test with a small batch, a switch over date, and when to cancel the old tool. Note that migrations usually take longer than expected because automations, links, and templates connected to the old tool are easy to forget, history and attachments sometimes do not transfer at all, and cancelling the old tool too early can lose data that turns out to be needed, so keeping read access for a month or two after switching is a sensible safety margin. Give me the migration plan.
description: Move to a new tool without losing data, links, or automations.
useCase: Use this when switching tools. Migrations take longer than expected because connected automations, links, and templates are easy to forget, history and attachments sometimes do not transfer, and cancelling too early can lose needed data, so keep read access for a month or two after switching.
variables: E.G. CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, HISTORY, FILES, TEMPLATES, AUTOMATIONS

title: Clean Data Before Connecting or Importing It
promptText: Help me clean data before I connect or import it into a new tool for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The data is [E.G. CUSTOMER LIST, PRODUCT CATALOG, CONTACTS], here are its columns and a few sample rows: [PASTE SAMPLE], and the problems I know about are [E.G. DUPLICATES, MIXED DATE FORMATS, PHONE NUMBERS WITHOUT COUNTRY CODES, NAMES IN DIFFERENT SCRIPTS, EMPTY FIELDS]. Give me a cleanup checklist and specific spreadsheet steps or formulas for each problem, plus rules to keep the data clean going forward. Note that importing messy data spreads the mess into every connected tool, where it is harder to fix, so cleaning first saves time, and names and addresses in different scripts, like Khmer and English versions of the same customer, often create hidden duplicates that simple matching will not catch, so a manual review of likely matches is worth doing. Give me the cleanup plan.
description: Fix duplicates, formats, and mixed scripts before importing data.
useCase: Use this before any import or new integration. Messy data spreads into every connected tool where it is harder to fix, and names in different scripts, like Khmer and English versions of one customer, create hidden duplicates simple matching misses, so manually review likely matches.
variables: E.G. CUSTOMER LIST, PRODUCT CATALOG, CONTACTS
E.G. DUPLICATES, MIXED DATE FORMATS, PHONE NUMBERS WITHOUT COUNTRY CODES, NAMES IN DIFFERENT SCRIPTS, EMPTY FIELDS

title: Plan Payment Integrations for Your Market
promptText: Help me plan how payments connect to the rest of my tools at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Where I am registered is [COUNTRY], where my customers are is [CUSTOMER COUNTRIES], the payment methods customers expect are [E.G. CARDS, LOCAL QR PAYMENTS, BANK APPS, MOBILE WALLETS, PAYPAL, CASH ON DELIVERY], and the tools payments must reach are [E.G. STORE, INVOICING, ACCOUNTING, CRM]. Compare payment providers available to businesses in my country, how each integrates with my tools, fees, payout times, and currencies, and suggest how to record payments that do not integrate automatically. Note that popular global providers are not available to businesses registered in every country, local QR and bank app payments are often what customers prefer but may have limited integrations, so some payments will need a manual or semi automated recording step, and provider availability and fees change, so current terms should be confirmed directly. Give me the payment integration plan.
description: Match payment providers available in your country to your tools.
useCase: Use this when setting up or changing how you get paid. Global providers are not available to businesses in every country, and local QR or bank app payments customers prefer may have limited integrations, so plan a recording step for those, and confirm current availability and fees directly.
variables: E.G. CARDS, LOCAL QR PAYMENTS, BANK APPS, MOBILE WALLETS, PAYPAL, CASH ON DELIVERY

title: Connect Sales Tools to Your Accounting
promptText: Help me plan how my sales tools connect to my accounting for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Where sales happen is [E.G. STORE, MARKETPLACES, INVOICES, POINT OF SALE, CHAT ORDERS], my accounting tool is [E.G. XERO, QUICKBOOKS, WAVE, A SPREADSHEET, AN ACCOUNTANT], the currencies involved are [CURRENCIES], and my month end process now is [CURRENT PROCESS]. Suggest whether to sync each order, daily summaries, or payouts, how to handle fees, refunds, and currency conversion, and a monthly reconciliation routine. Note that syncing every order can flood the books and duplicate entries, while syncing only payouts hides fees and refunds, so many small businesses use daily or payout level summaries with fees recorded separately, and mixed currencies need a consistent exchange rate rule, so I should agree the approach with my accountant before automating. Give me the accounting integration plan.
description: Decide how sales, fees, refunds, and currencies flow into the books.
useCase: Use this before connecting your store or marketplaces to accounting. Syncing every order can flood the books and duplicate entries, while syncing only payouts hides fees and refunds, mixed currencies need a consistent rate rule, so agree the approach with your accountant first.
variables: E.G. STORE, MARKETPLACES, INVOICES, POINT OF SALE, CHAT ORDERS
E.G. XERO, QUICKBOOKS, WAVE, A SPREADSHEET, AN ACCOUNTANT

title: Manage Logins, Permissions, and Offboarding Across Tools
promptText: Help me manage who has access to which tools at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tools are [TOOLS], the people with access are [TEAM, FREELANCERS, AGENCIES, FAMILY], how logins are shared now is [E.G. SHARED PASSWORDS, INDIVIDUAL ACCOUNTS, A PASSWORD MANAGER], and the integrations that run on someone's personal login are [IF KNOWN]. Create an access table, recommend changes like individual accounts, a password manager, two factor login, and least access permissions, and write an offboarding checklist for when someone leaves. Note that shared passwords make it impossible to remove one person's access cleanly, and integrations connected through a departing person's account can stop working the day their access is removed, so connections should run on business owned accounts, and the offboarding checklist should include changing shared passwords and checking which automations depend on that person. Give me the access plan.
description: Map who can access what and offboard people without breaking things.
useCase: Use this once more than one person touches your tools. Shared passwords make removing one person's access impossible, and integrations on a departing person's account can break the day they leave, so run connections on business owned accounts and check automation dependencies when offboarding.
variables: E.G. SHARED PASSWORDS, INDIVIDUAL ACCOUNTS, A PASSWORD MANAGER

title: Test a New Integration and Plan a Rollback
promptText: Help me test a new integration and prepare a rollback plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The integration connects [TOOLS] to do [WHAT IT DOES], the data affected is [DATA], and what would break if it went wrong is [IMPACT]. Give me a test plan with test records, edge cases, checks on both sides, a backup step before going live, a gradual rollout, signs that something is wrong, and exactly how to switch it off and restore data if needed. Note that integrations that write or overwrite data can damage many records quickly, so taking a backup or export before turning it on, starting with a small subset, and knowing in advance how to undo it turns a potential disaster into a minor fix. Give me the test and rollback plan.
description: Test with a small subset, back up first, and know how to undo it.
useCase: Use this before turning on any integration that writes data. Integrations that write or overwrite data can damage many records quickly, so back up first, start with a small subset, and know in advance how to undo it, which turns a potential disaster into a minor fix.

title: Cut Tool Costs by Consolidating Your Stack
promptText: Help me reduce software costs by consolidating tools at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My tools with costs and purposes are [PASTE YOUR TOOL INVENTORY], how much I actually use each is [USAGE NOTES], and my monthly software budget goal is [TARGET]. Identify overlapping tools, tools that could be replaced by features in ones I already pay for, cheaper plans that would still cover my needs, and annual versus monthly savings, then estimate total savings and the effort to switch. Note that consolidating saves money and reduces integrations to maintain, but switching tools costs time and can break workflows, so small savings may not be worth a big migration, and annual plans save money only if I am sure I will keep the tool for the full year. Give me the consolidation plan.
description: Find overlapping tools and cheaper plans worth switching to.
useCase: Use this when software bills creep up. Consolidating saves money and reduces integrations to maintain, but switching costs time and can break workflows, so small savings may not justify a big migration, and annual plans only save money if you will keep the tool all year.

title: Plan Your Exit From Any Tool Before You Need It
promptText: Help me plan how I would leave each important tool if I needed to for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The tools my business depends on are [CRITICAL TOOLS], what data each holds is [DATA], and the risks I worry about are [E.G. PRICE INCREASES, SHUTDOWN, ACCOUNT SUSPENSION, LOSING ACCESS FROM MY COUNTRY]. For each tool, describe how to export the data, what format it comes in, what would not transfer, a likely replacement, and a regular export routine to keep a current copy. Note that tools can raise prices, change terms, shut down, or restrict access by country with little warning, and some make exporting difficult or incomplete on purpose, so knowing the exit route in advance and keeping regular exports of essential data reduces the risk of being trapped. Give me the exit plan.
description: Know how to export and replace every tool your business depends on.
useCase: Use this for tools your business cannot run without. Tools can raise prices, change terms, shut down, or restrict access by country with little warning, and some make exports hard on purpose, so know each exit route in advance and keep regular exports of essential data.
variables: E.G. PRICE INCREASES, SHUTDOWN, ACCOUNT SUSPENSION, LOSING ACCESS FROM MY COUNTRY

title: Build a Tool Integration Roadmap
promptText: Help me build a step by step integration roadmap for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current tools and data flows are [SUMMARY OR PASTE YOUR MAP], the biggest manual work and errors are [PAIN POINTS], my budget is [BUDGET], and my time or help available is [CAPACITY]. Prioritize integrations by time saved, error reduction, cost, and effort, group them into phases over the next few months, and note dependencies, like choosing a source of truth before syncing. Note that trying to connect everything at once creates a fragile web that is hard to fix when something breaks, so a few well tested integrations that remove the most manual work beat many half working ones, and each phase should be stable before starting the next. Give me the integration roadmap.
description: Phase integrations by impact and effort, one stable step at a time.
useCase: Use this to plan integrations over the coming months. Connecting everything at once creates a fragile web that is hard to fix, so a few well tested integrations removing the most manual work beat many half working ones, and each phase should be stable before the next.

title: Turn a Repeating Process Into a Reusable Template
promptText: Help me turn a process I repeat into a reusable template for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The process is [PROCESS NAME], how often it happens is [FREQUENCY], here is how I did it last time: [DESCRIBE THE STEPS], and the tool where I want the template is [E.G. NOTION, TRELLO, ASANA, CLICKUP, GOOGLE DOCS, A PAPER CHECKLIST]. Create a template with a checklist of steps in order, the owner and rough time for each, inputs needed before starting, a definition of done, and a short notes section to record what changed this time. Note that a recurring template only saves time if it is short enough to actually use, so it should list the steps that are easy to forget rather than explaining every obvious action, and updating it right after each run, while problems are fresh, is what keeps it accurate. Give me the recurring template.
description: Convert a repeated process into a short checklist template you will use.
useCase: Use this for anything you do on a regular schedule. A template only saves time if short enough to use, so list the steps that are easy to forget rather than every obvious action, and update it right after each run, while problems are fresh, to keep it accurate.
variables: E.G. NOTION, TRELLO, ASANA, CLICKUP, GOOGLE DOCS, A PAPER CHECKLIST

title: Get a Quick Recurring Checklist
promptText: Give me a quick recurring checklist. The task is [RECURRING TASK], I do it every [FREQUENCY], and my business is [BUSINESS TYPE]. List ten or fewer steps in order as short checkbox items, no explanation. Give me the checklist.
description: Get a short checkbox list for any recurring task, fast.
useCase: Use this when you need a checklist right now. A short generic list gets you started, but adjust it after the first real run, since your own business will have steps a generic checklist misses.

title: Build a Calendar of All Recurring Business Tasks
promptText: Help me build one calendar of every recurring task in my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The recurring work I know of is [LIST DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, QUARTERLY, AND YEARLY TASKS], the people involved are [WHO DOES WHAT], and busy periods I should avoid are [E.G. HOLIDAYS, PEAK SEASONS, PERSONAL COMMITMENTS]. Organize them by frequency with suggested days, estimated time, and owner, spread the load so no single week is overloaded, and flag anything that is easy to forget. Note that recurring tasks tend to pile up at month end and year end, which creates stressful crunch periods, so spreading them across the month helps, and seeing everything in one place often reveals tasks that are no longer needed or could be done less often. Give me the cadence calendar.
description: Lay out every daily to yearly task and spread the load evenly.
useCase: Use this to see all your recurring work in one place. Tasks pile up at month and year end, creating crunch periods, so spreading them across the month helps, and seeing everything together often reveals tasks no longer needed or that could be done less often.
variables: LIST DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, QUARTERLY, AND YEARLY TASKS
E.G. HOLIDAYS, PEAK SEASONS, PERSONAL COMMITMENTS

title: Set Up Recurring Templates in Your Task Tool
promptText: Help me set up recurring process templates in [TASK TOOL, E.G. ASANA, TRELLO, CLICKUP, NOTION, TODOIST, MICROSOFT PLANNER, GOOGLE TASKS] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The recurring processes are [PROCESSES AND FREQUENCIES], each has these steps: [STEPS OR PASTE TEMPLATES], and who should be assigned is [OWNERS]. Explain how to create the template, make it repeat automatically, set due dates relative to the start, assign owners, and get reminders, using my tool's features. Note that task tools handle recurrence differently, some repeat a single task while others can copy a whole checklist or project, and some features are only on paid plans, so the setup may need a workaround, and recurring tasks that keep appearing but never get done are a sign the frequency or the process itself needs rethinking. Give me the task tool setup.
description: Make process templates repeat automatically with owners and due dates.
useCase: Use this to stop recreating the same checklists. Task tools handle recurrence differently, some repeat single tasks while others copy whole checklists, and some features need paid plans, while recurring tasks that keep appearing undone signal the frequency or process needs rethinking.
variables: TASK TOOL, E.G. ASANA, TRELLO, CLICKUP, NOTION, TODOIST, MICROSOFT PLANNER, GOOGLE TASKS

title: Create Daily Opening and Closing Checklists
promptText: Help me create daily start of day and end of day checklists for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The business runs [E.G. ONLINE ONLY, A SHOP, A CAFE, A HOME STUDIO, A SERVICE BUSINESS], what must happen every day is [DAILY ESSENTIALS, E.G. CHECK ORDERS, REPLY TO MESSAGES, COUNT CASH, BACK UP FILES, LOCK UP], and who opens and closes is [PEOPLE]. Write two short checklists, one to start the day and one to end it, ordered so the most important items come first. Note that daily checklists work best when they take a few minutes and focus on things that cause real trouble if missed, like unanswered orders, cash differences, or unlocked doors, and a checklist that grows too long gets skipped, so trimming it to the essentials keeps people actually using it. Give me the daily checklists.
description: Write short start and end of day checklists of the essentials.
useCase: Use this for anything that must happen every day. Daily checklists work best when they take minutes and focus on things causing real trouble if missed, like unanswered orders or cash differences, and a checklist that grows too long gets skipped, so keep it to essentials.
variables: E.G. ONLINE ONLY, A SHOP, A CAFE, A HOME STUDIO, A SERVICE BUSINESS
DAILY ESSENTIALS, E.G. CHECK ORDERS, REPLY TO MESSAGES, COUNT CASH, BACK UP FILES, LOCK UP

title: Create a Weekly Business Operations Review
promptText: Help me create a weekly operations review template for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The numbers I can check weekly are [E.G. SALES, ORDERS, LEADS, CASH IN BANK, OVERDUE INVOICES, OPEN SUPPORT TICKETS], the areas I want to review are [E.G. SALES, DELIVERY, MARKETING, FINANCE, ADMIN], and how long I can spend is [TIME]. Create a short review agenda with the key numbers, questions to ask, decisions to make, and a section for next week's top priorities. Note that a weekly review is useful only if it leads to decisions, so a few key numbers and questions like what is stuck and what needs attention beat a long report nobody acts on, and it is different from personal weekly planning, since it looks at how the business is running rather than my own task list. Give me the weekly operations review.
description: Review key business numbers weekly and turn them into decisions.
useCase: Use this to check how the business is running each week. A review only helps if it leads to decisions, so a few key numbers and questions like what is stuck beat a long report nobody acts on, and it looks at the business rather than your personal task list.
variables: E.G. SALES, ORDERS, LEADS, CASH IN BANK, OVERDUE INVOICES, OPEN SUPPORT TICKETS
E.G. SALES, DELIVERY, MARKETING, FINANCE, ADMIN

title: Create a Monthly Bookkeeping Close Routine
promptText: Help me create a monthly bookkeeping close routine for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My accounting setup is [E.G. XERO, QUICKBOOKS, WAVE, A SPREADSHEET, AN ACCOUNTANT DOES IT], my income comes through [E.G. BANK TRANSFERS, CARDS, MARKETPLACES, CASH, PAYMENT APPS], the currencies I deal with are [CURRENCIES], and what my accountant needs from me is [IF KNOWN]. Write a step by step checklist for the first days of each month, covering collecting receipts, matching bank transactions, chasing unpaid invoices, recording cash, checking marketplace payouts against sales, and sending what the accountant needs. Note that doing this monthly takes far less time than sorting a whole year at tax time, cash and mixed currency transactions are where records most often go wrong, so they need a consistent rule, and tax deadlines and record keeping rules depend on my country, so my accountant should confirm the routine fits local requirements. Give me the monthly close routine.
description: Close the books monthly with receipts, matching, cash, and payouts.
useCase: Use this to keep your books tidy month by month. It takes far less time than sorting a whole year at tax time, cash and mixed currency transactions are where records most often go wrong, so use a consistent rule, and confirm with your accountant that the routine fits local requirements.
variables: E.G. XERO, QUICKBOOKS, WAVE, A SPREADSHEET, AN ACCOUNTANT DOES IT
E.G. BANK TRANSFERS, CARDS, MARKETPLACES, CASH, PAYMENT APPS

title: Create a Monthly Invoicing and Collection Run
promptText: Help me create a recurring invoicing run for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. How I bill clients is [E.G. MONTHLY RETAINERS, HOURLY, MILESTONES, SUBSCRIPTIONS], my invoicing tool is [TOOL], my payment terms are [TERMS], and the payment methods clients use are [METHODS, INCLUDING CROSS BORDER IF ANY]. title: Replace Rereading With Active Recall
promptText: Help me change how I study [SUBJECT] from rereading to active recall. How I study now is [CURRENT METHOD, E.G. REREADING NOTES, HIGHLIGHTING, WATCHING LECTURES AGAIN], the material is [NOTES, TEXTBOOK, LECTURES], and the time per session is [MINUTES]. description: Schedule practice tests under real conditions and review mistakes by type.

title: Make a Catch Up Plan When You Have Fallen Behind

title: Build Rest Into a Demanding Study Plan
promptText: Help me adjust my study plan so it is sustainable and I do not burn out. My current plan is [PASTE OR DESCRIBE IT], how I am feeling is [E.G. TIRED, STRESSED, LOSING MOTIVATION, FINE BUT WORRIED], my sleep and rest look like [SLEEP AND BREAKS], and what I need to achieve is [GOAL AND DEADLINE]. Suggest changes like scheduled breaks, a rest day, realistic daily targets, and signs that I need to ease off, while still meeting my goal. Note that studying longer while exhausted produces less learning than shorter focused sessions after rest, since sleep is when much of memory forms, so cutting sleep to study usually backfires, and persistent exhaustion, low mood, or anxiety that does not lift with rest deserves attention and, if it continues, a conversation with a doctor or counselor. Give me the sustainable study plan.
description: Add breaks, sleep, and realistic targets so studying stays sustainable.

title: Track Study Progress and Adjust the Plan
promptText: Help me track my study progress and adjust my plan. My goal is [GOAL AND DEADLINE], my plan is [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE PLAN], what I have done so far is [SESSIONS COMPLETED, TOPICS COVERED, PRACTICE SCORES], and where I am struggling is [PROBLEMS]. Create a simple tracker I can update weekly, review my current progress against the plan, and suggest adjustments for the next two weeks. Note that tracking hours studied can be misleading, since time spent is not the same as progress, so practice scores and topics I can explain from memory are better signs, and a weekly check lets me adjust early instead of discovering in the last week that I am far behind. Give me the tracker and adjustments.
description: Track real progress weekly and adjust before it is too late.
useCase: Use this weekly while preparing for any goal. Hours studied can mislead, since time spent is not progress, so practice scores and topics you can explain from memory are better signs, and a weekly check lets you adjust early rather than discover in the last week that you are far behind.
variables: SESSIONS COMPLETED, TOPICS COVERED, PRACTICE SCORES
